Comment 10 (source ID 433462218) | Participant 3 | created 2018-10-26T16:15:04Z | updated 2018-10-26T16:15:04Z
Source: https://github.com/opensupports/opensupports/issues/363#issuecomment-433462218
I was able to recover the password while it was not even verified, it seems it's working correctly.
@Mte90 Please make sure the user has its account verified. It should show a warning on its profile if it's not.
![screenshot](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/6447076/47578320-79793400-d91f-11e8-809c-7faec0923626.png)
You can manually verify an user on the database by changing the `verification_token` row on `ticket` table to `NULL`.
If the email is not verified, the user will not be able to log in and a message `Email is not verified` will appear. I'm thinking we should maybe add a "resend verification email" button like other websites do, because currently it's only sent once.

Even if we're talking about users without expertise. Email verification it's still necessary because we need to very the authenticity of the email, of course this won't be always needed when we implement #207.

@kedarchinchvalkar There are two relatively small steps:

1. Register your DB context for DI using the overload provided for specifying the abstract `DbConnection`, constructing instead a `Microsoft.Data.SqlClient.SqlConnection` (probably optional).
2. Replace the `ISqlServerConnection` service with one targeting `Microsoft.Data.SqlClient` for both `SqlConnection` and `SqlConnectionStringBuilder`.

I lifted the code from GitHub for the last Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.SqlServer 2.x release for `SqlServerConnection` and updated it with proper targets as follows:

```
using Microsoft.Data.SqlClient;
using Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore;
using Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.SqlServer.Storage.Internal;
using Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.Storage;
using System.Data.Common;

namespace My.Storage
{
    /// <summary>
    ///     This API supports the Entity Framework Core infrastructure.
    /// </summary>
    public class SqlServerConnection : RelationalConnection, ISqlServerConnection
    {
        private bool? _multipleActiveResultSetsEnabled;

        // Compensate for slow SQL Server database creation
        private const int DefaultMasterConnectionCommandTimeout = 60;

        /// <summary>
        ///     This API supports the Entity Framework Core infrastructure and is not intended to be used
        ///     directly from your code. This API may change or be removed in future releases.
        /// </summary>
        public SqlServerConnection(RelationalConnectionDependencies dependencies)
            : base(dependencies)
        {
        }

        /// <summary>
        ///     This API supports the Entity Framework Core infrastructure and is not intended to be used
        ///     directly from your code. This API may change or be removed in future releases.
        /// </summary>
        protected override DbConnection CreateDbConnection() => new SqlConnection(ConnectionString);

        /// <summary>
        ///     This API supports the Entity Framework Core infrastructure and is not intended to be used
        ///     directly from your code. This API may change or be removed in future releases.
        /// </summary>
        public virtual ISqlServerConnection CreateMasterConnection()
        {
            var connectionStringBuilder = new SqlConnectionStringBuilder(ConnectionString)
            {
                InitialCatalog = "master"
            };
            connectionStringBuilder.Remove("AttachDBFilename");

            var contextOptions = new DbContextOptionsBuilder()
                .UseSqlServer(
                    connectionStringBuilder.ConnectionString,
                    b => b.CommandTimeout(CommandTimeout ?? DefaultMasterConnectionCommandTimeout))
                .Options;

            return new SqlServerConnection(Dependencies.With(contextOptions));
        }

        /// <summary>
        ///     This API supports the Entity Framework Core infrastructure and is not intended to be used
        ///     directly from your code. This API may change or be removed in future releases.
        /// </summary>
        public override bool IsMultipleActiveResultSetsEnabled
            => (bool)(_multipleActiveResultSetsEnabled
                      ?? (_multipleActiveResultSetsEnabled
                          = new SqlConnectionStringBuilder(ConnectionString).MultipleActiveResultSets));

        /// <summary>
        ///     Indicates whether the store connection supports ambient transactions
        /// </summary>
        protected override bool SupportsAmbientTransactions => true;
    }
}
```

Then I updated my service registration for AddDbContext as follows, where I construct a `Microsoft.Data.SqlClient.SqlConnection` and `SqlServerConnection` is `using SqlServerConnection = My.Storage.SqlServerConnection;`:
```
public void ConfigureServices(IServiceCollection services)
{
    services
        .AddDbContext<MyContext>(opts =>
            opts
                .UseSqlServer(new SqlConnection(Configuration.GetConnectionString("DefaultConnection")))
                .ReplaceService<ISqlServerConnection, SqlServerConnection>()) // TODO: Remove after transition to Core 3
}
```

Works like a charm. I even think the step of constructing the DbConnection may be unnecessary and you can use the raw string value for UseSqlServer(), but haven't tried it. Feel free to experiment.

<!--
If you've never submitted an issue to the SORMAS repository before or this is your first time using this template, please read the Contributing guidelines (https://github.com/hzi-braunschweig/SORMAS-Project/blob/development/docs/CONTRIBUTING.md) for an explanation of the information we need you to provide. You don't have to remove this comment or any other comment from this issue as they will automatically be hidden.
-->
### Problem Description
<!-- Mandatory -->
Retrieving data via ReST during the mobile app synchronisation process can take a lot of time (with as few as 1000 cases taking several minutes to synchronize). We've also received reports (and witnessed) the web app directories taking more than a few seconds to load on systems with a lot of data (e.g. more than 500,000 entries in a directory).

### Proposed Solution
<!-- Mandatory -->
In preparation of potential refactorings and code improvements, analyse the performance of the getAllAfter and getIndexList methods of the following entities:

* Case
* Contact
* Sample
* Person

This should include all EJBs called in the process, and also especially include the pseudonymisation logic because this was already identified as a huge bottleneck at least for the synchronisation process.

Step 1: Activate `PerformanceLoggingInterceptor` on TRACE level to analyse call hierarchy and where time is spent. Document execution times.
Step 2: Dive deeper into hotspot method to find costly transformations (probably in `toDto`/`pseudonymize` methods).

### Possible Alternatives
<!-- Optional -->

### Additional Information
<!-- Optional -->
A potential follow-up issue to improve the pseudonymisation process could include the following action points:
- Skip pseudonymisation completely for entites that we know will not be pseudonymised based on the user's user rights (e.g. an entity inside the user's jurisdiction does not need to be checked for pseudonymisation if the user has both the SEE_PERSONAL_DATA_IN_JURISDICTION and SEE_SENSITIVE_DATA_IN_JURISDICTION user rights)
- Create a cache per entity of all fields that need to be considered during pseudonymisation in order to reduce the usage of reflection

Since the toDto logic also takes some time, another possible change could be to directly select into DTOs, even though that would potentially introduce a significantly increased maintenance effort.

As database where we want to reproduce  the perf. issues and measure the improvements we are using the pseudonymized data from France.

### Deliverables
Confirm that pseudonymization is one cause 
Explore what else causes performance issues
Document KPI (Key performance indicators) and preconditions to be able to measure the improvement
Create follow-up tickets that are obvious

==>
- pseudonymization can be ruled out as a relevant impact on performance
- long runtimes are mainly caused by long running SQL queries with massive joins
- follow-up issues: #8938 for `getIndexList` methods, #8946 for `getAll` methods in the REST API

Comment 2 (source ID 599540514) | Participant 3 | created 2020-03-16T13:37:24Z | updated 2020-03-16T13:37:24Z
Source: https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/issues/53578#issuecomment-599540514
@fbaligand, a few comments on work we've done or considered in ES that's related to your suggestion for a fingerprint ingest processor--

You mention both content fingerprinting and content anonymization (esp. in a GDPR context) as use cases for such a processor. While both scenarios commonly perform some type of hashing on the document content, there are important differences between the two use cases.

For content fingerprinting, we want to produce a single, stable token useful either for comparison or as a unique identifier that is based on the document content. This is commonly done by taking the SHA-256 or similar hash across all the relevant fields of the document (and this is what the Logstash `fingerprint` filter does). Notably, we want to make it easy to go from document content to the fingerprint token.

With content anonymization, we also want to produce from one or more sensitive fields within the document stable token(s) useful for comparison or aggregation. The big difference is that we want it to be very hard to derive the original content from the token, especially in the context of GDPR or HIPAA where there is an obligation to safeguard personally identifying or other sensitive information. In such conditions, a simple hash such as SHA-256 could be susceptible to a brute force attack, especially when the set of possible input values is relatively small or when some of the input values are known such as patient names for a particular doctor.

That susceptibility to brute force attacks can be eliminated by using a hash with a secret key. We did some work on such a processor in https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/pull/31087 but it was ultimately pulled before release because there was no mechanism to ensure that the secret key was consistent across all ingest nodes. Without a guarantee of key consistency across nodes, different hashes for the same input data could be produced on different ingest nodes which would make the anonymized tokens useless for comparison or aggregation. We have some ideas about how to ensure consistency of secret keys across ingest nodes, but it is not a trivially easy problem to solve in the context of a distributed system such as ES.


Comment 3 (source ID 599692655) | Participant 1 | created 2020-03-16T18:24:48Z | updated 2020-03-16T18:25:49Z
Source: https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/issues/53578#issuecomment-599692655
First, thank you very much for your detailed answer.

I understand that it is not easy to provide a hash mechanism strong enough for anonymization use case.
And I understand that SHA2 is not really strong enough for anonymization use case.

That said, on a more global point of view, I think that it is very important to have a homogeneous filter/process offer between Logstash and Ingest Pipelines.

I mean that I would find very sad to have fingerprint filter in Logstash and fingerprint processor in ingest pipeline with different options and behavior.

That's why a first step would be to provide fingerprint processor with same features and behavior than Logstash.

And later, maybe a nice idea to have a strong anonymization hash will emerge :)

Comment 4 (source ID 647467717) | Participant 4 | created 2020-06-22T11:50:56Z | updated 2021-02-09T12:17:37Z
Source: https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/issues/53578#issuecomment-647467717
From my understanding, we are talking about pseudonymization in the GDPR context here because even with the more suitable version of fingerprinting with a secret key (HMAC), users could still be re-identified with the knowledge of the secret key. Maybe add a way to rotate this key at defined intervals? This would provide strong pseudonymization properties after the rotation period. Note that this is just an idea. I have not checked if others are using such a design and what possible downsides are.


> That's why a first step would be to provide fingerprint processor with same features and behavior than Logstash.

Not sure that you would really want that as the Logstash fingerprint filter is currently non-stable/none-deterministic for nested fields. Ref: https://github.com/logstash-plugins/logstash-filter-fingerprint/pull/41

Source: https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/issues/53578#issuecomment-775872866
Note that the processor introduced in https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/pull/68415 is suitable for the use case of content fingerprinting. Despite having "fingerprint" in this issue title, the issue description describes the content anonymization use case which is different as explained in the [comment above](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/issues/53578#issuecomment-599540514). The fingerprint processor is not intended for content anonymization. The work on a processor intended for that use case is tracked in #34085.

Issue body:
Crates.io does not currently display a privacy notice, and I am concerned that crates.io may be operating in violation of data protection legislation in the EU (and elsewhere).
 
A privacy notice should be added so that people know what data is collected about them when they use the crates.io website (I see that Google Analytics is used, for example, (see #460) with no notification to users that their personal data is being processed.) and/or use cargo to fetch crates listed by the service.

Hi @aidanhs 

As I read that judgment, paras 20 and 21 are outlining the position of a lower court.

If you read further in to that judgment - at paragraph 49 and repeated again as a ruling on the question referred to it - the court states a different interpretation:

>Having regard to all the foregoing considerations, the answer to the first question is that Article 2(a) of Directive 95/46 must be interpreted as meaning that a dynamic IP address registered by an online media services provider when a person accesses a website that the provider makes accessible to the public constitutes personal data within the meaning of that provision, in relation to that provider, where the latter has the legal means which enable it to identify the data subject with additional data which the internet service provider has about that person.

The case also appears to have revolved around the fact that the IP address(es) in question were dynamic. Many people - myself included - have _static_ IP addresses which would more obviously identity us as individuals. In my case my IP address is also registered with RIPE under my name which is trivially available if one were to look up my IP address.

That judgment is also pre-GDPR (the reference to Directive 95/46/EC is to the Data Protection Directive which was repealed and replaced in May by the GDPR)

You point out the definition of personal data in the GDPR. That definition references "online identifiers" and as such should be read in the light of recital 30 of that Regulation:

>Natural persons may be associated with **online identifiers provided by their devices, applications, tools and protocols, such as internet protocol addresses**, cookie identifiers or other identifiers such as radio frequency identification tags. This may leave traces which, in particular when combined with unique identifiers and other information received by the servers, may be used to create profiles of the natural persons and identify them

(emphasis mine)

Of course, I am not a lawyer so I'll leave that final determination as to whether this situation constitutes processing of personal data to your legal counsel and to the supervisory authorities.

@aturon also mentioned that you were working on a set of language that would cover all of Rust's web properties, including the internals and users forums which are hosted on rust-lang.org (albeit on subdomains) which is why I mentioned rust-lang.org in my comment.

Comment 12 (source ID 447603789) | Participant 4 | created 2018-12-15T22:56:36Z | updated 2018-12-15T22:57:18Z
Source: https://github.com/rust-lang/crates.io/issues/955#issuecomment-447603789
> The case also appears to have revolved around the fact that the IP address(es) in question were dynamic. Many people - myself included - have static IP addresses which would more obviously identity us as individuals. In my case my IP address is also registered with RIPE under my name which is trivially available if one were to look up my IP address.

Thanks for pointing that out. I think in this case we will likely pursue something similar to https://support.google.com/analytics/answer/2763052?hl=en, which appears to be accepted best practice in the analytics world as it throws away the ability to uniquely identify a user.

(for crates.io I expect we will retain full collection of IP addresses (documented in privacy policy) under recital 49)

> (emphasis mine)

Minor comment: the language in your extract is oriented around the 'traces' being used in combination with other information received by the servers, which is not the case. However, recital 26 does apply, requiring consideration of "all means reasonably likely to be used [...] to identify the natural person directly".

> including the internals and users forums which are hosted on rust-lang.org (albeit on subdomains) which is why I mentioned rust-lang.org in my comment

Ah, understood.

@M2Ys4U It's been on the meeting agenda every week since December 12 (our meetings are open to attend every Thursday, and you can find agendas at https://github.com/rust-lang/crates-io-cargo-teams). After the 12th, we performed an audit of any PII we store, which was completed in early January. Shortly after the audit we discovered that our logs are being retained for longer than intended, and we're looking into what the original reason for that was. The person who is taking the lead on writing the final policy has also been away for the past week or so.

If you're interested in following the progress, I highly recommend attending our team meetings as an observer. Here are the results of the audit if you're interested.

PII you explicitly give us:

- Email address(es)
  - Stored indefinitely, you can edit at any time. It can be removed by emailing support (unless the account has published crates, in which case we need to keep a verified email for legal reasons)

PII you implicitly give us:

- GitHub username
- Full name as displayed in GitHub
- GitHub avatar

All GitHub related data is stored indefinitely. It can be updated in our database by modifying it in GitHub, logging out of crates.io, and logging back in.
It can be removed by emailing support (unless the account has published crates, which needs further discussion)

Stuff we log:

- IP address and user agent header
  - For most requests, this information cannot be associated with your username or any other PII

Logs are stored for 1 year.

We also intend to log additional information when a crate is uploaded, such as the username and crate name.

Issue body:
We want to implement eLabFTW at our university and need to take care of data privacy. The requested feature would be an optional additional page before the actual registration with the data privacy statement. Ideally, the following requirements are met:

* activate optional data privacy statement from system admin panel, similar to enabling account creation 
* add a field where an individual data privacy statement can be entered, e.g. with markdown or html format
* the privacy statement has to be explicitly approved, e.g. with a button press on a page before or via checking a box
* after successful registration the data privacy statement is mailed to the user and preferably, has to be confirmed again upon confirming the mail adress (i.e. double opt-in)
* add an optional additional link to the data privacy statement of the institution, a good position would be in the footer of the page where the links for admin pages are - currently, this can be achieved by exchanging the documentation link from the admin panel 

Thanks

However, a single opt-in upon registration i.e. "If you continue with the registration you agree to the above terms" with a confirmation e.g. via button-press or checking a box is sufficient. In any case, the confirmation has to be saved with the data privacy statement, ideally in a printable form to be archived locally.
But I can ask the specific requirements in these regards, ideally with a link to an official site.

Comment 4 (source ID 422284772) | Participant 1 | created 2018-09-18T07:27:49Z | updated 2018-09-18T07:27:49Z
Source: https://github.com/elabftw/elabftw/issues/870#issuecomment-422284772
This is the link to the official site of the European Union: [European Commission - Legal Grounds](https://ec.europa.eu/info/law/law-topic/data-protection/reform/rules-business-and-organisations/legal-grounds-processing-data/grounds-processing) 

In the section "When is consent valid?" there are some requirements on how to have a valid consent which are:

1. it must be **freely given;**
2. it must be **informed**;
3. it must be given for a **specific purpose**;
4. all the reasons for the processing must be clearly stated;
5. it is **explicit** and given via a positive act (for example an electronic tick-box that the individual has to explicitly check online or a signature on a form);
6. it **uses clear and plain language** and is clearly visible;
7. it is possible to **withdraw consent** and that fact is explained (for example an unsubscribe link at the end of an electronic newsletter email).

Bullet points 2 - 7 have to be covered by the organisations data privacy statement, but maybe a default statement can be provided, i.e. which personal data is collected (mail, name, optional phone number etc, maybe IP/browser at login?!). Comment 1 (source ID 436967312) | Participant 2 | created 2018-11-08T11:44:35Z | updated 2018-11-08T11:44:35Z
Source: https://github.com/MetaMask/metamask-extension/issues/5699#issuecomment-436967312
Hi @DaneWiid1, thanks for taking the time to file this issue. We recently simplified our implementation of the "privacy mode" settings option. Specifically, turning this option "off" makes it so your accounts are always exposed to the dapps you visit, but this doesn't prevent the approval popup from showing if a dapp explicitly calls `ethereum.enable()`. The "privacy mode" settings option was only ever meant to allow users to continue to use legacy dapps that may be slow to update to the new API. However, if a dapp is already calling the new API, meaning their code is already updated to handle the approval popup, users will still see the approval popup regardless of whether "privacy mode" is "on" or "off". It should also be noted that this settings option is temporary: it will eventually be defaulted to "on" and ultimately removed altogether in future releases, making private browsing the only option for users.

Thanks again for reaching out. Let us know if you have any additional questions while testing.

Comment 2 (source ID 437539274) | Participant 3 | created 2018-11-10T00:43:21Z | updated 2018-11-10T00:43:21Z

Thanks for the explanation @bitpshr. I think it's easy to misunderstand the behavior of "Privacy mode" given the name. We also expected connect requests to not show as long as this was off.

Perhaps something like "Legacy Support" with the on/off meanings switched (Privacy mode "off" == Legacy support "on") would've reduced confusion a bit. I guess either way it'll all be removed soon, so it's no big deal.

Source: https://github.com/MetaMask/metamask-extension/issues/5699#issuecomment-445480857
For future visitors: 
You can avoid the popup if privacy mode is turned off by checking if window.ethereum.selectedAccount is undefined. If it is undefined, then attempt to enable.

Something like:
```javascript
if (window.ethereum) {
      try {
         if (typeof window.ethereum.selectedAddress === 'undefined') {
                await window.ethereum.enable();
                window.web3 = new Web3(window.ethereum);
          }
          else {
                window.web3 = new Web3(window.ethereum);
          }
      } catch (error) {
            alert('You denied access to your metamask. You will not be able to utilize the site.');
      }
}

```

Comment 4 (source ID 450892985) | Participant 5 | created 2019-01-02T15:28:27Z | updated 2019-01-02T15:28:27Z
Source: https://github.com/MetaMask/metamask-extension/issues/5699#issuecomment-450892985
If enabling or disabling Privacy Mode has no effect, why include it in the interface at all? The user has no meaningful choice, so the option should just be removed OR the behavior of the option should be made consistent with all the documentation that clearly says what the behavior should be.

I agree with the original rationale behind adding this option and progressing toward making it on by default.  This gives dapp developers a chance to make the necessary changes and test them out.  However, if the option is going to be in the interface, it should give users a meaningful choice where the meaning matches all the documentation of what the meaning is supposed to be, in many places, that are not updated and show no sign that they are going to be.  I believe it would be significantly better to restore the original, well-documented behavior of the Privacy Mode setting.

Source: https://github.com/MetaMask/metamask-extension/issues/5699#issuecomment-451133558
@wbt,

> If enabling or disabling Privacy Mode has no effect, why include it in the interface at all?

This settings option does have an effect, just not a visual one: accounts are either automatically exposed to dapps if this option is disabled, or not automatically exposed if this option is enabled.

Also, as stated earlier, this settings option is purely temporary so legacy dapps can work for the time being, and was never meant to reduce user-facing prompts on dapps that already call the new API. Our privacy mode [blog post](https://medium.com/metamask/introducing-privacy-mode-42549d4870fa) also states that users may still see the prompt with the option disabled as dapps update proactively:

> At first, Privacy Mode will be opt-in (and turned “off” by default). Even if you haven’t turned Privacy Mode “on” yet, we want to make it clear what’s happening under the hood, so you may start seeing the “Connect to this site” dialog as you use your favorite dapps.

Source: https://github.com/MetaMask/metamask-extension/issues/5699#issuecomment-451343626
> This settings option does have an effect, just not a visual one: **accounts are** either **automatically exposed to dapps if this option is disabled**, or not automatically exposed if this option is enabled.

That's what I expected, too, based on all the documentation and logical software behavior.  That's apparently not how the software actually behaves.  If the option is disabled, accounts are apparently **not** automatically exposed to dapps, and if the user clicks "cancel" on the popup the dapp apparently does not ever get the account exposed unless the user later returns and clicks "connect."  

This disconnect between our and even your expert expectations of how the software *should* behave and how it actually *does* behave is the basis and trigger for my bug report (#5971) and apparently this one as well. 

Comment 7 (source ID 487706906) | Participant 6 | created 2019-04-29T19:13:20Z | updated 2019-04-29T19:13:20Z

It is an unavoidable, meaningless popup that is presented to the user for no explainable reason, and the app has no means of ameliorating the situation.

Source: https://github.com/MetaMask/metamask-extension/issues/5699#issuecomment-487730576
@dkent600:

> nor any way of anticipating that the popup is going to be shown

For now, you can use `ethereum._metamask.isApproved` to know if calling `ethereum.enable` will trigger a popup to show. `ethereum._metamask.isApproved` returns a `Promise` that resolves to `true` or `false` depending on if a user has previously approved a given dapp. Also, "privacy mode" was never part of the underlying EIP and was added as an afterthought to ease the transition from the old API to the new API. Unfortunately, we're now in a difficult spot where dapps are split between the two. Ideally, "privacy mode" would go away entirely since it was never meant to be a longterm feature, negating the issue you identified above re: divergent logic paths / UX flows.

Issue body:
These suggestions are from Matthew Davis @ https://discourse.mozilla.org/t/upload-of-screenshot-without-asking-for-permission-or-even-warning-me/16451/7

On [this page](https://screenshots.firefox.com/#hello), under “Save and Share”, it should say something like:

> When you take a shot **and click on the Cloud Share button**, Firefox posts your screenshot to your online Screenshots library and copies the link to your clipboard. We automatically store **shared** screenshots for two weeks, but you can delete shots at any time or change the expiration date to keep them in your library for longer. If you don’t click on the share button, your image doesn’t leave your computer.

Of course, only put that if it’s true.

And the “[privacy notice](https://www.mozilla.org/en-US/privacy/firefox/)” link at the bottom of [that page](https://screenshots.firefox.com/shots) should take the user to a page which actually tells the user something useful, which is specific to Firefox screenshots. Privacy notices have one purpose, and the current one fails to fulfill that. It should tell me what happens to my data. i.e. when are my photos uploaded to the cloud? And when are they not?

Similarly, there should be a question on [the FAQ page](https://wiki.mozilla.org/Firefox/Screenshots/FAQs) which says something like:

> Q: Which images are uploaded to the cloud?
> 
> A: By default, images do not leave your machine. Images are uploaded only if you click ‘share’ to generate a URL. You can choose to sync all screenshots with the cloud by going into settings and clicking on

The “download” button should have it’s hovertext changed from “download” to “save to filesystem”. Maybe also change the download icon to a hard disk shaped save icon?

Functionally, I’d like “My Shots” to show me all the shots that I’ve saved locally, even if I didn’t upload them to the cloud.

/cc @flodolo

Issue body:
We need a page for an imprint. 
If we don't have one, we can get in trouble with German and European laws.

- [ ] Imprint information like address, contact and legal information
- [ ] Disclaimer for external links

Further, we should discuss whether we use cookies.

Issue discussion (chronological; participant names pseudonymized within the case):
Comment 1 (source ID 279235799) | Participant 2 | created 2017-02-12T17:59:12Z | updated 2017-02-12T17:59:12Z
Source: https://github.com/TeamNewPipe/website/issues/4#issuecomment-279235799

Comment 2 (source ID 279236341) | Participant 3 | created 2017-02-12T18:08:04Z | updated 2017-02-12T18:08:04Z
Source: https://github.com/TeamNewPipe/website/issues/4#issuecomment-279236341
Your justification is quite vague. I am going to clarify that.

First of all, let's regard German law: The first relevant one is the Telemediengesetz (TMG). Having a look at [§ 5 TMG](https://dejure.org/gesetze/TMG/5.html) which cares about the internet presence as a whole, an imprint is required for "geschäftsmäßige Online-Inhalte". As Newpipe and its website are all non-commercial, there is no need for an imprint due to TMG.
The other relevant law is the Rundfunkstaatsvertrag (RStV), more precisely [§ 55 RStV](http://www.dvtm.net/fileadmin/pdf/gesetze/13._RStV.pdf), which takes care of a website's contents. § 55 (1) is about "Telemedien", "die nicht ausschließlich persönlichen oder familiären Zwecken dienen" (that are not exclusively about personal or family purposes). As this software project is just a personal one for @theScrabi and the contributors, there is no need for an imprint (as long as there's no journalistic content like a blog, which would be dealt with by § 55 (2)).

About EU laws: Actually, there is no such thing like EU laws. There's the EU regulations that have to be implemented by national laws in a specified period of time (this depends on a regulation's type (yes, there's more than one, welcome to bureaucracy hell), if you are interested, you can read this [Wikipedia article](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regulation_(European_Union)). As a consequence, laws in the German jurisdiction are compatible to EU regulations, which implies that if you don't need an imprint for German laws, you won't need one for any EU regulations.

TL;DR: This website does not need an imprint in its current form (an informational, static page). As soon as this changes, we will have to rethink this decision.

About the disclaimer: I cannot count the times how often I read those, and thought "this is a waste of webspace". Many of them share the exact same wording. The bad thing about some of these wordings is: They are often illegitimate and thus ineffective. External links stuff is dealt with by (surprise) Telemediengesetz, more precise [§§ 7 ff. TMG](https://dejure.org/gesetze/TMG/7.html). This topic is even more complicated than the question whether you need an imprint or not (and if yes, what you have to put in it). You can read a summary [here (German)](http://blog-it-recht.de/2013/09/27/datenschutzklausel-und-haftungsausschluss-im-impressum/).

TL;DR: disclaimers are not necessary, because all they could do is inform the user about the contents of 
§§ 7 ff. TMG, which they could just look up themselves. It is better to not have one on your website than having a potentially illegal and abstruse wording that is in the end ineffective.

About the "use of cookies": I am not quite sure why this is a thing at the moment. The page is purely informational, and uses static HTML pages. There is no code that could even create cookies, or make use of them. Apart from that, this is a completely separate issue and should be discussed in a separate thread as soon as it gets relevant.

And last but not least the most important question: What about data privacy and the privacy notice things you can spot on may websites?
Well, surprise, TMG covers that part too. [§ 13 (1) TMG](https://dejure.org/gesetze/TMG/13.html) describes how a service provider has to inform their users about "Art, Umfang und Zwecke der Erhebung personenbezogener Daten" (type, amount and purpose of the collection of personal data). As the site does not collect any necessary data except for the webserver logs (which is verified to be legal), there is nothing to inform the user about.

**TL;DR: We don't need an imprint, we don't need a disclaimer, and we don't need a privacy note as long as the website remains a purely informational (and ideally static) website. As soon as this changes, we will have to discuss this issue again.**

@theScrabi next time, gimme a few minutes to write my wall of text.

Btw: apps [can be required](http://rechtsanwalt-schwenke.de/shocking-kaum-eine-mobile-app-hat-ein-zulaessiges-impressum/) to include an imprint, too. We should discuss that for Newpipe some day. (Although I'm quite sure that this is covered by Youtube's imprint as they are responsible for the content, perhaps we just need to include a link to Google's imprint.)

I am not a lawyer and this is not legal advice; however, I do work in information security and have privacy engineering experience as well as security event incident management experience (i.e. security log acquisition, retention, search/alerting.)

Logs can certainly reveal sensitive information, but exactly what is sensitive and shouldn't be logged should be based on a combination of existing laws and the potential harm to a _natural person_ which may come from the information being logged, which could potentially be leaked or shared inappropriately. Considering GDPR, CCPA, LGPD, PDPA, and HIPAA (privacy laws from many geographic areas)  -- the common thread is the potential harm to the natural person.

So in regards to logging information, one should always avoid logging: passwords, email addresses, IP-addresses associated with end-users (i.e. POD IP address is ok to log), individual-person health information, credit card numbers, national ID numbers, driver's license number, etc. Most of the information that a Kubernetes cluster deals with would not contain any of this sensitive information, as the cluster, pods, and containers pertain to system components and not a natural person. 

The real challenge is posed by the workloads running within the containers; they are very likely to ingest and handle personally identifiable information and potentially log it inappropriately; what this data might be would depend on the specific workload and the geography where the end user resides (example: end-user IP address is PII for EU data subjects but not for US residents!) Many companies end up writing their own logging routines to help filter out the sensitive information that their business processes from their logs. An extensible logging framework could help your customers greatly by allowing them to write their own logging filters which deal exactly with the types of PHI or PII their organization is ingesting. 

If in doubt, consult your info sec or legal team.

Title at retrieval: Should we include user information?
Status at retrieval: closed

Issue body:
I apologise if this has been discussed before; I could not find an issue for it.

Currently the spec specifically refers to users who have produced/uploaded the burrito, by name and by unique identifier.  I am not really a fan of this, for several reasons, but willing to be convinced otherwise.

Firstly, including personally identifiable information may mean that burritos are affected by data protection regulations such as GDPR, which may place legal limits on the ability to transfer burritos to servers in other countries.  IANAL, so I do not know how far-reaching the implications are (and I might be completely wrong on this).

Secondly, from a purely conceptual level I am not sure that it should be considered in-scope for the burrito metadata to say something that is not descriptive of the contents but rather of the person who created it.  Including the name and version of the software that generated it is useful because it may say something meaningful about the contents thereof, but the identity of the person who did it does not.  (And when burritos are offered for wider distribution, people who publish burritos on behalf of their organisation may not even want their personal names attached.)

Thirdly, I can't see how it's *useful*.  The fact that identifiers are system-specific, and privacy considerations mean that user information cannot just be queried by an arbitrary party from a public API without the user's consent, effectively means that a system is likely storing this purely for its own consumption, but a system that needs this will likely already be storing its own event log accompanying the actual metadata.  But, this is purely my own speculation, so it would be valuable for others to weigh in.

Issue discussion (chronological; participant names pseudonymized within the case):
Comment 1 (source ID 556149864) | Participant 2 | created 2019-11-20T17:35:35Z | updated 2019-11-20T17:35:35Z
Source: https://github.com/bible-technology/scripture-burrito/issues/91#issuecomment-556149864
I can confirm that having the archivist name often turns out to be in DBL, for example to work out how things ended up the way they did. This works without user ids because there's only one DBL. Giving user ids may or not enable DBL to identify the user - it might well do so if the user is in the Registry. But, in all cases, it tells me that I can't assume org-x's John Smith is DBL's John Smith, and that's something.

For GDPR I'd have thought that the name of the user is more of the problem than a somewhat opaque user id (unless someone is using SS numbers as keys or something.)

We should probably make these fields optional though.

Comment 2 (source ID 557492284) | Participant 1 | created 2019-11-22T11:11:18Z | updated 2019-11-22T11:11:18Z
Source: https://github.com/bible-technology/scripture-burrito/issues/91#issuecomment-557492284
Is it often the case in DBL's situation that the uploader may be a different person than the person who produced the bundle?  I'm wondering whether it might perhaps be sufficient for DBL to record the uploader name alongside the bundle based on their authentication credentials.

For the record, GDPR is quite broad when it determines the meaning of personal data; even including the hair colour of the burrito producer would already become tricky.  Identifiers fall under it because they indirectly refer to a personal identity and can be used to track that individual.  Article 4 is unambiguous about this (emphasis mine):
> ‘Personal data’ means any information relating to an identified or identifiable natural person (‘data subject’); an identifiable natural person is one who can be identified, **directly or indirectly**, in particular by reference to an identifier such as a name, an **identification number**, location data, an **online identifier** or to one or more factors specific to the physical, physiological, genetic, mental, economic, cultural or social identity of that natural person.

This would mean that burritos do fall under data protection laws, and anyone processing burritos containing references to EU citizens and sharing them with third parties would have to abide by the stipulations of the GDPR, such as requiring explicit (and withdrawable) consent to share them with specifically enumerated third-party recipients of the data for specifically enumerated purposes.

This is not the responsibility of the SBWG but of whoever produces and processes burritos, so we could simply make these fields optional and not concern ourselves further with it, but these considerations may add a practical barrier to the usefulness of this field.

Comment 3 (source ID 557494185) | Participant 2 | created 2019-11-22T11:17:31Z | updated 2019-11-22T11:17:31Z
Source: https://github.com/bible-technology/scripture-burrito/issues/91#issuecomment-557494185
We added a second user identifier because the project archivist may not be the person uploading to DBL. (The total number of users who have uploaded to DBL is just over 100, with the vast majority of entries being uploaded by less than 20 users - these figures are orders of magnitude lower than the number of archivists who have prepared projects now in DBL.)

I think it's good to flag GDPR but I agree that we should not make GDPR compliance a SB problem. In some cases, SBs may never be seen by anyone but the owner, in others they could potentially appear all over the place. So GDPR seems to me to be partly an ecosystem question rather than a data representation question. I would imagine that a DBL approach to this would be to extend the current "strip on export" mechanisms used to provide specific users with a suitable subset of information.

Source: https://github.com/saleor/saleor/issues/4039#issuecomment-487550087
IIRC we are allowed to log the customer's name during its deletion, even if they asked us to remove their data as it's not an information that could directly be used to identify a single person, a full name can return multiple persons (depending of the scope, of course). I'm believing it's fine for the GDPR as long we don't have any other information about this customer, other than their name. But I'm unsure.

We discussed about this issue during our previous meeting, and it was mentioned that @patrys may have an answer to bring us. What do you think about this matter?

We still have, of course, the issue of the orders; but that's another matter.

Comment 2 (source ID 487574671) | Participant 2 | created 2019-04-29T13:14:28Z | updated 2019-04-29T13:14:28Z
Source: https://github.com/saleor/saleor/issues/4039#issuecomment-487574671
We are allowed to process a person's name as part of an order for the purpose of fulfilling a contract. We can do so even if the user requests that their data is deleted, otherwise it would be possible for me to demand that my data is erased from an unpaid invoice. We can use the buyer's data for as long as it's required: to process payments, dispatch packages for shipping, process complaints, returns, refunds, etc.

We can not use the information for any other purpose once the contract is fulfilled unless the user explicitly consents to such use (and that consent can be forfeited by requesting erasure). To me, that means we should probably avoid storing the information outside of the context where it's absolutely necessary for reasons required by law (order details, invoices, etc.). For events, it's probably safer to say "notified the customer" instead of "sent email to john.doe@example.com". We can't reasonably claim that it's absolutely necessary for us to put the name there for the purpose of fulfilling the contractual requirements (delivering purchased goods or services).

As for whether someone's full name constitutes personally identifiable information that really depends on the person. The regulation states that it applies to information that makes it reasonably easy to identify an individual. "Queen Elisabeth II", "Arnold Schwarzenegger", "Danny DeVito", "Taylor Swift" are all easily identifiable based on the name alone.

Retrieved issue comments: 12/12

Issue body:
I work on confidential projects, where the thought of accidentally pushing to a GitHub remote is horrifying.

As a safety measure I have defined local versions of wflow_git_remote() and wflow_git_push() that call stop("Don't do that!). However, that doesn't prevent some function calling workflowr::wflow_git_push().

Would it be possible to add a local_only=TRUE argument to wflow_start() that takes steps to ensure that workflowr never tries to have dealings with a remote repo?

Issue discussion (chronological; participant names pseudonymized within the case):
Comment 1 (source ID 451622003) | Participant 2 | created 2019-01-05T02:53:20Z | updated 2019-01-05T02:53:20Z
Source: https://github.com/workflowr/workflowr/issues/141#issuecomment-451622003
> The thought of accidentally pushing to a GitHub remote is horrifying.

@rgayler If this is a concern, it seems that the simplest option would be to remove the GitHub remote, and at that point `wflow_git_push` should no longer work. For more details, run `git remote  --help`.

Comment 2 (source ID 451627322) | Participant 1 | created 2019-01-05T04:39:03Z | updated 2019-01-05T04:39:03Z
Source: https://github.com/workflowr/workflowr/issues/141#issuecomment-451627322
I never even created a GitHub remote in the first place, but I will eventually be handing over the project directory to people who are even more clueless than I am about workflowr and git - so I redefined wflow_git_remote() to avoid accidents via that route (although, obviously, that doesn't stop somebody using git to push directly to a remote).

Given that lots of research projects have confidentiality constraints I thought it might provide a degree of comfort for workflowr users if there was some project-level configuration that could be set to indicate the project is confidential and prevent pushing to a remote repo.

(Maybe a [git pre-push hook](https://blog.ghost.org/prevent-master-push/ could be used to prevent git from pushing to a remote.)

Comment 3 (source ID 451980854) | Participant 3 | created 2019-01-07T15:53:41Z | updated 2019-01-07T15:53:41Z
Source: https://github.com/workflowr/workflowr/issues/141#issuecomment-451980854
> I work on confidential projects, where the thought of accidentally pushing to a GitHub remote is horrifying.

@rgayler Could you please describe your use case some more so that we can better understand how to support your use of workflowr? For example, how are you sharing the workflowr website with your collaborators? Do you have a private web server or are you sending files over email? Did you use a remote Git hosting service of any kind, or do you plan to only use Git locally? How do you plan to share the code/data with your collaborators?

> Would it be possible to add a local_only=TRUE argument to wflow_start() that takes steps to ensure that workflowr never tries to have dealings with a remote repo?

Since this is the first request for this feature, I'm not ready to add an argument for it. For more complicated Git behavior, I think it is best to directly use Git (see below).

> (Maybe a [git pre-push hook](https://blog.ghost.org/prevent-master-push/ could be used to prevent git from pushing to a remote.)

I think this is the right solution. I saved the file below as `.git/hooks/pre-push`, made it executable with `chmod +x .git/hooks/pre-push`, and confirmed that it prevents pushing to a remote repository.

```
#!/bin/bash

echo "This is a confidential project. Do not push the files to a remote server"
echo "For details, contact Ross Gayler via ..."
exit 1
```

Now this hook file is not transferred using the traditional Git commands (`push`, `pull`, `clone`), but I think that is ok for your use case since you don't seem to be using those commands. If you share the workflowr project directly with your collaborators (e.g. using a file sharing service or emailing a tarball), the pre-push hook will prevent them from pushing to GitHub or any other Git hosting website.

Comment 4 (source ID 452511843) | Participant 1 | created 2019-01-09T00:21:02Z | updated 2019-01-09T00:21:02Z
Source: https://github.com/workflowr/workflowr/issues/141#issuecomment-452511843
**Use case:**
My current use case is that I am working on a project for a third party. The project is contractually constrained to be confidential - I can only share project materials with the third party.
During the course of the project I need to repeatedly share results (but not code) for feedback.
At the end of the project the entire project directory is sent to the third party so they have the ability to reproduce and modify the analyses if they wish.

I like the [Dat/Beakersuggestion](https://jdblischak.github.io/workflowr/articles/wflow-05-faq.html#can-i-share-workflowr-websites-directly-with-collaborators-in-a-secure-fashion) in the FAQ,
but the third-parties I work with tend to have a hard time getting anything non-standard into their IT environments.

I use Git locally in the project directory to track changes to the code base. I protect against data loss with encrypted backup.

I currently share the knitted results with the third party by sending an encrypted archive of the `docs` directory.

At the end of the project I will send an encrypted archive of the whole project directory to the third party.

Generalising my use case to more likely scientific scenarios, I think the key features are:

1. The project contains or may generate information that must be kept confidential. This would be fairly common in any field that deals with human data, because there is a risk of having personally identifiable information. Even if you expect the analyses to only generate unidentifiable aggregate figures there is a risk that someone will accidentally slip some PII into the output text, e.g. when identifying an aberrant case that needs to be followed up ("John Smith has negative age").

2. The project has collaborators who don't need to modify the code, e.g. subject-matter experts. They only need to review the outputs.

> Since this is the first request for this feature, I'm not ready to add an argument for it.

I think what I was after was firstly a declarative statement of intent to keep the project local. E.g. it could be a line in `_workflowr.yml` or the existence of a file named `CONFIDENTIAL.txt` in the project directory. Then given the declaration that the project is not to be published (unintentionally) any mechanisms to prevent accidental publication via Git are essentially implementation detail.

> I think [a Git pre-push hook] is the right solution.

So the suggestion was that something like that might be built in to `workflowr` so that users who know almost nothing about Git (e.g. me) might have more confidence in using `workflowr` for confidential projects.

Comment 5 (source ID 452898668) | Participant 3 | created 2019-01-09T22:48:34Z | updated 2019-01-09T22:48:34Z
Source: https://github.com/workflowr/workflowr/issues/141#issuecomment-452898668
@rgayler Thanks for the explanation. It is very insightful to learn the various ways that workflowr is being used.

> At the end of the project I will send an encrypted archive of the whole project directory to the third party.

Great. This means that the pre-push hook is a good solution for this situation.

> The project contains or may generate information that must be kept confidential.

I agree this is a common situation. My problem trying to generalize it is that disabling Git is not necessarily required in this situation. For example, if the organization uses [GitHub Enterprise](https://github.com/enterprise), then the analysts can push to the remote repository even though the data is confidential.

> it could be a line in _workflowr.yml or the existence of a file named CONFIDENTIAL.txt in the project directory.

I think adding such a file is best done manually. It's not as common as say a README.md file.

> So the suggestion was that something like that might be built in to workflowr so that users who know almost nothing about Git (e.g. me) might have more confidence in using workflowr for confidential projects.

How about an argument to `wflow_start()` named something like `disable_remote`? When set to `TRUE`, it would create the file `.git/hooks/pre-push` and make it executable. I'd propose the file contain something like the following (suggestions welcome):

```
#!/bin/bash

# This hook prevents pushing to a remote repository, which is ideal for a
# project containing confidential data. It was created by wflow_start() with the
# argument disable_remote = TRUE. If you decide you want to be able to push this
# repository, delete this file.

echo "This is a confidential project. Do not push the files to a remote server"
exit 1
```


Comment 6 (source ID 452945551) | Participant 1 | created 2019-01-10T02:18:58Z | updated 2019-01-10T02:18:58Z
Source: https://github.com/workflowr/workflowr/issues/141#issuecomment-452945551
> if the organization uses GitHub Enterprise, then the analysts can push to the remote repository even though the data is confidential.

1. So the core concept is "not to be pushed to a public repo" (which may follow from confidentiality).
2. The feature is aimed at users who are not technically sophisticated (or have access to technical sophistication).

> wflow_start() named something like disable_remote? When set to TRUE, it would create the file .git/hooks/pre-push

That sounds great. The existence of the argument makes it clear that the possibility exists and absolves the technically naive user of having to come up with a technical solution. I just redefined `wflow_git_remote()` and `wflow_git_push()` to give an error message, but the pre-push hook prevents pushing by any mechanism. The mechanism doesn't have to be absolutely watertight (a malign actor can always find a workaround) it just needs to give a degree of well-founded confidence that the user is unlikely to accidentally expose the project.

Issue body:
Right now, Guppy has no tracking at all. As a result, we don't know how many people are using it =(

This has been discussed much in Gitter, and I think we should move towards using a pre-built service. The obvious choice is Google Analytics, but because Google uses this product to follow users around the web (and beyond), I don't feel great about adding another data point for them through Guppy.

I've been turned on to some other services though:
- https://heapanalytics.com
- https://mixpanel.com
- https://usefathom.com/

Fathom is essentially a fancy counter, it tells you how many people are using your thing, although it's very web-focused and doesn't seem to have additional info about what folks are doing. Plus it doesn't offer a hosted solution yet, so we'd need to figure out where to put it.

The other two are analytics products; you wire it up to track certain events (launch dev server, build, test, etc). Now that I think about it, that info would be really good to have; it could help us prioritize features based on how people are using Guppy, for example. And I feel OK about it from a privacy perspective because we still aren't collecting any personally-identifiable information, although we will definitely add this to our privacy policy.

Both Heap and Mixpanel have a free tier, but are paid beyond that, and are quite expensive. In the future I imagine we might have a Patreon or similar to fund services like this, but for now we should assume that we might need to switch providers if we outgrow the one we pick, and find a cheaper alternative.

I think our solution should be an abstraction over one of those services, so that we can easily swap it out later if needed. So I imagine we will have a new Redux Saga that will watch for specific actions, and when it sees them, will call a method in a new `analytics.service.js` file. That way, if our analytics provider ever changes, we just need to update that service file.

I'm gonna take a quick stab at implementing it this morning. I'll start with Heap Analytics, since I've heard good things from a trusted source, but I'm not married to that solution if anyone has alternative suggestions.

------------

- [x] Add new analytics saga
- [x] Add new analytics service
- [x] Add Mixpanel client library, wire it up with some of the service calls
- [ ] Add Privacy Policy

Thanks for creating the issue.

I briefly checked Heap and one thing we'll need to add is an identification `heap.identify(userId)` of the installation. I think we can do this with an uuid that we'll generate on first start because electronStore will not contain that id or do we have another option to do this because clearing the store would always create a new userId?
But I think that's the easiest way with-out a login and probably won't happen often. Or maybe we can read an id from the computer (e.g. network MAC address) and use this as identifier.

Comment 3 (source ID 420270895) | Participant 1 | created 2018-09-11T13:17:25Z | updated 2018-09-11T13:17:25Z
Source: https://github.com/joshwcomeau/guppy/issues/242#issuecomment-420270895
> why a saga instead of a redux middleware? Seems like the perfect use case for a middleware

The reason I want to try a saga is just to reduce the amount of potentially-foreign concepts this repo uses (new contributors shouldn't have to learn about both middlewares _and_ sagas, ideally). 

I think we can create something very similar if we `takeEvery('*', handleAnalytics)`; inside `handleAnalytics` we can `switch` on the action type, the same way we would in a middleware.

But yeah, if the ergonomics of it are weird, I can switch it to a middleware.

>I briefly checked Heap and one thing we'll need to add is an identification heap.identify(userId) of the installation

Yep! I decided to generate a UUID (feels less personally invasive than finding some sort of device identifier), and store it in `electron-store`. I don't think Redux needs to know about it since it never affects the UI. It's true that if the user clears their state, they'll be treated as a brand-new user, but I think that's OK.

---------

First PR is up: #244.

After playing with Heap, I realized it's not great for what we need. They do a bunch of stuff for you, to be helpful, but it winds up making things more complicated. For example, they do page-tracking automatically, but it doesn't work since in our desktop app, we don't have routes. They do have a custom events system, but it feels bolted on, and we'd get a bunch of noise from all their wrong assumptions.

Mixpanel is much closer to what I was looking for. You just submit events with a `.track` call. Plus, their UI is much cleaner, and I actually have experience working with them (It's been a couple years, but I remember having good experiences with their client library).

Issue body:
If we are going to get set up as a data wrangler of various data sources, I want to be able to check that we are following any MITA or CMS standards that are appropriate for handling provider info. I presume that *provider* info could not possibly constitute sensitive PII but I would like to double-check this!

I started looking at [the MITA framework](https://www.medicaid.gov/medicaid/data-and-systems/mita/mita-30/index.html) but think it does not address this question.

I am beginning to think that the relevant standards might well be ["Minimum Acceptable Risk Standards for Exchanges (MARS-E) 2.0 Framework"](https://www.cms.gov/CCIIO/Resources/Regulations-and-Guidance/Downloads/2-MARS-E-v2-0-Minimum-Acceptable-Risk-Standards-for-Exchanges-11102015.pdf) -- discussed privately [on CALT]( https://calt.cms.gov/sf/projects/cms_aca_program_security_privacy/) and publicly listed in [cms.gov's Regulations and Guidance](https://www.cms.gov/cciio/resources/regulations-and-guidance/#MinimumAcceptableRiskStandards), explained in [this summary from CMS (pdf)](https://www.medicaid.gov/federal-policy-guidance/downloads/cib-09-23-2015.pdf) and described in [this surprisingly cogent Microsoft compliance page](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/TrustCenter/Compliance/Mars-E). But I haven't gone deeply enough into it to understand whether it applies just to patients or includes any discussion of providers as well.

And I stumbled across a [NIST standard, "Guide to Protecting the Confidentiality of Personally Identifiable Information (PII)" (pdf)](http://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/Legacy/SP/nistspecialpublication800-122.pdf) -- but this only applies if any of the data we deal with counts as PII.

The resolution of this issue may depend on which federal data services we integrate with, in which case we can close it as a duplicate of #17.

Relates to #10.

We don't need to do specific work on this issue except to continue our work on building secure infrastructure with sane access controls.

Those NIST guidelines are pretty good.  We should aspire to meet them. :)

The proposal is __not__  for a special kind of account but for special kinds of posts/comments for which there would be no record of the author. The accounts created by the current methods are not anonymous but __pseudonymous__.

The problems with pseudonymous accounts are,

- The moment you identify the person, you can identify all his posts/comments.
- Any hint from one post/comment can exposes the real identity.
- Even a transaction of Steem can be traced back.

The anonymous posts/comments would not have any record of the author. And there wouldn't be any rewards connected to them. Thus the author cannot be identified.

If an account has a null authority (no keys, or threshold 0), then it can post without a signature. Yes, there is a name associated with it, but anyone can use it. So it is anonymous. Several users have set up accounts like this in the past. If you are asking for comments that are not even traced on the blockchain, then this is not the repository you are looking for because this is only for things on the blockchain.

The problem with no author being listed on a comment is that we have no way of rate limiting via Steem Power (no account means no Steem Power). It opens up an attack vector against the blockchain.

If there is a reason why the null authority scheme does not work, I would be interested to hear it, but I believe all of the tools to implement what you want already exist.

Well, the description for this repo says "OpenID Connect (OIDC) and OAuth2 protocol support for browser-based JavaScript applications" :)

But sure, if I knew what that was more, then I'd love to hear what support is needed. Is isomorphic a native framework for running JS & react?


Comment 2 (source ID 260052368) | Participant 1 | created 2016-11-11T20:50:15Z | updated 2016-11-11T20:53:33Z
Source: https://github.com/DuendeArchive/identity-model-oidc-client-js/issues/178#issuecomment-260052368
Isomorphic React isn't a framework. It just means writing your code so it runs both on the client and the server. The server obviously doesn't have things like localStorage/sessionStorage/cookies, at least not out of the box (there are many polyfills for Node to fill in some of this functionality, but they vary widely in quality and how recenlty they've been updated). So writing your library in such a way that it assumes those things exist means your library just can't be easily used isomorphically.

Source: https://github.com/DuendeArchive/identity-model-oidc-client-js/issues/178#issuecomment-260052719
The reason this is desirable is because it means that a React application can benefit from all the speed of a cached application on initial pageload, but subsequent interactions/routes/etc can be handled within the browser. In addition to performance benefits, it also has SEO benefits.

That sort of grew into what info can we provide for general Tech FAQ-like topics from freshdesk. I added a lot of canned responses to freshdesk to address those topics. W.r.t. information security/ safety, we might want to clarify our existing FAQ & CG (as well as having the longer, more detailed responses to specific questions I added to freshdesk). @kaschm already thumbs-up'd these changes, but I thought other people - @SpeakkVisually, @thisandagain, potentially others as well - should approve before any changes are made to the FAQ/ CG.

These suggestions result from https://github.com/LLK/scratch-www/issues/1007.

### Updating FAQ/ CG page

We already cover the information at a high level that I was considering adding to the FAQ. I don't know if it makes sense to include the details in the FAQ, but maybe we can re-word some of the existing FAQ questions to be a little stronger/ more specific.

**Existing FAQ & CG**
https://scratch.mit.edu/info/faq/
https://scratch.mit.edu/community_guidelines/

> **What information can I share on / with my account?**
Please don’t share personal contact information, such as your physical address, email, phone number, or anything else that can be used to make contact outside of the Scratch website. Please report projects, comments, or forum posts that contain this kind of information so the Scratch team can remove it, and remind the author of our policy.

> **Is it OK to have more than one person logged into an account?**
This is discouraged, because the website and project editor can easily get confused when more than one person is logged into the same account.

> **What information do you ask for during account registration?**
To protect the privacy of our community members, we limit what we collect and what we publish on the website. During the registration process, we ask for the following information:
> * username - We ask that users avoid using their real names or other identifying information.
country
> * birth month and year - We use this to confirm ownership of the account if the owner loses the password and email or asks to close an account.
> * gender
> * contact email address - If the account holder is younger than 13, we ask for the email address of their parent or guardian. We do not send email to this address except when someone requests to have the account password reset.

> The username and country of the account holder are displayed publicly on their profile page. The birth month / year, email address, and gender associated with the account are not displayed publicly. We collect this info so we can know the age and gender of our users in aggregate, and for research purposes. We do not sell or rent information about our users to anyone.

(From the CG)
> **Keep personal info private.**
For safety reasons, don't give out any information that could be used for private communication - such as real last names, phone numbers, addresses, email addresses, links to social media sites or websites with unmoderated chat.

**Proposed FAQ & CG Changes**

> **What information can I share on / with my account?**
Please don’t share personally identifiable information, such as your name, address, email, phone number, school, links to social media sites, websites with unmoderated chat, or anything else that could be used to identify, find, or contact you outside of the Scratch website. Please report projects, comments, or forum posts that contain or request this kind of information so the Scratch team can remove it, and remind the author of our Community Guidelines (link to Community Guidelines).

> **Is it OK to share a single Scratch account with multiple people?**
This is discouraged, because the website and project editor can easily get confused when more than one person is using the same account. Because Scratch wasn’t designed with this use in mind, you are increasing your likelihood of your work not being saved.

> **What information do you ask for during account registration?**
To protect the privacy of our community members, we limit what we collect and what we publish on the website. During the registration process, we ask for the following information:
> * username
> * country
> * birth month and year - We use this to confirm ownership of the account if the owner loses the password and email or asks to delete an account.
> * gender
> * contact email address - If the account holder is younger than 13, we ask for the email address of their parent or guardian. We do not send email to this address except when someone requests to have the account password reset, or if they have opted into receiving updates from the Scratch Team.

> We collect this info so we can know the age and gender of our users in aggregate, and for research purposes. We do not sell or rent information about our users to anyone.
The username and country of the account holder are displayed publicly on the user's profile page. The birth month / year, email address, and gender associated with the account are not displayed publicly. We keep this information private as a means of keeping Scratch safe. For the same reason, we ask users to keep this information private as part of our Community Guidelines (link).

(On the CG)
> **Keep personal info private.**
For safety reasons, don't give out any information that could be used to identify, find, or contact you outside of Scratch. This personally identifiable information includes real names, the name of your school, phone numbers, addresses, email addresses, links to social media sites or websites with unmoderated chat.

Issue body:
This is a feature that we haven't tackled so far because of its relative complexity. Instead of building this, we've always suggested that users take advantage of existing video hosting platforms such as YouTube and Vimeo to upload their video content and then _embed_ them inside targets. The argument has been that these platforms have done an enormous amount of work into making the video upload / hosting easy, fast, accessible, and cheap.

However, there could be use-cases where this isn't practical, and where the user would prefer that these large files be managed directly by the LMS. In almost all cases, these large files appear to be videos, and the use is to stream video content.

The main "pain" driving this feature appears to be the inconvenience of uploading videos to another service - It would be really nice to be be able to use Pupilfirst to directly manage video content - something that is frequently an integral part of a course's content. To me, this looks like a good problem to solve.

However, another major driver appears to be to disallow students from sharing or downloading videos to their local systems - as a form of _Digital Rights Management_. The issue with this, is that whatever measures we take, there will always be ways around it, and to a technically capable user such measure are merely inconveniences. I'm unsure as to whether this is a direction we should even attempt to take.

### Options that I can see:

1. Build the feature-set in-house. This means building a direct-upload system (Rails [has good support for this, as of v6](https://edgeguides.rubyonrails.org/active_storage_overview.html#direct-uploads)), **and also** the content-delivery side of it; I'm unfamiliar with the complexities of global streaming delivery of video - I'm sure there are plenty.
2. Integrate with a third-party service to manage video uploads and content delivery. For example: [Cloudflare Stream](https://www.cloudflare.com/products/cloudflare-stream).
3. Build both - i.e., build a direct upload system to handle generic large files (but only allow simple "downloads" of these), and seperately, integrate with a video upload & streaming service to handle hosting of streaming video content.

Options 2 & 3 look preferable to me, but IMHO, more research is required here.

@harigopal , thanks for these ideas, very well captured and articulated , I digged in a bit to gather additional useful thoughts on option 2 & 3.

 [Cloudflare Stream](https://developers.cloudflare.com/stream/getting-started) seems to have some good reviews based on scalability, cost and functionality. It also disables downloading which is useful from _digital rights management_ perspective. Also, they use  [tus protocol](https://tus.io/) (recommended )  for resumable downloads  for files heavier than 200M

I checked  [GStreamer ](https://gstreamer.freedesktop.org/)which is an open source multi-media framework and i think this may have a huge learning curve , but maybe of interest in the future is that it supports  webRTC should we think in that direction in future. 

Also, I checked [ Amazon Elastic Transcoder ](https://aws.amazon.com/elastictranscoder/), which is not cheap at all and doesn't look all that straightforward.

Like you rightly mentioned, this feature seems to be ubiquitous  across most LMS and something worth looking into,but careful considerations be made to avoid unnecessary complications and especially it has to help the roadmap of pupilfirst.
