Title at retrieval: Attribution windows in conversion reports
Status at retrieval: closed
Retrieved issue comments: 11/11

Issue body:
Hi @csharrison and @michaelkleber, 

A few weeks ago on the W3C web-adv call, we discussed the possibility of adding random reporting delays. During that call, I asked if we could include the actual window a particular conversion came from (i.e. `conversion-window=7d`) in the conversion report.

Advertisers want to know the window to which their conversions attributed. They also optimize their campaigns for conversions within a particular window. While a small random delay (on the order of an hour or two) relative to a large attribution window (on the order of days or weeks) may have a small impact on accuracy, a large random delay relative to a small attribution window (on the order of a day or two) would have a significantly detrimental impact on accuracy.

@csharrison suggested we follow up on Github to iron out any potential privacy concerns. I'm fairly confident that revealing just the conversion window would not leak personally identifiable information if we round it to a granularity we are comfortable with (days?)

Do you see any potential privacy concerns? How do we make progress here? Thanks



Issue discussion (chronological; participant names pseudonymized within the case):
Comment 1 (source ID 635528441) | Participant 2 | created 2020-05-28T18:45:33Z | updated 2020-05-28T18:45:33Z
Source: https://github.com/WICG/attribution-reporting-api/issues/47#issuecomment-635528441
I think this really hinges on whether we need to add random noise to report delays, since the existing API does not have any noise except to stagger queued reports at browser startup.

If we implement what is currently describe in the explainer, then this proposal doesn't seem necessary. If you get a report associated with a click you can tell which report window it came from by looking at the time delta from the click time. The only source of noise here is from browser up-time / startup staggering which hopefully should be minimal.

However, if we feel we want to add noise to the API, we should be analyzing why we are doing it and whether reporting the `conversion-window` makes the noise less effective. For instance, in PCM noise is needed because click-time information is not known from a report and conversions are reported based on some delay relative to the conversion-time. We may consider unifying this mode of delay (see https://github.com/privacycg/private-click-measurement/issues/29 for more context) by e.g. adding noise on top of the conversion windows.

If we did something like that, the main thing we want to achieve is for PCM's privacy model to hold (i.e. your click time and your conversion time are well hidden). However, we may be able to come up with other solutions here that don't involve just adding the two delay mechanisms together.

Comment 2 (source ID 635686988) | Participant 1 | created 2020-05-29T00:25:32Z | updated 2020-05-29T00:25:32Z
Source: https://github.com/WICG/attribution-reporting-api/issues/47#issuecomment-635686988
Thanks for the thoughtful response @csharrison !

> The only source of noise here is from browser up-time / startup staggering which hopefully should be minimal.

This is entirely possible though I don't have the data to confirm one way or another. 

On the other hand, even small inaccuracies in our reports can be significantly problematic for our trust with advertisers. In the past, Facebook has been criticized for inaccuracies in its metrics (of this range) so I hope you can see why I'm keen on trying to get the most accurate data as possible, subject to privacy constraints. 

> If we did something like that, the main thing we want to achieve is for PCM's privacy model to hold (i.e. your click time and your conversion time are well hidden).

If we report the `conversion-window` at a day level resolution, I think we can maintain the privacy of the click time and conversion time. For instance, suppose there's a random delay of 0-24 hours for conversion reports. If we got a conversion with a 7-day window, we would know that the click happened 8-7 days ago, still a 24-hour window, and that the conversion happened in the past 8 days. When you add in the additional noise of browsers being offline at the end of the window, it becomes unknowable. 

What do you think? If that doesn't work, how do you think we can move forward here? I'm really keen on finding solutions to let us credit conversions to the right window because advertisers have different targets based on them. Thanks!

Comment 3 (source ID 636175313) | Participant 2 | created 2020-05-29T20:22:53Z | updated 2020-05-29T20:22:53Z
Source: https://github.com/WICG/attribution-reporting-api/issues/47#issuecomment-636175313
Good point. I thought about this with @johnivdel and I think we concluded that reporting a time that omits browser downtime (and associated randomized report delays at startup) is fine for the privacy model of preventing identity joining, but it unfortunately leaks information about user behavior that we might not want to leak: how long it has been since the user last used their browser. This is an unexpected thing to be able to learn from the API so I would be cautious adding it unless it's very necessary.

Note that this problem only exists for the event-level API. For the aggregate API I believe we can send along the time the report was "scheduled" to be sent, since no report can be tied to any individual (unlike the event level API).

However, I wonder how big a problem this is really? e.g. with a reporting window of 1, 7, 28 days you would need a user who converts between day 1-7 to be offline for >2 weeks before they are "mixed in" with users that convert in the 7-28 day window. I think this should be pretty rare.


Comment 4 (source ID 636179051) | Participant 2 | created 2020-05-29T20:31:51Z | updated 2020-05-29T20:31:51Z
Source: https://github.com/WICG/attribution-reporting-api/issues/47#issuecomment-636179051
Though I suppose in some sense you will be able to learn this with any implementation of the event level API to some extent, especially if you configure just a single reporting window. In the existing case if a report comes T time after the last reporting window you know (% some complexity with startup scheduling) that the user hasn't started the browser for T time, so maybe this is moot.

Still, I think I would be interested in seeing if this "implicit noise" is a problem in practice, since it does boost some of the privacy guarantees (like learning the true conversion delay).

Comment 5 (source ID 636620643) | Participant 1 | created 2020-06-01T05:28:24Z | updated 2020-06-01T05:28:24Z
Source: https://github.com/WICG/attribution-reporting-api/issues/47#issuecomment-636620643
> Though I suppose in some sense you will be able to learn this with any implementation of the event level API to some extent, especially if you configure just a single reporting window. In the existing case if a report comes T time after the last reporting window you know (% some complexity with startup scheduling) that the user hasn't started the browser for T time, so maybe this is moot.

Yeah, this is why I didn't consider it a new risk. We could always somewhat mitigate the problem by adding some random delay to firing off the report even after the browser is restarted.

You are right that in practice the cross-window case should be pretty rare. If we think the value of being 100% accurate outweighs the potential privacy risks, I'd still prefer this if possible.

> Note that this problem only exists for the event-level API. For the aggregate API I believe we can send along the time the report was "scheduled" to be sent, since no report can be tied to any individual (unlike the event level API).

That's great to hear. 

Comment 6 (source ID 639775341) | Participant 2 | created 2020-06-05T20:14:08Z | updated 2020-06-05T20:14:08Z
Source: https://github.com/WICG/attribution-reporting-api/issues/47#issuecomment-639775341
Yes I think the natural way to solve this is to introduce some noise to startup that hides browser-uptime a bit more. Right now we add uniform noise to simulate a shuffle, but it might make sense to alter it to be exponential noise, with the key property that it has an unbounded tail, so a user always has _some_ plausible deniability that they got really unlucky but were actually online.

Right now Chrome's uniform delay is between [0 and 5 minutes](https://source.chromium.org/chromium/chromium/src/+/master:content/browser/conversions/conversion_policy.cc;drc=bdab6517e19d8d2e81ae45d93fd4d5109d60e195;l=89), so maybe Exponential[1/3] minutes is a reasonable (somewhat conservative) starting point so the mean delay is 3 minutes and there is only a ~3% chance a report will be delayed more than 10 minutes at startup.

The only problem with this approach is that it bunches up reports a bit more than the uniform noise we have currently (lower variance), so timing attacks may be more effective to join impressions from different publishers. We should weigh these two approaches or maybe consider summing the noise from two noise sources to get best of both worlds.

Comment 7 (source ID 641730406) | Participant 1 | created 2020-06-10T05:27:16Z | updated 2020-06-10T05:27:16Z
Source: https://github.com/WICG/attribution-reporting-api/issues/47#issuecomment-641730406
If we label the conversion window, I think we would be tolerant of a wider delay than Exponential[1/3]. We're not trying to figure out when people's browsers are back online; we just want to be able to assign conversions to the right bucket. What do you think?

Comment 8 (source ID 642295879) | Participant 2 | created 2020-06-10T22:15:41Z | updated 2020-06-10T22:15:41Z
Source: https://github.com/WICG/attribution-reporting-api/issues/47#issuecomment-642295879
It seems reasonable to me, but one problem with wider delays is that it has a chance of perpetually delaying conversions from users that use the browser for very short periods of time before closing it (e.g. via Android killing the process). We will likely need to tune some of the parameters with data to make sure we're making the right trade-offs here.

Comment 9 (source ID 642847263) | Participant 1 | created 2020-06-11T18:09:37Z | updated 2020-06-11T18:09:37Z
Source: https://github.com/WICG/attribution-reporting-api/issues/47#issuecomment-642847263
That makes sense. Do you think that will give us enough protections to include the attribution window in the conversion report? 

Comment 10 (source ID 642855694) | Participant 2 | created 2020-06-11T18:27:38Z | updated 2020-06-11T18:27:38Z
Source: https://github.com/WICG/attribution-reporting-api/issues/47#issuecomment-642855694
Yes I think it should provide enough protection (just my own opinion). If we can we should validate with real-world testing to see if the data is really necessary though, as I think even without this you should be able to estimate the window with pretty high accuracy.

@johnivdel FYI. 

Comment 11 (source ID 888496625) | Participant 3 | created 2021-07-28T17:42:14Z | updated 2021-07-28T17:42:14Z
Source: https://github.com/WICG/attribution-reporting-api/issues/47#issuecomment-888496625
Following up on this:

We've gone in the direction on not adding substantial random delays to reports. In the Aggregate explainer reports are annotated with their `scheduled_report_time`.

For parity between the two, it seems useful to also send the scheduled_report_time for event level reports. 

This would also be helpful for debugging as it lets the reporting endpoint know what state the browser was working with sending the report.

As noted above in some scenarios you may be learning additional information than before (e.g. a report in the 7 day window that got reported on day 40 because the browser was shutdown can now be tied back to the 7 day window), but this should not affect the worst/"standard" case because the report time is derived from the impression-side data.

Not really true, because if someone contacts you (via Contact Us Page), the visitor is doing an action on his own behalf.
There are many discussions about adding a checkbox to a form (like this), some of them say yes, most of them say no.
The more, because the standard contact form in OpenCart has no further actions combined (e.g. answering through the system, or assigning it to an order, or doing more like in a CRM).

And finally, 
1. IF there would be a checkbox, the consent has to be stored! 
2. And the customer/visitor should be able to withdraw his consent.

General: a contact form is something every visitor should know that further actions are done electronically.
No more consent is required.

More helpfully would be an additional text (with link) what this form can be used for - and the link points to the Privacy Statement.

See also Article 6 GDPR

But (!), if the contact form would have required fields like phone number, company name etc. > then a Checkbox is required.

Issue body:
### Describe the issue

Plan gives the following error for new installs as of December 30th 2019.
```
[ERROR]: [Plan] Plan Requires internet access on first run to download GeoLite2 Geolocation database.
```

This causes the geolocation of the plugin to not function.

### Additional information

MaxMind have changed their distribution model on a very short notice by [posting a blog post on December 18](https://blog.maxmind.com/2019/12/18/significant-changes-to-accessing-and-using-geolite2-databases/) - stating the change is due to having to comply with The California Consumer Privacy Act (CCPA)

The changes mentioned in the blog post include disabling public distribution of the GeoIP2 database and change of license.

----

An account must be created to get a distribution key for the database. (By the developer)

To solve the issue on client side, MaxMind eula acceptance policy setting needs to be introduced. - The EULA can be found here: https://www.maxmind.com/en/geolite2/eula

To comply with the eula, the GeoIP database needs to be updated on a regular basis (point 3 under Additional Restrictions).

----

Unfortunately this will take a while to fix, sorry for any inconvenience. Temporary solution is to obtain a copy of GeoIP2 database from MaxMind and placing `GeoIP.dat` in the Plan plugin folder.

GDPR consent must be freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous, by a clear affirmative action.

> ‘consent’ of the data subject means any freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous indication of the data subject’s wishes by which he or she, by a statement or by a clear affirmative action, signifies agreement to the processing of personal data relating to him or her

All subscriptions are double opt-in, and as such the person entering an email address has to click the button that says, 'Yes, I want to receive email updates', under the paragraph, 'You've signed up to receive email updates from Wellcome Collection. Issue body:
user Jtuttle found a major 'hole' in geoprivacy...

from their post on http://www.inaturalist.org/posts/6518-a-new-way-to-add-observations#activity_comment_548803:

_the locational privacy issue I'm referring to is this: For anyone I follow, when she/he posts several observations with location obscured or private, the _actual_ locations, down to the address and/or coordinates, are listed beneath the set of observations in my dashboard. So I have to assume that this is occurring with others for _my_ obscured/private observations as well. For example, if my husband uses the app (and probably also the website) to upload observations made at our home address, even if he has made the location obscured or private, our home address will display underneath his observations in my dashboard (e.g., "See whiteoak's observations from {FULL ADDRESS}...")! When I go to individual observations, the location is obscured or blocked, but the location information is still right there on my dashboard. If I upload obscured or private observations via the website and enter my own location name (e.g., "Chatham County", but not otherwise overriding the coordinates pulled from the photo), I _think_ it gets around this issue, but I'm not really sure of that._

I just checked this and it is true. it doesn't show the address when i look but does show the street name. See screenshot below:

![image](https://cloud.githubusercontent.com/assets/7171475/16275330/8e8f4dfc-3877-11e6-8373-5cc0f2c2547c.png)

here's the observation:

http://www.inaturalist.org/observations/3493779

![image](https://cloud.githubusercontent.com/assets/7171475/16275383/c47378da-3877-11e6-95af-0631b7d2f631.png)

I just checked by viewing my account from a different account and it is true for observations I've made and obscured at my home as well. In this case it doesn't matter because I literally live on 'main street' of a state capital (albeit a small one) and that is all it says for mine, so not a big deal there. But for a small, short street it could be a much bigger issue.


Issue discussion (chronological; participant names pseudonymized within the case):
Comment 1 (source ID 227846316) | Participant 2 | created 2016-06-22T19:08:19Z | updated 2016-06-22T19:08:19Z
Source: https://github.com/inaturalist/inaturalist/issues/1012#issuecomment-227846316
The only thing we do to the "place guess" or "locality notes" when you obscure the coordinates is strip leading numbers, and that's the way it's been (by design) since the days before we had a performative way to access more conventional place names. Think about how one could deal with this problem: if you have an arbitrary string of text, how are you supposed to choose what parts are very specific and what parts aren't? "1234 Bogus St., Oakland, CA" is pretty well structured and we could remove the street from that, but what about "1234 The Cedars Oakland/Orinda Califarnia" or worse,  "Oakland, CA, the only red house on Bogus St., behind the rosemary bush by the garage"? Free, user-editable text is hard for machines to make sense of, and while we can sort of control the street addresses the apps generate, we can't absolutely stop people from entering very specific locality information that we simply cannot parse. And if you think my made-up examples are obtuse, here are some real place guesses:
- 209-1 Dogok-ri, Maepo-eup Danyang-gun, Chungcheongbuk-do
- Kepler track above Iris Burn in beech forest
- Thalkirchner Straße 240 81371 München
- wind turbine
- -47.20516       167.681383 (yes, people put coordinates in this field)

All that being said, these days we _could_ treat the `place_guess` in the same way that we do `private_latitude`, while still showing _some_ textual description of the place in the form of names of the admin-level places that contain the coordinates. But even then the system is imperfect when the true coordinates are right at the edge of the obscuration cell and revealing the name of the containing places gives the viewer a very exact idea of where the true coordinates are.

My point here is that while we could perhaps improve the situation, perfection is impossible, so I would not describe this as a "major hole". As we've tried to say from the beginning of the debates over revealing coordinates, if you really don't want to disclose information, don't post it to the Internet. We try to do what we can, but we can't stop people from revealing locations _and_ allow them to communicate openly.


Comment 2 (source ID 227854065) | Participant 1 | created 2016-06-22T19:40:00Z | updated 2016-06-22T19:40:00Z
Source: https://github.com/inaturalist/inaturalist/issues/1012#issuecomment-227854065
I know the system isn't perfect and isn't meant for 'super top secret'
anything. Maybe major hole is excessive. However, in this case it seems
quite clear to me at least that the downsides of sharing that sort of info
in the dashboard far outweigh the upsides. Why even have the place guess in
the dashboard notification at all? If I want to see where my friend
observed something, I click on it. Then all obscuring rules apply. Removing
that little text string would offer a lot more geoprivacy without a real
downside that I see.

Overall, I don't understand the sentiment "if you really don't want to
disclose information, don't post it to the Internet". I use websites for
all sorts of variably personal information... bank accounts, credit card
numbers sent to Amazon, private email, semi-private Facebook posts,
whatever. Perhaps more relevant, I've posted a LOT of private biodiversity
data to the Internet via NatureServe Biotics. My point isn't that iNat
should replace BIOTICS but if you have a button that says 'private
location' it seems to me that it's best to take reasonable non odious
efforts to keep the data private. Like not posting that seemingly
unnecessary string of text on the dashboard. There's certainly a happy
medium between 'location says private but anyone who tries can easily see
it' and the obnoxious 12 step authentication and security questions stupid
bank websites have. And this issue isn't stopping people from revealing
locations... this is people revealing locations without necessarily knowing
it. At least in the case of two users (that other person and me) there was
information being shared that the user wasn't aware was being shared.

More broadly, I've lately been discussing iNaturalist with a lot of really
wonderful ecologists, scientists, and land managers. It's a hard sell to
get people to use inat when they aren't tech types, despite the fact that
it's probably the most powerful tool for naturalists since field notebooks
were invented, but interest is starting to rise. However almost EVERY time
the conversation comes up, geoprivacy comes up as a concern. Concern about
species prone to collection but also brought up when proposing the idea
that we can use iNat to help landowners learn about their land. If I visit
a wetland on private land, iNat is a wonderful way to collect data that can
easily and quickly be provided to the landowner for their own knowledge,
education, and enjoyment of the biodiversity on their land. The landowner
can add to it too, or can post things and share them with us for ID help.
The data will also be shared with the rest of the world - except the
location will be obscured. Vermont has a ton of rural roads with just one
or two homes along them and privacy leaks like this are dealbreakers for
probably thousands of people here who want a reasonable measure of privacy
(else they wouldn't live on a road with just two houses on it). In my mind,
if a few small changes mean a potential flowering of the scientific
community (which means much better ID help and a stronger community) as
well as a wide expansion of the ability to use iNat for land management and
private lands issues, it seems worth allowing this little bit of 'mission
creep' to the site. But of course that's your call, not mine.

I know I kind of have a history of requesting bizzare obscure features that
like, no one else ever will use but I can tell you this is different. I've
talked to a lot of current and potential users... not in a seditious way
but just casually... and this stuff comes up more often than I can count.
In the least I think it's worthy of further discussion... though since I'm
not sure what forum is best for that I will leave it at this for now:
stronger (but not obscenely secret) geoprivacy means more data for everyone.

Thanks, as always!

Issue body:
### Is your proposal related to a problem?

Some users want to auto-delete their post and/or comments after a period of time to avoid potential brigading, stalking, doxxing and other abuse.

### Describe the solution you'd like

A compromise between content deletion for privacy reasons and maintaining content for the community:

**_Allow posts to be anonymized after a period of time._**

This should be opt-in. The time limit before content anonymization could be set by the developers to maintain a universal standard, by the instance admins or the users themselves. There should be a warning for inexperienced users that this only deletes content on the lemmy network and does not "scrub" it from the internet.

### Describe alternatives you've considered

- Manually deleting comments and posts
- Using scripts like on reddit
- Not using lemmy or social media for privacy reasons

### Additional context

Original discussion
https://github.com/LemmyNet/lemmy/issues/2415

> My personal reasoning for this is just annoyance; the main page of an app I use for extended periods of time, changing based on what I've been browsing, annoys me.
>
>However, there is also a privacy issue at play: an eavesdropper can see what you've been browsing if they manage to look at your screen when you open a new tab.

>I understand that for a lot of people this may be a wanted feature. I just don't see why it can't be toggled on and off. So, please, add such an option to this otherwise awesome app.

## Type

- Feature

## Problem description

GDPR is almost there.
It is our task to provide solutions in Fork CMS for when a data leak has occurred.

1. User sessions must be deleted.

2. Users must reset their password.
When a data leak has occurred (database credentials leaked, ...),

Until they have reset their password, using a received "reset your password" mail.

Issue body:
In https://github.com/pypa/warehouse/pull/4468 we've started blocking new passwords (via registration, reset, or password change) that have previously been in a data breach of a compromised website. However, that validation currently only occurs server side, it would be nice to also have it occur client side.

This can happen in two ways:

* Have the client JS hit the HIBP API directly, effectively re-implementing the logic that exists in the Python code.
* Have the client JS hit a private API endpoint on Warehouse, that calls into the logic that exists there.
  * If we do this, what should this API look like? Do we want to just send the password over the wire (since that's going to happen on submit anyways?), do we want to prehash it with sha1 and send that over the wire? Or do we want to reimplement the HIBP api in Warehouse? (this would only prevent leaking our users PII via additional http requests to an external service).

Of course, the other question is whether we want to do this or not. It's hard to do it without either reimplementing logic, or sending the password to Warehouse as the user is typing it, neither of which are ideal. Maybe having this validation happen only server side is ok?

The service `payum` is created thanks to a factory `payum.builder` managed by a series of `addMethodCall` into `Payum\Bundle\PayumBundle\DependencyInjection\Compiler\BuildConfigsPass`.
So if you want to override a specific default config by adding a default one you can build a `CompilerPass` like this one :

```
<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

namespace App\DependencyInjection\Compiler;

use Symfony\Component\DependencyInjection\Compiler\CompilerPassInterface;
use Symfony\Component\DependencyInjection\ContainerBuilder;

final class PayumGatewayConfigOverride implements CompilerPassInterface
{
    /** @var array */
    private $gatewayConfigs;

    /**
     * @param array $gatewayConfigs
     */
    public function __construct(array $gatewayConfigs)
    {
        $this->gatewayConfigs = $gatewayConfigs;
    }

    /**
     * {@inheritDoc}
     */
    public function process(ContainerBuilder $container)
    {
        $builder = $container->getDefinition('payum.builder');
        foreach ($this->gatewayConfigs as $gatewayName => $factoryConfig) {
            $builder->addMethodCall('addGatewayFactoryConfig', [$gatewayName, $factoryConfig]);
        }
    }
}

```

Then use this `CompilerPass` into your `src/Kernel.php` :

```
protected function build(ContainerBuilder $container)
    {
        $container->addCompilerPass(new PayumGatewayConfigOverride([
            'stripe_checkout' => [
                'sca_flow' => true,
                'payum.template.obtain_token' => '@SyliusPayum/Action/Stripe/obtainCheckoutToken.html.twig',
            ],
        ]));
        parent::build($container);
    }
```

Maybe we can add a new feature to `SyliusPayumBundle` to handle this kind of specific overrides, something based on a `sylius_payum` config for exemple.

Issue body:
# Information

What data does GPDR Apply to:
 - Any file or database that has a person's name or an ID in it.

Terms:

    * Personal Data – anything that you could conceivably use to identify a person within a larger group. This is likely broader than you think they consider combining data to be personal. aka while being left handed necessarily call you out, being a left handed male making between 30k to 60k who lives in the village of Shropshire on Lee may well.


    * Profiling – learning anything about a person’s preferences or inclinations. Seems mostly concerned with predicting behavior or future actions.


    * Controller – if you’re reading this, most likely this means you. It’s whoever decides what to do with the data that’s been collected. If you run a website that uses any marketing or analytics services you’re a controller.


    * Processor – typically this is any company that the controller tells to handle their data for any purpose. If you run a website and use Google Analytics, Google is the processor as they are acting at your direction.

# How To

Personal data should be kept:

    – Accurate and up to date

    – Secured

    – Transparent about how it’s going to be used

    – Restricted to the minimum needed to do the job

So you should:

    * Review what you’re doing with any collected data- Track where you received it

    * Get consent (opt in) for using it

    * Have a plan for deleting stale or out of date data

For stale unstructured files consider using an automated application like the Data Transport Engine to continuously purge dangerous data.

Unless required by some other law (employment or real estate) – don’t collect any data about race, politics, religion, union status, health data, sex life or sexual orientation.

Unless you’re working for a legal organization you shouldn’t keep any data regarding convictions, or offenses about a person.

# People's Data Rights

In your online forms (or anywhere you collect data from people), provide:

    – Contact information for the company (and ideally the Data Privacy Officer)

    – Describe what you’re going to use the data for

    – List what categories of data you’re collecting

    – How long you’re going to keep the data

    – How to contact you about issues or to remove the data

    – If the data is going to be used for profiling and in general terms the logic involved.

    – You just need to do all this the first time, if they fill out a second form 30 seconds after the first we can assume they haven’t forgotten it all yet.

All of the above should be available even if you’re not collecting personal information.

People are allowed to ask if you have their data and you need to respond whether or not you do.

    * If you do have their personal data, you need to provide them on demand:

        – Why you have it

        – What categories of personal data you have

        – Who in your organization or third-parties accessed it (in particular if they were in another country)

        – How long you plan on keeping their data

        – That they’re able to request to have their data deleted or fixed as requested

        – Source of where data was obtained

        – That they have the right to lodge a complaint with the EU Commission if they’re displeased with your response.

        – Unless something weird is going on, provide the data electronically

        – Don’t compromise other people’s data while doing this

If any of the following apply, you need to be able to remove their data from your system ‘without undue delay’ which while they don’t come out and say it here, probably means within in 30 days.

    – They withdraw consent (aka they feel like it) and there’s not a legal reason to keep it

    – Data has been unlawfully processed (used for a purpose beyond what it was intended)

People can request the data that you have about them

    - The data should be machine readable (CSV, XLS, XML, JSON).

    - The data should be structured and the entire process automated if possible

People can opt out of entirely machine made decisions about themselves.

# Controller and Processor

You need to document what you’re doing to comply with GDPR and be and be able to prove that in cases where it’s not self evident.

If you’re routinely collecting data (and for sure if it’s special category or criminal data) you need to designate a person in the EU as your representative for these matters.

SO YOU SHOULD

Hire someone who resides in an EU country.

Services (Processors) that you (as the Controller) use need to be GDPR compliant.

Make sure all the services you use are GDPR compliant.

Most services should now have some page on their website that indicates their GDPR compliance status. On your own GDPR compliance page you should list and link to theirs.

You need to track what is happening with personal data across your organization and any services it goes to. Including to what purpose.

If you have less than 250 employees and aren’t collecting data every day and aren’t dealing with special categories or criminal data you don’t have to do do this.

If your countries supervising authority asks to see your GDPR homework, you need to show them.

Implement modern digital security methods.

    – Secure Data Storage

    – Entitlement reviews

    – Data Breach plans

Once you become aware of a data breach (loss of data control) you have 72 hours to notify the [supervisory authority](https://blog.varonis.com/gdpr-data-protection-authority-supervisory-listing/)

You need to tell people ‘without undue delay’ if their data has been breached.

Issue body:
Hi!

I have found with great interest this golang implementation of some of the concepts behind Magic Wormhole. As a user of the latter (and maintainer of the Debian package), I am happy to see other implementations pop up, especially if it means it's easier for others to share files and use those concepts.

Unfortunately, I am concerned with the current implementation of croc, as I explained in https://github.com/schollz/croc/issues/15#issuecomment-399301454

I see two main issues:

 * compatibility concerns
 * security concerns

Compatibility
----------------

While it's great croc reuses some concepts behind magic-wormhole, it doesn't exactly implement the same protocol. This means the problem space is fragmented: a user of croc can't talk with a user of wormhole and vice-versa, which makes it needlessly hard for users to talk to each other.

I understand the idea behind it: a different implementation means more decentralization, for example. But that doesn't mean it *has* to be a different implementation to be decentralized. Wormhole, out of the box, supports using different relay (e.g. "discovery") and transfer (e.g. "nat trasversal") servers and croc could still implement the wormhole protocol while not being dependent on @warner's infrastructure as a single point of failure (SPOF). In fact, he explicitly said it would be good if other projects would make use of different DNS aliases for those services so they can easily be switched to different backends if traffic would become unmanageable for his services. This is how the debian packages work: the transit server is patched to be `tcp:magic-wormhole-transit.debian.net:4001:priority=2.0` instead of the upstream `tcp:transit.magic-wormhole.io:4001`. Then on Debian's infrastructure, that DNS entry is just a pointer to the normal transit server. The relay server server is the same, however (`ws://relay.magic-wormhole.io:4000/v1`).

Implementing this would mean adding Wormhole support in croc, specifically the capability of talking with transit and, more importantly, relay servers so that croc would share the same key namespace as Wormhole.

Security
----------

But this would also require reimplementing the key exchange using PAKE instead of the home-grown, SHA256-based key exchanged. As I explained in my previous comments, I am unsure of the security properties of croc as it is done right now. A lot of care was given to the way Wormhole implements the key exchange: it uses a low-entropy ephemeral and weak key to establish a strong session key: that is the PAKE protocol which was published in multiple papers and seems to be solid at the cryptographic layer. I am not sure the SHA256-checksum croc implements has similar properties. For example, does it allow multiple attempts or does it bail on first try? Wouldn't it be possible for an attacker to build a rainbow table of all possible keys and just use that to access the files?

I haven't reviewed croc's security properties in details, so maybe my concerns are misplaced. But as a general principle, rolling out a different cryptosystem for another project seems an idea fraught with dangers that should generally be avoided. In that regard, I also think that PAKE exchange support should be implemented as well as the above network compatibility.

I hope this is useful for you and thanks for working on all of this!

Comment 1 (source ID 399542922) | Participant 2 | created 2018-06-22T18:46:00Z | updated 2018-06-22T18:46:00Z
Source: https://github.com/schollz/croc/issues/71#issuecomment-399542922
@anarcat 

As to compatibility with *magic-wormhole* that was never really a goal for *croc*. When I started building *croc* I couldn't find good documentation or source code on how the *magic-wormhole* relay worked, so I gave up trying to port it. 

As to security, you're right that *croc* is not as secure as *magic-wormhole* in general. There are several points of vulnerability in a program like this:

- MITM attacker (between sender/receiver and relay)
- Evil relay attacker (the relay can try to decrypt things with the knowledge it has)
- Brute force attacker (someone can spam "code phrases" against the relay trying to trick a sender into sending stuff to them)

AFAIK PAKE will help against MITM and the Evil Relay but not against the Brute force - that is neither can determine the encryption key because that was generated using PAKE between the final recipient and sender. However someone could easily just spam the relay with code phrases hoping to get one right, which is only mitigated by a rate limiter.

I could see that someone could place a MITM in the *croc* encrypted stream (or a nefarious relay could do this) and they could eventually decode the stream by trying all 5 million possibilities of code phrases. Eventually they could decode it. However, if you use custom code phrases it becomes harder and only the relay could probably decipher it (because the relay has the hash so they could presumably do a rainbow attack). Currently because of the time window for the transfer is so short, I was never really worried about this.

## Croc 2.0

I think something better is worth striving for, something that could handle all three such cases.

One thing that comes to mind is a public-private key + code phrase protocol. It would work like this:

1. A generates public/private key (Apub, Apriv) and sends to the relay a code phrase + Apub.
2. B generates a public/private key (Bpub,Bpriv) and sends to the relay the same code phrase + Bpub.
3. The relay tells A that Bpub is interested in downloading the file and asks if thats okay. A says okay.
4. The relay tells B that Apub will send the file and B says okay.
5. Once both parties agree, then A encrypts the file against Bpub.

In this case, there is an extra interaction - the sender is asked if they want to send the file to the recipient. That means that brute force attacks won't work because if you have multiple recipients the sender could verify with the recipient what their public key is. Of course this also prevents MITM and nefarious relays because the private keys are never shared, so I believe it is better than PAKE.

@anarcat Sorry, compatibility with wormhole was never a goal. I put on the readme that this is "similar in spirit and design" but I really mean *similar* design and not exact. I'll just remove that altogether.

I think the new changes do address your concerns but I'm happy to hear otherwise. Here's specifically what I thought your concerns were:

> For example, does it allow multiple attempts or does it bail on first try? 

The transfer is now double-authenticated with user-specific keys. So you can just check with your recipient that you are encrypting for their key. If not, you can bail and nothing is transferred. 

> Wouldn't it be possible for an attacker to build a rainbow table of all possible keys and just use that to access the files?

This is no longer possible. The data is encrypted using AES-256 with an encryption key that is encrypted with the public key / private key of the recipient / sender. The private keys are never shared so only the recipient can decrypt the data. 

An attacker could still try to spam all possible code phrases to to pose as a recipient. However, the sender can easily discover this as the public key of the fake recipient won't match the one of the real recipient they want to send to. AFAIK, this doesn't exist in wormhole. I think that wormhole just subverts this attack by rate-limiting and actually there is no way to guarantee that the recipient is really the true recipient (its basically whoever gets to the code phrase first).

In fact, public/private keys actually provide *more* security than PAKE - in addition to encrypting the file for a single recipient they also provide a means to authenticate the recipient (wormhole cannot do this - anyone with a code phrase could receive the file! On 2018-06-27 15:22:06, Zack wrote:
> Key signing here is unnecessary, because the public key is authenticated by the source (the person who generated it) over the channel of communication that is already open between the two people (i.e. the phone/text). I.e. you can just tell someone your public key and see if matches. Public/private keys, by their nature, assures that the public key corresponds only to one private key, which cannot be generated by a MITM, and only exists on the recipient machine.

This is the problem right here. Croc is introduced like this in the
README:

> croc allows any two computers to directly and securely transfer files
> and folders. When sending a file, croc generates a random code phrase
> which must be shared with the recipient so they can receive the
> file. The code phrase encrypts all data and metadata and also serves
> to authorize the connection between the two computers in a
> intermediary relay. The relay connects the TCP ports between the two
> computers and does not store any information (and all information
> passing through it is encrypted).

Nowhere does it mention that public keys must be authenticated as
well. At best, deep below in the README, does it say that public keys
serve as "a second method of authentication" and gently encourages users
to authenticate those keys. I have a long experience working with public
key systems, mostly with TLS, X509, GnuPG and OpenPGP, and I can tell
you: no one will ever do that.

So the security of the system entirely resides over the original short
key exchange, which does not follow established standards (PAKE).

By the way, Wormhole also uses strong session keys, which you can
authenticate if you really want to. Wormhole does not do that because
it's inconvenient and would defeat the purpose of the lighter key
exchange, which is to leverage an easy to use key to establish a
stronger shared secret.

If you bypass all of this and simply relies on users to exchange their
public keys, you are missing the point of Wormhole and PAKE
altogether. You are creating a system with unclear security properties
which, at best, introduce a false sense of security for users and at
worse, exposes vulnerable users to serious data breaches.

Either you rely on the short code and implement PAKE, in which case you
don't need to validate public keys, or you implement public keys and
then users need to validate public keys. Doing half of both is the worst
of both worlds and needlessly exposes your users to serious security
issues.

Here's an evil relay scenario. The short code is easy to guess. Say A wants to send to B through the relay. A generates a code phrase. The wormhole says that there is only one guess at a time. Does this mean that the wormhole relay only allows a single transfer to happen a time?

All of these are business processes that you can build on top of allauth....

@IrfanBaqui @altsang  @rlisagor 
the stormpath article 
https://stormpath.com/blog/secure-your-rest-api-right-way

1) Speed
Best practices say to encrypt your passwords in the database to limit a potential data breach.  This increases overhead for each request when authenticating a user.  Unique API keys authentication skips the hashing step and therefore speeds up your calls

2) At Stormpath, we use what we call “Url62” for UUID generation.  This is basically a globally unique generated byte array encoded using 62 ‘url-safe’ characters.  This allows IDs to be safely used in URLs without having to worry about encoding problems

and the way they generate the key is also interesting.
they download file with the key, so no copy pasting is involved 
and they even assign read permission to only current user
https://stormpath.com/blog/top-six-reasons-use-api-keys-and-how

## Privacy Policy
This privacy policy has been compiled to better serve those who are concerned with how their 'Personally Identifiable Information' (PII) is being used online. PII, as described in US privacy law and information security, is information that can be used on its own or with other information to identify, contact, or locate a single person, or to identify an individual in context. Please read our privacy policy carefully to get a clear understanding of how we collect, use, protect or otherwise handle your Personally Identifiable Information in accordance with our website.

### What personal information do we collect from the people that visit our blog, website or app?

When ordering or registering on our site, as appropriate, you may be asked to enter your name, email address or other details to help you with your experience.

### When do we collect information?

We collect information from you when you register on our site or enter information on our site.

### How do we use your information?

We may use the information we collect from you when you register, make a purchase, sign up for our newsletter, respond to a survey or marketing communication, surf the website, or use certain other site features in the following ways:

      • To personalize your experience and to allow us to deliver the type of content in which you are most interested.
      • To send periodic emails regarding new hangouts or study groups.

### Do we use 'cookies'?

We do not use cookies for tracking purposes.

### Third-party disclosure

We do not sell, trade, or otherwise transfer to outside parties your Personally Identifiable Information unless we provide users with advance notice. This does not include website hosting partners and other parties who assist us in operating our website, conducting our business, or serving our users, so long as those parties agree to keep this information confidential. We may also release information when it's release is appropriate to comply with the law, enforce our site policies, or protect ours or others' rights, property or safety. 

### Third-party links

We do not include or offer third-party products or services on our website.

### Google

Google's advertising requirements can be summed up by Google's Advertising Principles. They are put in place to provide a positive experience for users. https://support.google.com/adwordspolicy/answer/1316548?hl=en 

### California Online Privacy Protection Act

CalOPPA is the first state law in the nation to require commercial websites and online services to post a privacy policy. The law's reach stretches well beyond California to require any person or company in the United States (and conceivably the world) that operates websites collecting Personally Identifiable Information from California consumers to post a conspicuous privacy policy on its website stating exactly the information being collected and those individuals or companies with whom it is being shared. - See more at: http://consumercal.org/california-online-privacy-protection-act-caloppa/#sthash.0FdRbT51.dpuf

According to CalOPPA, we agree to the following:

- Users can visit our site anonymously.
- Once this privacy policy is created, we will add a link to it on our home page or as a minimum, on the first significant page after entering our website.
- Our Privacy Policy link includes the word 'Privacy' and can easily be found on the page specified above.

You will be notified of any Privacy Policy changes:
      • On our Privacy Policy Page
Can change your personal information:
      • By logging in to your account

### How does our site handle Do Not Track signals?
We honor Do Not Track signals and Do Not Track, plant cookies, or use advertising when a Do Not Track (DNT) browser mechanism is in place.

### Does our site allow third-party behavioral tracking?
It's also important to note that we do not allow third-party behavioral tracking

### COPPA (Children Online Privacy Protection Act)

When it comes to the collection of personal information from children under the age of 13 years old, the Children's Online Privacy Protection Act (COPPA) puts parents in control. The Federal Trade Commission, United States' consumer protection agency, enforces the COPPA Rule, which spells out what operators of websites and online services must do to protect children's privacy and safety online.

We do not specifically market to children under the age of 13 years old.

### Fair Information Practices

The Fair Information Practices Principles form the backbone of privacy law in the United States and the concepts they include have played a significant role in the development of data protection laws around the globe. Understanding the Fair Information Practice Principles and how they should be implemented is critical to comply with the various privacy laws that protect personal information.

In order to be in line with Fair Information Practices we will take the following responsive action, should a data breach occur:
      • Within 7 business days
We will notify the users via in-site notification
      • Within 7 business days

We also agree to the Individual Redress Principle which requires that individuals have the right to legally pursue enforceable rights against data collectors and processors who fail to adhere to the law. This principle requires not only that individuals have enforceable rights against data users, but also that individuals have recourse to courts or government agencies to investigate and/or prosecute non-compliance by data processors.

### CAN SPAM Act

The CAN-SPAM Act is a law that sets the rules for commercial email, establishes requirements for commercial messages, gives recipients the right to have emails stopped from being sent to them, and spells out tough penalties for violations.

We collect your email address in order to:
      • Send information, respond to inquiries, and/or other requests or questions
      • Market to our mailing list or continue to send emails to our clients after the original transaction has occurred.

To be in accordance with CANSPAM, we agree to the following:
      • Not use false or misleading subjects or email addresses.
      • Identify the message as an advertisement in some reasonable way.
      • Include the physical address of our business or site headquarters.
      • Monitor third-party email marketing services for compliance, if one is used.
      • Honor opt-out/unsubscribe requests quickly.
      • Allow users to unsubscribe by using the link at the bottom of each email.

### Expected behavior
Setting config.viewProfileDates should not only remove the date axis from the profile view, but the tooltip should also not show 'start date' or any specific dates.

### Actual behavior
The top x-axis hides the dates properly but hovering over a data point shows the date in the tooltip.

### Steps to reproduce behavior
1. Configure env to viewProfileDates = false
2. Open a profile from a cohort
3. Observe: profile plot does not show a date on a timeline, however, tooltip does.

Reason for this restriction:
The rule about PHI is that names, SSN, full date of birth,  and all dates of medical services is considerred protected information. We made the profile specifically so it wouldn't show any of that information (showed age relative to an index 0, where you didn't know the index date so it was 'safe'). ## 📝 Provide a description of the new feature

_What is the expected behavior of the proposed feature?  What is the scenario this would be used?_

I find myself frequently juggling with URLs which get pasted to the clipboard and then inserted into some browser-window, so (just as a proof-of-concept) I wrote a little tool (independ of PT) which observes the clipboard and if it finds one, suggests to open - which I can then accept of neglect. I was unsure whether this would be practical of if I would get bombarded with prompts that I don't use. But after a few wks of using this, I still like the idea and would like to take it further - and that is beyond my level of knowledge, beyond the capabilities of the environment I worked on etc., and it also feels like PT Run would be a more obvious home for such functionality. Which is why I opened this issue.

I suggest that PT Run should observe the clipboard and if it finds a new entry commencing with `http[s]:`, it should display a dialog that offers a choice of browsers (either as "found on the system" or configured by the user) which could open this URL. The dialog also has a Cancel-Button. Ideally there should be a configurable timeout after which the dialog will close.

As a milder form (if the observer is disabled through a config-option), it would be good if when entering such URLs into PTs Search-Field there was a choice of browser to open the URL with.

If you'd like to see this feature implemented, add a 👍 reaction to this post.

Issue retrieved at: 2026-10-18T19:11:35.417324+00:00 Issue last updated at: 2022-03-30T13:46:38Z Title at retrieval: Anonymous Consent [master] Status at retrieval: closed Retrieved issue comments: 4/4 Issue body: Master ticket for implementing Anonymous Consent. Project is https://github.com/SAP/cloud-commerce-spartacus-storefront/projects/35 Issue discussion (chronological; participant names pseudonymized within the case): Comment 1 (source ID 517213271) | Participant 2 | created 2019-08-01T09:49:46Z | updated 2020-06-23T14:32:40Z Source: https://github.com/SAP/spartacus/issues/3800#issuecomment-517213271 # Anonymous consents ## Basic idea The idea is to display a consent dialog to an anonymous user, once they visit Spartacus. The dialog should contain a list of all anonymous consents (anonymous consents are the same as regular consents, but with `exposed` property set to `true`; see the last column [here](https://github.tools.sap/cx-commerce/spartacussampledataaddon/pull/7/files#diff-dba233f251920eb8938641e1468fdef2R14)) and an option to give/withdraw each consent. The anonymous user should be able to close and re-open the dialog at any time, in case they change their mind. The anonymous consents are exchanged between Spartacus and the server in a stateless way, using `X-Anonymous-Consents` HTTP header. With each request to the server, the `X-Anonymous-Consents` should be sent to the server. When an anonymous user gives/withdraws a consent, the corresponding consent's `consentState` field is changed to reflect the new state. (if we want to support the case when the user logs out and the previously given anonymous consents are restored, the only way to do that is to append the `X-Anonymous-Consents` header with **every** request, not just anonymous ones.). ## Limitations and edge cases There are three edge cases: 1. Moving from Anonymous User to Logged In Customer - once the user logs in, the consents that were given as an anonymous user are ignored, and the consents of the currently logged in user are restored, see ["Moving from Anonymous User to Logged In Customer"](https://help.sap.com/viewer/9d346683b0084da2938be8a285c0c27a/1905/en-US/fbf047927e8845038581d49c22d37bc3.html). 2. The case when a user is moving from an anonymous user to a registered user, the consents _should_ be transferred (see [Moving from Anonymous User to Registered Customer](https://help.sap.com/viewer/9d346683b0084da2938be8a285c0c27a/1905/en-US/fbf047927e8845038581d49c22d37bc3.html)). E.g. if an anonymous user gave a tracking consent, and then the user decided to register, the tracking consent should be _automatically given on the back-end_ once the user registers. However, this is not working as intended when using the OCC APIs. [? Bill: Pawel from Ray says this is an accelerator issue, and that they can't do anything until it's resolved (if they need to do something at all)]. 3. In the old accelerator, when an authenticated user logs out, the previously given consents are restored (when the user was anonymous, i.e. was not logged in). See ["Moving from Logged In Customer to Anonymous User When Logging Out"](https://help.sap.com/viewer/9d346683b0084da2938be8a285c0c27a/1905/en-US/fbf047927e8845038581d49c22d37bc3.html). In order to support this, we need to keep the anonymous consents in the state even after the anonymous users decides to regiser/log in. ## Flow - User visits Spartacus for the first time - Spartacus pulls the anonymous consents from the API: `/users/anonymous/consenttemplates` - _NOTE_: this API endpoint only returns consents that are _exposed_ for an anonymous user, see the last column in [this impex](https://github.tools.sap/cx-commerce/c3po-legacy-spartacussampledataaddon/pull/7/files). - Once the anonymous consents are retrieved, put them into the state, and sync them with `localStorage`. - Use a different state slice than the regular consents. The reason for this is that when a user logs out, the whole `user` state slice is cleared. The state slice for anonymous consents should be a new feature state called e.g. `anonymous-consents`. - The anonymous consents dialog is presented to the user - it contains a list of all the anonymous consents with their corresponding state (given/withdrawn). If the user didn't even interact with a particular consent, the state of it should clearly indicate the fact that a consent is neither given nor withdrawn (there should be some kind of a neutral state, similar to the old accelerator, see the image below) - When to present the anonymous consents dialog to the user? - If the user didn't previously close it by clicking on an `x` button. This toggle information should be stored in the `dialogs.anonymous-consents`. - If an anonymous user has already given a consent, but there's a new version of that consent available on the server, the dialog should be displayed again to the user. [? What's the `consentState` of it? Should the state be the same as before, e.g. if it was given before, should the `consentState` be `GIVEN`? Or it should `null`, because it's the new version?] - The user should be able to re-open the anonymous consents dialog. [? There should a link somewhere that can open the dialog again. Maybe in the header/footer?] ## UI Pending. Some WIP wireframes can be seen [here](https://98qkkl.axshare.com/#g=1&p=m_anonymous_consent_behavior_on_page). ## Changes to the current consents implementation - The consent that is shown to the user while registering is not "wired" with the back-end; meaning that when the user visits the consent management page after registration, the state of the consent will not reflect the user's decision while registering. Once anonymous consents are pulled from the back-end, this consent can be retrieved from `localStorage` in the `register.component.ts` and wired, so that when a user registers, the consent's state is persisted and the user can see that the status of it on the consent management page. ## Implementation details and notes To see the flow in action, use [this postman collection](https://github.tools.sap/cx-commerce/postman-collections/blob/master/OCC%20Account%20Profile.postman_collection.json#L563), starting from the linked API call ("Anonymous consents - Get List"). To have the necessary anonymous consents in your local back-end, you can use [this impex](https://github.tools.sap/cx-commerce/c3po-legacy-spartacussampledataaddon/pull/7/files). - the anonymous consents received from the API are serialized in JSON format and URL encoded in UTF-8. To decode them, use JavaScript's `decodeURIComponent()`. When sending the anonymous consents back to the server, use `encodeURIComponent()`. _NOTE_ that these methods are **not** available in `SSR` mode. - When changing a consent's status, the `consentState` property of the corresponding consent should be changed: - When giving a consent, the `consentState` should have `GIVEN` string value. - When withdrawing a consent, the `consentState` should have `WITHDRAWN` string value. - In order for the server to understand the header that Spartacus is sending, **all** consents must be sent to the server, regardless of how many consents have changed. - In case an `X-Anonymous-Consents` header is _not_ sent to the server, and the request is for an anonymous user, the server will respond with all anonymous consents (but their status is going to be set to `null`) - An Angular's http interceptor (e.g.`AnonymousConsentsInterceptor`) should handle the exchange of `X-Anonymous-Consents` header between Spartacus and the server by storing/pulling the consents to/from `localStorage`. Please, consider the fact that the `Window` object is not available in `SSR` mode, thus making the `localStorage` API also not available in `SSR` mode. - The language change should not affect the anonymous consents state. The language of the consents should change, but not their `consentState` properties. An e2e test should cover this case. - The anonymous consents can leverage the processing/loading mechanism in Spartacus which will handle `loading`, `loaded` and `success` flags. - As consents might change on the back-end (e.g. there's an updated version), it might be necessary to check the response header for an updated JSON. ## Anonymous consent vs. "cookie" consent "Cookie" consent is not the topic here, this section is just a clarification. _A quick note about "cookie" being quoted in this section: we're probably not going to use the actual cookies as an authentication method and a way to track user's sessions._ The cookie banner in the old accelerator looks like this: Looking at the old accelerator implementation, it seems that the "cookie" consent is not implemented using consents per se. "Cookie consent" is just a CMS component that's rendered on [a `jsp`](https://github.tools.sap/cx-commerce/b2caccelerator/blob/develop/yacceleratorstorefront/web/webroot/WEB-INF/views/responsive/pages/consent/cookienotification.jsp#L11) page. The consent text is pulled from a `*properties` file using a translation key. After giving the consent (or maybe even just closing the cookie banner), a [javascript is activated](https://github.tools.sap/cx-commerce/b2caccelerator/blob/edeead005039963f24b7b25f24fd9f54cdc05c52/yacceleratorstorefront/web/webroot/WEB-INF/_ui-src/responsive/lib/ybase-0.1.0/js/acc.cookienotification.js) that places a cookie in the browser. There's no actual way of declining the cookie, and the decision is enforced to the user. We could improve this by leveraging the actual consents: - pull a dedicated consent (could be exposed to anonymous users) with an ID of e.g. `STORE_USER_INFORMATION` (this requires from clients to put this consent as part of their "sample" data) - the result of the user's consent decision will be stored on the back-end (in case the user is logged in) - we can re-use the consents dialog for showing this "cookie" banner that we will implement as part of the `anonymous consents` effort - users can easily revoke the `STORE_USER_INFORMATION` consent from the consent management page More about the cookie consent issue [here](https://github.com/SAP/cloud-commerce-spartacus-storefront/issues/1323). ## Useful links - [Postman collection](https://github.tools.sap/cx-commerce/postman-collections/blob/master/OCC%20Account%20Profile.postman_collection.json#L563) - [Anonymous consents sample data](https://github.tools.sap/cx-commerce/c3po-legacy-spartacussampledataaddon/pull/7/files) - [wire frames](https://98qkkl.axshare.com/#g=1&p=m_anonymous_consent_behavior_on_page) - [Visuals](https://zpl.io/bAGG8me) - hybris help - [anonymous consent management](https://help.sap.com/viewer/9d346683b0084da2938be8a285c0c27a/1905/en-US/a9f387f70d484c19971aca001dc71bc5.html) and [main user cases](https://help.sap.com/viewer/9d346683b0084da2938be8a285c0c27a/1905/en-US/fbf047927e8845038581d49c22d37bc3.html) - Old accelerator - [https://electronics.dev-com-6.accdemo.b2c.ydev.hybris.com:9002/electronics/en/](https://electronics.dev-com-6.accdemo.b2c.ydev.hybris.com:9002/electronics/en/) - Back-end issues: [https://jira.hybris.com/browse/RAY-214](https://jira.hybris.com/browse/RAY-214) and [https://jira.hybris.com/browse/RAY-222](https://jira.hybris.com/browse/RAY-222) ## Tickets - The simorgh consent banner sets cookies to `www.bbc.com` whereas the pal sets them to `.bbc.com`. This causes weird behaviour where we read from 1 domain, but write to another. This means the cookie banner cant be dismissed in some cases

Simorgh sets cookies the same place that the pal does

Issue body:
**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**
GNL are making changes to how the Cookie Banner works in the EU/EEA (but not UK) - we need to make some changes as well.

**Describe the solution you'd like**
Currently, we display the cookie banner if the ckns_explicit cookie's value is not `1` (ie it is `0` or not set)

We now need to consider a value of 2 as also reflecting acceptance of the cookie banner.

**Describe alternatives you've considered**
N/A

**Implementation detail:**
We currently have [this function](https://github.com/bbc/simorgh/blob/latest/src/app/containers/ConsentBanner/CanonicalLogic/index.js#L30)
```js
const showCookieBanner = () =>
  Cookie.get(EXPLICIT_COOKIE) !== COOKIE_BANNER_APPROVED;
```

This may need to change to
```js
const EXPLICIT_COOKIE_ACCEPTED_VALUES = ['1', '2'];

const showCookieBanner = () =>
  !EXPLICIT_COOKIE_ACCEPTED_VALUES.includes(Cookie.get(EXPLICIT_COOKIE));
```

i.e. if `EXPLICIT_COOKIE` (ckns_explicit) isnt `1` or `2`, show the banner

I noticed that Gatsby's websites (gatsbyjs.org and gatsbyjs.com) save cookies without user consent – like `GA`.

Issue body:
### Preconditions
1. Reproduced on a Magento 2.2 EE with a custom theme based on luma

### Steps to reproduce
1. Enabled Cookie restriction mode (`bin/magento config:set web/cookie/cookie_restriction	1`) & cleanup cache
    * the cookie banner should now display in FO
2. With a clean profile (private navigation for example) do ***not*** clic on "OK" in this cookie banner
3. try to checkout anything

### Expected result
1. checkout should be fine

### Actual result
1. when validating the shipping page, the checkout is now blocked in an intermediate, empty, state
2. the error `TypeError: window.dataLayer is undefined` is displayed in JS console

While doing some analysis, I found that the dataLayer object is not created here `vendor/magento/module-google-tag-manager/view/frontend/web/js/google-tag-manager.js:40` if the banner has not be checked. Later in the code `window.dataLayer.push` is directly called and fail.

For now I've only wrapped those calls in conditions, but maybe it should be catched earlier. In attachments, you will find the patches I intend to test and use on `magento/google-tag-manager` module.
* [patch on Magento_GoogleTagManager/js/action/checkout](https://github.com/magento/magento2/files/1967840/mg_cookie.txt)
* [patch on Magento_GoogleTagManager/js/action/product-details](https://github.com/magento/magento2/files/1967841/mg_cookie2.txt)

Issue retrieved at: 2026-10-18T20:11:00.598701+00:00 Issue last updated at: 2022-12-22T00:01:21Z Title at retrieval: setValidityState doesn't work correctly on tab removal page Status at retrieval: closed Retrieved issue comments: 15/15 Issue body: Given: a removeUrl is set with `setSettings` and the user clicks "Remove" from the tab menu Expected: The Remove form button is not activated until `setValidityState(true)` is called Actual: The Remove form button is activated after a timeout no matter what. Subsequent calls to `setValidityState(false)` do not deactivate the form button I tested using the example code here: https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoftteams/platform/tabs/how-to/create-tab-pages/removal-page My specific code, I am using older js, not es6, but that shouldn't affect anything: ```html ``` Issue discussion (chronological; participant names pseudonymized within the case): Comment 1 (source ID 576110408) | Participant 2 | created 2020-01-20T05:17:49Z | updated 2020-01-20T05:18:48Z Source: https://github.com/OfficeDev/microsoft-teams-library-js/issues/303#issuecomment-576110408 @synth , When a user selects Remove from the tab's drop-down menu, Teams will load the optional removeUrl page (designated in your configuration page) into an IFrame. Here, the user is presented with a button loaded with the onClick() function that calls microsoftTeams.settings.setValidityState(true) and enables the Remove button located near the bottom of the removal page IFrame. Please try to set contentUrl within setSettings. Teams enables the Remove button after 5 seconds, even if your tab hasn't called setValidityState(). When the user selects Remove Teams removes the tab after 30 seconds regardless of whether your actions have completed. Comment 2 (source ID 576391020) | Participant 1 | created 2020-01-20T18:40:48Z | updated 2020-01-20T18:40:48Z Source: https://github.com/OfficeDev/microsoft-teams-library-js/issues/303#issuecomment-576391020 Hi @Trinetra-MSFT Thx for response. > Teams enables the Remove button after 5 seconds, even if your tab hasn't called setValidityState(). This is very strange. 5 seconds is a very short time. What's the point of having app's call setValidityState if it will have no effect after 5 seconds? I get that you probably want to allow end users to remove Tab regardless of app logic (like in case of app error). However, I feel either: 1. That there should be an alternative mechanism for end user to hard remove tab 2. Or, the documentation should not recommend app developers to call `setValidityState` as its confusing and has no ultimate effect. 3. Or, There should be a longer timeout to enable the remove button. Thx for your consideration Comment 3 (source ID 577162713) | Participant 2 | created 2020-01-22T12:42:17Z | updated 2020-01-22T12:42:17Z Source: https://github.com/OfficeDev/microsoft-teams-library-js/issues/303#issuecomment-577162713 @synth , What do you mean by removal of app logic? Below piece of code helps to remove the entire tab and all data which is configured in a channel. ``` microsoftTeams.settings.registerOnRemoveHandler((removeEvent) => { // Here you can designate the tab content to be removed and/or archived. microsoftTeams.settings.getSettings((settings) => { settings.contentUrl = "..." }); removeEvent.notifySuccess(); }); ``` Btw Teams will load the optional removeUrl page (designated in your configuration page) into an IFrame. when setValidityState is set to true it will enable remove button as configuration page loads. but if you have not enabled the setValidityState it will take some time for sure as mentioned in the document. Currently this is the only way to remove a tab from channel. Comment 4 (source ID 577358873) | Participant 1 | created 2020-01-22T19:57:32Z | updated 2020-01-22T19:57:32Z Source: https://github.com/OfficeDev/microsoft-teams-library-js/issues/303#issuecomment-577358873 @Trinetra-MSFT I'm referring to this: A user clicks "Manage Team", then clicks "Apps", then deletes the App. This causes (correctly) all the tabs to be removed from the team. However, the tab removal logic is not called during this flow. Comment 5 (source ID 577361403) | Participant 3 | created 2020-01-22T20:03:57Z | updated 2020-01-22T20:03:57Z Source: https://github.com/OfficeDev/microsoft-teams-library-js/issues/303#issuecomment-577361403 @synth, removing an app doesn’t actually cause all the tabs to be removed. They are simply hidden and get re-shown if/when the app is installed into the team again. Comment 6 (source ID 577484591) | Participant 1 | created 2020-01-23T03:07:56Z | updated 2020-01-23T03:07:56Z Source: https://github.com/OfficeDev/microsoft-teams-library-js/issues/303#issuecomment-577484591 Thanks for letting us know this. Is there documentation on this? Seems problematic. Companies will expect that uninstalling an app hard deletes all data. Imagine one user adds the app and installs several tabs. That user ends up leaving the org and the app is subsequently uninstalled. Then another user later installs the app...then all of the previous tabs are restored unbeknownst to the current user. In a team with a lot of channels, it would be near impossible to manage - let alone the compliance issues with the 3rd party app holding onto data it shouldn't (if the app is uninstalled). There should be a full app uninstall hook that notifies the app to clean up all of its component references and data. Comment 7 (source ID 577506704) | Participant 3 | created 2020-01-23T05:11:51Z | updated 2020-01-23T05:13:08Z Source: https://github.com/OfficeDev/microsoft-teams-library-js/issues/303#issuecomment-577506704 @synth, thank you for the feedback. We are aware of the asks for an app/tab removal hook and is something we will be looking into. It’s important to keep in mind that tabs in and of themselves do not store any data; they are just pointers to external sites which store the data (not that different from contextually relevant bookmarks). Data access, compliance, and retention policies need to be handled by the external sites. You should not be relying on Teams to do that for you. Comment 8 (source ID 577537988) | Participant 1 | created 2020-01-23T07:20:58Z | updated 2020-01-23T07:22:49Z Source: https://github.com/OfficeDev/microsoft-teams-library-js/issues/303#issuecomment-577537988 Thanks @ydogandjiev. It's good to know an app removal hook is on your radar. It's true the tab itself doesn't store any data, and it's us, as third parties, that are storing data. This is precisely the reason for a need for an app removal hook. In other words, the app removal hook can help 3rd parties to clean out data that should no longer be stored which follows international compliance requirements (gdpr, ccpa, etc). Comment 10 (source ID 1320277913) | Participant 1 | created 2022-11-18T16:52:12Z | updated 2022-11-18T16:52:12Z Source: https://github.com/OfficeDev/microsoft-teams-library-js/issues/303#issuecomment-1320277913 @Meghana-MSFT This seems like a bug not a feature request, which is why I posted here. Comment 11 (source ID 1321533401) | Participant 4 | created 2022-11-21T06:45:23Z | updated 2022-11-21T06:45:23Z Source: https://github.com/OfficeDev/microsoft-teams-library-js/issues/303#issuecomment-1321533401 Engineering team has considered this as a feature request. Comment 12 (source ID 1321568839) | Participant 1 | created 2022-11-21T07:28:56Z | updated 2022-11-21T07:28:56Z Source: https://github.com/OfficeDev/microsoft-teams-library-js/issues/303#issuecomment-1321568839 Hmm, the issue described here follows Microsoft's own documentation which does not work as described. I'm unclear how that is a feature request - the documentation itself describes it as an existing feature... Comment 13 (source ID 1321600532) | Participant 3 | created 2022-11-21T07:53:06Z | updated 2022-11-21T07:57:40Z Source: https://github.com/OfficeDev/microsoft-teams-library-js/issues/303#issuecomment-1321600532 Hi @synth, thank you for takin the time to report this issue. The specific behavior of setValidityState that you have described is by design. ## 🚀 Feature Proposal

In https://github.com/fastify/fastify/blob/d06287a9a612d218d26e3a94b248b5035d5c44cb/lib/request.js#L27-L29 there are the `ip`, `ips` and `hostname` properties that are currently set to `null`. Those are 3 pointers of 64 bytes each that we are carrying around with no specific needs as most code does not need them.

Those are defined and set in https://github.com/fastify/fastify/blob/bf18412f2ba838fc06e3162a13ebcf88b5a283be/lib/route.js#L304-L315.

I recommend that we move those definitions to getters similar to https://github.com/fastify/fastify/blob/bf18412f2ba838fc06e3162a13ebcf88b5a283be/lib/request.js#L36-L58. In order to support the `trustProxy`, I recommend those definitions to be overridden with another `Object.defineProperty()`.

Note that the logger use them: https://github.com/fastify/fastify/blob/bf18412f2ba838fc06e3162a13ebcf88b5a283be/lib/logger.js#L54-L55
