## Describe the new feature or change to an existing feature you'd like to see

On January 1st, 2020 the CCPA comes into effect. One of the provisions of the law is that residents of California must be granted the ability to opt out of their data being sold. It is not immediately clear how to implement such functionality in AMP. Having looked at various approaches, at least the following items are potential issues or blockers:

* `amp-geo` only works at a country level; in order to offer California-specific affordances (for those who choose to implement it that way) it would require the ability to also provide US state-level results (for instance by placing a separate state-specific `class`).
* There can only be one `amp-consent` instance on page, so anyone already using `amp-consent` for other purposes, typically GDPR, cannot also use it for CCPA. (CCPA is an opt out mechanism, but this could be represented through a consent affordance triggered by a button, on which the options are reject and close). `amp-consent` was designed to support multiple instances but that seems to have never been implemented.
* Both `amp-analytics` and `amp-ads` seem to support opt-in behaviour whereby they are off until an `amp-consent` is agreed to, but they do not seem to support opt-out behaviour in which they run until an opt out is effected (equivalent to an `amp-consent` reject) at which point they can be selectively disabled or modified. They would need to support that behaviour.
* `amp-ads` does not currently appear to have the ability to pass the IAB flag to signal opted-out users.

Given the short time frame remaining, we would appreciate reassurance that the AMP team intends for it to be possible to run AMP legally in 2020.

## Describe alternatives you've considered

We have tried to hack this together every which way and it does not seem possible to make it work.

Good point on share the design ideas in the thread and get feedback. Thank you @tobie for the suggestion. 

Two major challenges we are facing. 

Challenge 1. opt-out 
opt out is difficult because unlike opt-in decision, opt-out decision in theory should not be purged from storage. This is extremely difficult with AMP's limited localStorage space. AMP's localStorage is implemented by the AMP viewer, and it's up to the AMP viewer to purge unused storage entries without advance notice. We can improve the AMP viewer's implementation to support LRU logic and also expand the storage space for AMP, but this issue will still exist. 
Client side storage is preferred because otherwise there will always be a roundtrip delay to render any AMP pages (even if users are not from EEA or CA). We want to get publisher's feedback on the AMP localStorage limitation, and the risk of opt-out decision not being persisted.

Challenge 2: Handle multiple consents.
In the case there are multiple user consents (GDPR and CCPA). It's should be up to publisher or CMP to decide what to respect. This may involve some complicate logic including interpreting consent string and return different result based on users geo location. AMP may provide a very conservative way to combine boolean based consent state. But for more advanced features, one idea is to have publishers use `<amp-script>` to combine multiple consent decisions. 

Ideas, feedback and requests are very welcomed!

Comment 19 (source ID 551973914) | Participant 6 | created 2019-11-08T20:12:46Z | updated 2019-11-08T20:17:53Z
Source: https://github.com/ampproject/amphtml/issues/24910#issuecomment-551973914
Responding to @tobie as requested: 

### Challenge 1. opt-out

I agree with what is said above, we need to be able to have consistency in the opt-outs across platforms. If a user has opted-out on washingtonpost dot com, arrives on a WashPost AMP via Search and that AMP has `amp-access` or `amp-subscriptions` user IDs that are logged into our systems then we need to be able to make a decision on the logged-in users data before any possible tracking or ads are loaded. If the user is not logged in, and they log in via AMP and opt-out in AMP we need to receive a data payload that allows us to register that opt-out across all our systems. As such we have the following as requirements: 

- We must know if the user is logged in before anything that tracks them is loaded. 
- We must know if a logged-in user is opted out in our site (outside of AMP Cache/Viewer) before anything that tracks them is loaded. 
- We must know if a logged-in user has taken the action to opt-out from within AMP and be able to align that with their login inside our own systems. 
- If a non-logged-in user opts out on AMP's localStorage that opt-out should be stored persistently within AMP localStorage from that point forward and there should be an event registering that opt-out with our site along with the AMP reader id. 
- Finally I am pretty sure that if a non-logged-in user arrives on an AMP page it will need to send their AMP Reader ID to our API in order to assure we have not recorded a previous opt-out that would need to be retained. 

I think it would be reasonable to no longer 'phone-home' for that opt-out's status once it is set and sent to our API. 

If we want to find the most performant option, a solution might be: once the user's opt-out is registered and for as long as it is persistent in the AMP Viewer's storage the opt-out is the user's assumed state without an additional phone-home on each load. 

However, we'd want to register changes in that status so an async call to a publisher-based endpoint on every AMP view after the load to check if logged-in users have retained their opt-out status since the last AMP visit would be required.

### Challenge 2: Handle multiple consents.

I agree this is a decision best made by checking the AMP Reader ID against our database. However, I'm not sure what situation would be the case in which there are multiple relevant consents. That said, as @darobin notes, `amp-consent` or whatever element gets used should be geographically aware enough to only handle these requests within their locale. The case of an EU user arriving on our AMP page while visiting CA is definitely something that seems impossible to resolve to legal satisfaction without a DB check.

Further, I'm not sure how it would work with `amp-script` as these two consents are very different and GDPR would likely override CCPA. It seems best to make a single API request that included the Reader ID, and expects a return of GDPR and CCPA consent info and makes a decision based on that? 

More than the very specific question of CCPA vs GDPR we should assume more processes that have their own compliance parameters are likely to surface in the US and abroad and any system should be able to support not just two, but many potential consent situations. 

----

### Additional questions:

Beyond this question: AMP will also need to implement the IAB Consent Framework regardless of the state of consent, we will need to indicate that the CCPA IAB Consent framework is active, that we have displayed a compliant opt-out prompt and if the user has opted-out using their framework. We will also need that framework to explicitly signal that a user is not eligible for the opt-out process when they are outside the CCPA compliance area. The consent string of `1--` is needed on all ad HTTP requests (along with any other HTTP request to a potential user tracking service) so vendors can be sure we are checking for compliance and have determined a user is outside the zone. Further the system for a window level object and `postMessage` receiver will need to be in place. 

This is work is required to be complete by January 1 2020. Our team has also determined this will indeed be the enforcement date. 

EDIT: Also: this will need to work in AMP Stories.

In this case an API to update the local cached value can be provided. The local cached value can be updated every time the user visit the site, and the updated value will be used the next time the user visit the site again. 

> I'm am not sure: what is the value in using an iframe as opposed to calling a remote API with the right parameters and letting it state what is active/inactive? It would seem to be heavier?

I agree that an iframe seems to be heavier. I proposed iframe instead of a CORS request because of four reasons.
1. Iframe provides the flexibility. The iframe can handle showing different UIs, opt-in/opt-out user flow. 
2. AMP already support iframe solution for consent management platform. In the future, I assume many publishers will work with CMPs to collect their user consents. In such cases, iframe solution is preferred and easier to integrate with .
3. To combine multiple consents together, using an iframe provides publishers with the most flexibility. Also given the iframe is already up, it saves the delay of another potential roundtrip request.
4. To support the IAB consent string and its API client side, we need a service to interpret the consent string in the background. Which an iframe provided by a CMP sounds reasonable. 

However, we're only exploring the MVP solution right now. If the local storage one-time off solution is good with everyone, I would still propose the client side solution for MVP. Thank you

@AramZS thanks reviewing the spec. 

For CCPA integration, you basically need 4 things:
1) re-tag your AMP page with a new amp-consent configuration
2) set up a server endpoint for consent state syncing
3) provide a link on your AMP page to initiate the opt-out flow
4) tag the page with `data-block-on-consent`


(1)  amp-consent config
```
geoOverride: {
  "us": {
      checkConsentHref: "https://example.com/check-consent",
      consentRequired: "remote"
   }
}
```

(2) server endpoint
Your `checkConsentHref` server endpoint should return a response like:
```
{
  consentRequired: true/false, // depending on if the user is in CA
  consentStateValue: "accepted" / "rejected", // depending on if user has opted out
  consentString: "1YN", // the consent string that is accepted by the vendors used on the page
  expireCache: true/false, // depending on if you want to leverage client cache to improve latency for the next visit.
}
```
note that `sharedData` is not designed to carry consent string, as it will never be cached locally. It's to pass along other arbitrary one-time data that are agreed between vendor and publisher.

(3) opt-out flow
you need to add a link on your page that takes user to your own website to do the opt-out.

(4) data-block-on-consent
you will likely tag all `amp-ad` with this attribute so that their instantiation will be blocked until either a) amp-geo says the user is not in regulated region b) your endpoint returned a response. 


Let me know if you have further questions.

Comment 6 (source ID 496735280) | Participant 3 | created 2019-05-29T00:10:04Z | updated 2019-05-29T00:11:50Z
Source: https://github.com/uTox/uTox/issues/1274#issuecomment-496735280
_Not sure what some of your statements where addressing since they lack any references._

Here's my best guess at matching your replies...

**Avoiding False Security:**
> An IP isn't protected information. And if you have a threat model where it is, you need to be tunneling everything through an onion router.

But proxying is another means to obscure an IP and should warn the user if it the data is not going through the proxy as expected. Shouldn't we imply proxy services be desired if a proxy was entered? Based on that implication, isn't it fair to notify that the proxy is not being forced? _(granted, 1.0.2 is worded a little strange)_

_1.0.3 does not seem to be addressed..._

**Standardizing Avatar Usage:**
> Avatars shouldn't be standardized, clients should make a best effort, to display whatever it gets.

Avatars may not be standard and the app SHOULD show what it gets. But most apps do EXPECT a 1:1 ratio for avatars. Is it really unreasonable to warn the user that their new avatar is not a standard size?

_2.2.10 and 2.2.11 do not seem to be addressed..._

**Avoiding Group Spam:**
> IIRC, that was fixed

So [the page](https://hcoop.net/~docelic/tcs_full.html) has it wrong on 3.2.1 and 3.2.2?

**Avoiding Data Loss:**
> That's a problem that needs to be fixed with toxcore, not uTox

So ToxCore needs to show the client an alert before leaving a group?
That doesn't seem like the job of ToxCore to do anything related to the user interface...

**Ensuring Honoring Privacy:**
> uTox dosen't auto answer calls -_-

So 3.3.3 is also erroneously reported?

**Avoiding Shared System Privacy Breach:**
> No, message persistence is a feature, not a bug

So defaulting to message persistence to off **is not an option** because you want them to persist?

> That is an option

So 5.0.1 are erroneously reported?

**Providing Easy Data Access:**
> already done.

So 5.0.2 and 5.0.3 are erroneously reported too?

- - - -
**Conclusion:**
> The info from is BADLY out dated, and in some places simply wrong.

So the **items marked wrong** are:

- 3.2.1 - Explicit acceptance of group chat inclusion
- 3.2.2 - Defaulting auto-accept of group inclusion to false
- 3.3.3 - Defaulting auto-answering calls to false
- 5.0.1 - Exposing the option to encrypt .tox data file
- 5.0.2 - Exposing the option to decrypt encrypted profile data
- 5.0.3 - Storing profile data in standard locations

And the  **items considers stupid** are:

- 1.0.2 - Warning user IP may be exposed when proxy is set but not forced
- 1.0.3 - Enforcing ONLY proxy use when force proxy is set
- 2.2.6 - Standardizing expectation of square avatars
- 2.2.10 - Broadcast avatar removal to honor user intent
- 2.2.11 - Conforming to expected use of avatars
- 3.2.3 - Warning user of data loss before leaving a group
- 4.0.2 - Defaulting to message persistence to false

_Did I parse your message correctly?_ :-D

- - - -

**Commentary:**
> The goals for uTox are to be usable for sane humans... Paranoid/security nerds need not apply, and shouldn't be the ones writing standards. That being my original issue with TCS.

_I'm confused by this because it seemed that Tox was created precisely for paranoid security nerds..._

> From **[About Tox](https://tox.chat/about.html):** 
> Tox began a few years ago, in the wake of Edward Snowden's leaks regarding NSA spying activity. The idea was to create an instant messaging application that ran without requiring the use of central servers. The system would be distributed, peer-to-peer, and end-to-end encrypted, with no way to disable any of the encryption features; at the same time, the application would be easily usable by the layperson with no practical knowledge of cryptography or distributed systems. 

- Based on the above description it seems that forcing proxy use (when set by user) and avoiding unencrypted persistent messages (by default) and broadcasting the unset of user's avatars - _these are really expected features of Tox clients..._

- As for the non-security nerd stuff, warning user of unintentional consequences (on leaving groups or when not using a set proxy) and responding to avatar changes in a normal way - _these seem fair and reasonable to me..._

- It seems unfair to dismiss sane defaults for a security-focused instant messenger or to dismiss layperson's expectations of usage as unreasonable. But I guess this is all a matter of perspective...

- I'm also surprised to learn that a Tox client hates security nerds. I guess that's allowed. Just unexpected...

_Thanks for the in-depth response! Cheers!_

**Description of problem:**
On my network I block all outgoing external DNS requests (Ports 53 & 853). So requests to my local DNS server at 192.168.10.1 are allowed, but a request to 8.8.8.8:53 for example will be blocked. I do this to force all devices on my network to use my local DNS server which is assigned over DHCP, or static.
```
~ $ ha dns info
host: 172.30.32.3
locals:
- dns://192.168.10.1
servers: []
version: "9"
version_latest: "9"
```
My HA system functions perfectly, however I see constant DoT requests (10-16 per min) from HA to 1.1.1.1 and 1.0.0.1. This is apparently a fall back #1597 solution for when local DNS is 'messed up'. However, there is nothing wrong with my config, yet I see this constant traffic

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/59442445/90238573-158a6d00-de1e-11ea-9d2a-bfa2d100a0a3.png)

I block this kind of DNS traffic because its an issue of both Privacy & Performance. I don't believe systems should have hard coded DNS built in (eg. Google is huge offender...). I understand this is trying to fix a 'Problem', but I don't think hard coded DNS is the solution, especially when the existence of such settings is only apparent after searching the repo, because it's not in the docs, and its not displayed when running the above ```ha dns info``` command.

My personal opinions aside, there is clearly a bug in the 'fallback' solution, as my DNS setup is working fine.

Issue body:
**Who:** All users on the OFN
**Trigger:** User confirms their email address
**Goal:** To ensure that the enterprise can see the full order history for one email address (user), but protect the previous owner of the email address.

For epic #946, where any user at all has clicked on the 'confirm email address' link in the confirmation email they receive, the system must:
- Check if the email address is associated with any guest checkout orders.
- Where there have been previous guest checkout orders, the associated guest customer record must be linked to the newly registered user.
- The guest order history does not show in the registered user's order history.
- The enterprise can see the linkage between the guest orders and the subsequent registered user orders in their customer list.

Background on the design decision: Enterprises want to see the full order history of a customer. It doesn't matter if the customer was registered or not. It would also be very convenient to show all previous orders to the user. The problem is that we don't know which orders were really performed by the same person. We can't rely on the email address, because:

- People misspell email addresses.
- People change email addresses and email addresses change owners.
- People invent email addresses for guest checkouts that actually exist.

So if we would show all guest orders with the same email address to the newly registered customer, they may see orders that don't belong to them. That breaches the privacy of the person that ordered as guest.

-------
SPIKE
- How easy is this to implement? Will it work out of the box as @oeoeaio says?

@daniellemoorhead there is something I don't understand here, when you say

> To ensure that the enterprise can see the full order history for one email address (user), but protect the previous owner of the email address.

I understand your design proposal but sightly disagree. I see your arguments to say that a guest user -
- might have misspelt the email address used
- or might have used an email, then close his mailbox and then someone else might have open the same email address (I'm not sure that's authorized by email providers though so not sure about that argument)
- a customer might have used a random email and then it happens that the real people using that email creates an account

**BUT here are my objections:**
- If a guest user uses an email that happens to exist (point 3) the real user would have received an order confirmation email and would have write to us saying "I never ordered, how did you get my email, etc." So for me this can't happen, or if it does it woud be a mistake and we would treat it as a mistake.
- If a guest user misspelt her email (point 1) and this misspelt address happens to be a real one and the real user creates an account, we are in the same case as just described. Else there is no issue, she just didn't receive her previous order confirmations, and she wouldn't see when registering the orders made through that error email.
- Point 2 I think is impossibe, I checked and gmail for instance doesn't authorize to create an email address already used by someone else before even if this user has closed it (https://support.google.com/mail/answer/56256?hl=en&visit_id=1-636625089850149575-3195862716&rd=1) so this case for me can't happen.

So for me: "The guest order history does not show in the registered user's order history."  > I disagree, as a new registered user I want to see in my account the past orders I made with that same email address when I was still a guest and had no account.

**So I would simplify that story and just say that:**
- the previous guest records are associated with the new register user
- so manager see all info attached to user
- user see all info in his account

Do you agree @daniellemoorhead ?

Source: https://github.com/openfoodfoundation/openfoodnetwork/issues/1592#issuecomment-391226369
Maybe I can answer some of these questions.

> used an email, then close his mailbox and then someone else might have open the same email address (I'm not sure that's authorized by email providers though so not sure about that argument)

This is possible. Some email providers make the address available straight after deletion, most block it for a few months and some providers (Gmail) block it forever.

> the real user would have received an order confirmation email and would have write to us saying "I never ordered, how did you get my email, etc."

If I received an email like that, I would suspect some kind of scam. Maybe I would mark it as spam, but I wouldn't react to it, because that is how the bad guys get you.

I agree that the cases in which we don't want to associate the data are very rare. But they can happen and we would be doing the wrong thing in these cases. These issues have been real for bigger companies with more customers and therefore more email addresses. For me, this comes down to basic security measures. When you order as a guest, there is no authentication and all data is untrusted. We can display that to the manager for their information, but it's not right to display it to customers.

Comment 6 (source ID 391330187) | Participant 2 | created 2018-05-23T12:35:08Z | updated 2018-05-23T12:35:08Z

Ok I get your points @mkllnk 
Then my question is: can we just consider that all the records from before the account is created remain as guest and are not connected to the new account at all? Is it really a problem for the hub manager if she doesn't see the records associated to that customer? I mean the problems you mention on the user side will be the same on the hub manager side, if the email was used by someone esle the hub manager will see a wrong record associated to a customer.
**SO my proposal is: we don't associate any guest record to new accounts.** And we close this issue :-)
The hub manager will still see the past orders but they will not be associated with the account of the new user. I don't think it's really a problem, if the hub manager filter orders with the email she will see all the orders anyway, so why would she need to have the guest orders formally associated with the customer?

Think about saving to order notes instead and/or save to user meta in a data structure that saves each time they check the TOS box.

Issue discussion (chronological; participant names pseudonymized within the case):
Comment 1 (source ID 334241219) | Participant 2 | created 2017-10-04T18:05:49Z | updated 2017-10-04T18:05:49Z
Source: https://github.com/strangerstudios/paid-memberships-pro/issues/530#issuecomment-334241219
For this to make sense (be applicable as a legally valid means of tracking acceptance of the ToS), it will need to do more than simply track the fact that somebody clicked the checkbox. 

Not a lawyer, but from my corporate days, I recall it also needs to ask for positive confirmation of receipt of the ToS.

A checkbox isn't enough, it has to be "signed" and agreed to, using one of the legally accepted electronic signature options and in the context of the ToS text. Thus it can't use the supplied user email from the email field as a "signature". Also can't use IP address either since the IP address is by no means not unique to the user who agreed. 

Then it has to be stored somewhere with a clear audit trail associated with it. 

Adding a timestamp and/or IP address is not going to cut it in a dispute. Not even close, unfortunately.

Issue body:
On 25 May 2018, the [EU General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR)](https://www.eugdpr.org/) will come into enforcement. SilverStripe should decide to what extent it should change the core code to accommodate this change, to what extent it can provide advice about best practices, and to what extent it is left up to the individual site owners.

In addition, best practices can be established for what data is stored by default, what is done with that data, and how it is stored, processed, and disclosed.

At minimum a blogpost or docs update that addressed potential areas to look at or config settings to tweak would be a great bout of confidence for the community.

Comment 1 (source ID 359846189) | Participant 2 | created 2018-01-23T16:25:18Z | updated 2018-01-23T16:25:18Z
Source: https://github.com/silverstripe/silverstripe-framework/issues/7791#issuecomment-359846189
As a starting point, it's probably worth considering what the core system actually stores that falls under the regulation.   From what I can see, the following are the only issues:

Member table: Name, Email, etc.
LoginAttempt table:  IP, Email

As I understand it, the critical things we need for GDPR are statements about the use of the data, and means to expire it, etc.

For the second of the two, the simplest way to deal with it would be to take it out of the equation altogether.  If it were possible to disable the loginattempt logging with a configuration option, that solves the issue.   If the loginattempt data is needed, then some mechanism to expire/purge it periodically (maybe an add-on) would help.

I agree that GDPR compliance itself is critical (we've started reviewing our own systems like SilverStripe Platform and silverstripe.com/org back in November). But in the context of our open source software, my understaning is that the software itself is neither a "Data Processor" nor a "Data Controller". It really depends on what you build with it. I agree that some documentation about potential privacy impacts emerging from our software would be nice. But unless somebody thinks we need to change our APIs or system behaviour, it's not `impact/critical`. I'll raise a GDPR blog post with our marketing team! :)

You can turn off login recording via `Security.login_recording: false`. But in its default behaviour, it means that any website might need a privacy statement for CMS users, even if you're not collecting data from visitors or providing other login-based services. Maybe "business applications" like the CMS are exempt from GDPR, if the CMS user is employed by the "data controller" organisation?

Issue body:
## What's the issue?

If AMP is used for tracking and it is legally required to have opted in to tracking or for the user to at have least seen the cookie dialog the iframe can not contain custom tracking, unless a custom dialog is shown, since the iframe is unaware of the tracking state of the AMP document. 

The iframe also has to load additional tracking scripts which might impact the page/iframe performance. The duplicate implementation of tracking and unnecessary load of additional scripts might easily be avoided if the iframe could postMessage to the AMP page, where AMP-analytics could then execute a predefined trigger to handle the calls.    

## How do we reproduce the issue?

1. build simple amp page with amp-analytics trigger predefined
2. include amp-iframe in page
3. build simple iframe content page with post message implementation to trigger tracking event on link/button click
4. click button/link inside iframe
5. fire tracking request on AMP page prior to link navigation

## What browsers are affected?

All browsers for new feature.

## Which AMP version is affected?

Upcoming if implemented.

Source: https://github.com/ampproject/amphtml/issues/12607#issuecomment-358805665
If I'm understanding the requirements correctly, I think there's two separate ideas combined here.
* The first relates to enabling iframes to send their events so that they can be tracked as part of an amp-analytics configuration. As far as I know, this isn't supported today. It's somewhat related to the idea of the [video interface](https://github.com/ampproject/amphtml/blob/master/src/video-interface.js) supporting analytics, but asked for in a much more generic way, not specific to video. Would be interesting to get @choumx's feedback relating to 2-way messaging here.
* The second idea is related to disallowing tracking when the user has not yet consented to it. It is not reasonable to expect the iframed page to present the consent UI. Therefore, the AMP page needs to handle this by either blocking the iframe or informing it that it cannot perform its own tracking within.

Does this sound like an accurate summary?

@crssi: the indices that are changed in the audio data are usually picked at random. With the "fixed indices" you can pick some by yourself. The default is to chose one from 0-30 at random by browser start.
The basic idea there was that apparently some fingerprinters are only using the first 30 entries in the audio data and the you are always somewhat protected there. Otherwise it could by random that you are tracked because the random indices were not in that range.

TCP/IP fingerprinting works without Javascript/HTML/CSS; just by pinging a server that server can tell your OS and even rough version like WinNT X, Linux Kernel xx etc. That's the reason mozilla decided to keep the original OS even if privacy.resistFingerprinting is enabled.

Best bet is to use a VPN service with many users that is hosted in a trustworthy EU country (as in DACH or BENELUX). Everything else should be considered unsafe, while anything from the Five Eyes countries should be considered malicious. If you care any percent about privacy and then still pipe your traffic through any of UK/US/CA/AU/NZ you should really just stop using the internet and open your private home to the general public, including that Nigerian prince.

Issue body:
 I don't know if this is an issue or not, but it was a pain to debug and fix.  If you default to http, statehood is defaulting the cookie to be "Secure" so no browser will ever set the cookie, you have to set this.settings.state.isSecure = false.  I'm not sure if the system should default to secure, or, it should take into account http vs https when setting that default.

Issue discussion (chronological; participant names pseudonymized within the case):
Comment 1 (source ID 453877573) | Participant 2 | created 2019-01-13T23:55:58Z | updated 2019-01-13T23:55:58Z
Source: https://github.com/hapijs/hapi/issues/3902#issuecomment-453877573
The problem is that most production node deployment use HTTP not HTTPS (using an external front HTTPS LB). This means that you cannot decide if cookies should be secure based on the protocol level at the hapi server level.

If the docs can be clearer on that, please submit a PR. Otherwise, there isn't much I can do about this.

Comment 2 (source ID 453883217) | Participant 1 | created 2019-01-14T01:15:17Z | updated 2019-01-14T01:15:17Z
Source: https://github.com/hapijs/hapi/issues/3902#issuecomment-453883217
Why can't you? Why would you default to unable to set cookies?  Secure should only be used if certs are specified in the configuration for that connection i.e. { tls: { cert:"", key:"" }}.  Setting secure for any other reason will make cookies completely useless.  If most node production deployment use HTTP then I would think you wouldn't want secure set, as there is no browser that would even accept those cookies, ever.

Comment 3 (source ID 453883968) | Participant 3 | created 2019-01-14T01:24:32Z | updated 2019-01-14T01:26:06Z
Source: https://github.com/hapijs/hapi/issues/3902#issuecomment-453883968
The trick is that deployments often do use HTTPS, but terminate TLS _in front_ of the node server, i.e. at a reverse proxy or load balancer, and there's no way for hapi to know if that is going to be the case.  Notice how in this case secure cookies are still fully able to be used with hapi, even if the hapi server itself does not use TLS.

Comment 4 (source ID 453936690) | Participant 1 | created 2019-01-14T09:02:59Z | updated 2019-01-14T09:02:59Z
Source: https://github.com/hapijs/hapi/issues/3902#issuecomment-453936690
No I understand that, but then wouldn't the configurer TURN ON SECURE manually because they are going use it?  What i'm not understanding, i guess. Is why is the default to be in a broken state where cookies cannot be used. Non TLS/SSL should default to non secure, TLS/SSL should default to secure, with the ability to override that if needed.  I'm just saying the DEFAULT should take into account the state of the connection, instead of always saying true or false.

Comment 5 (source ID 454090647) | Participant 2 | created 2019-01-14T17:30:32Z | updated 2019-01-14T17:30:32Z
Source: https://github.com/hapijs/hapi/issues/3902#issuecomment-454090647
The default is always going to be the most secure.

Issue body:
Hi, 

This is a feature request for settings for Toots to automatically delete/expire within a certain amount of time. By expiry time I mean the amount of time which has to pass before a Toot is automatically deleted, rather than a specific date/time that a Toot expires on. 

I would suggest keeping the default to Toots never expiring unless a user deletes them, however it would be nice to get the option to set a default expiry time in your account settings, but also have the option to alter the time on a Toot-by-Toot basis. 

The range for expiry times would be pretty large and it could make an awkward input to design if a user can choose anything between an hour and 6 months, but the more flexibility the more useful the feature is. 

This is a feature that I (@jck@mastodon.social) and a few others thought would be useful and make Mastodon feel like a social network where you *actually* have control over your own data. 

There would obviously need to be exceptions of some sort for Toots that have been marked for moderation, so that the feature can't be used for harassment that auto-deletes before a moderator can get to it. 

Thanks for looking at this!

@thegranddesign I was able to reproduce the error you're experiencing. 
Given the following configuration, and assuming the module at the specified filepath attaches the supplied policies (Preconfigured AWS Policies) to generated iam_roles:
```
module "api_server_instance_profile" {
  source = "./modules/instance_profile"

  name = "api-server"
  policy_ids = "arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/IAMUserChangePassword,arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/service-role/AmazonEC2RoleforSSM,arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/service-role/AWSConfigRole,arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/AmazonAPIGatewa\
yAdministrator,arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/AmazonAPIGatewayInvokeFullAccess,arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/AmazonAppStreamReadOnlyAccess"
  policy_count = 6
}

module "bastion_instance_profile" {
  source = "./modules/instance_profile"
  name = "bastion"
  policy_ids = "arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/IAMUserChangePassword"
  policy_count = 1
}
```

I am able to continuously reproduce the error you are experiencing. However, if I change the list of policy id's passed in the second module declaration, to use policies that were not already attached in the first module's declaration, I can no longer get the issue to reproduce.

Ex:
```
module "api_server_instance_profile" {
  source = "./modules/instance_profile"

  name = "api-server"
  policy_ids = "arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/IAMUserChangePassword,arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/service-role/AmazonEC2RoleforSSM,arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/service-role/AWSConfigRole,arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/AmazonAPIGatewa\
yAdministrator,arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/AmazonAPIGatewayInvokeFullAccess,arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/AmazonAppStreamReadOnlyAccess"
  policy_count = 6
}

module "bastion_instance_profile" {
  source = "./modules/instance_profile"
  name = "bastion"
  policy_ids = "arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/AmazonZocaloFullAccess"
  policy_count = 1
}
```

This is because an `iam_policy` can only have at max 1 policy attachment resource bound to it, as the `iam_policy_attachment` resource will manage every attachment on that policy. This is why we were experiencing the diff between policy attachments for each attachment resource. 

To sum up, in order to fix the issue we need to ensure that each `iam_policy` has only one `iam_policy_attachment` attached to it. This may result in multiple policies that have the same content but different names, or restructuring the policy_attachment resource to maintain the 1-1 relationship between an `iam_policy` and the `iam_policy_attachment` resources.

Closing as not a bug, but happy to discuss further. Thanks!

Comment 13 (source ID 305927999) | Participant 4 | created 2017-06-02T23:02:18Z | updated 2017-06-02T23:02:18Z
Source: https://github.com/hashicorp/terraform/issues/11331#issuecomment-305927999
Hello! 

Can someone please provide for us a complete reproduction configuration (ideally using modules and no secret things exposed). I'd like to take a better look at what's happening here and hopefully provide additional guidance. 

`aws_iam_policy_attachment` is specifically and intentionally  designed to behave the way it is here. I can see how it may be confusing at first though. It is designed to explicitly control who/what/where a role is attached. It's mission statement could be summed up as "I have a policy, I want it to be attached to these things, and only these things." Having two `aws_iam_policy_attachment` with this mission statement for the same policy naturally conflict. 

From reading above it doesn't sound like that's your intent. If I understand, you want to construct modules to accept a policy as input and attach it to a variable amount of things. For that you need to use `aws_iam_role_policy_attachment`. 

A full example that I can look at and apply ourselves would better help us get on the same page and hopefully provide direction forward. 

Thanks!

Exposing the fava instance to the net is a plus, for me. Primarily because
this allows the user to not just input stuff, but also view the current
state of accounts. For example, how much has been spent in that category
this month.

Also delayed entry increases friction as there's manual additional steps to
undertake between the data entry and actually having the data available.

birds with one stone is to have the form on a separate route and only
exposing that route external to your home router or machine. So the only
thing you can do is enter data (but no need for manual upload later, the
data is automatically saved). Proper screening of inputs is important,
obviously.

Public web services are an additional resource (and privacy) hassle I think
may not be worth it.

I use beancount for my accounting now (switched from ledger-cli), but my family are not command-line people and rely on the web form I made for them in [ledgible](//github.com/lipidity/ledgible) for adding transactions. I actually really miss the convenience of it myself, too.

Please [check it out](https://lipidity.com/cgi/ledgible/app.py/add) (login demo/demo) -- my mother has been using this for over one year.

The main features of this approach are that:
1. It's super easy to enter transactions on the spot, so it gets to be a habit. I can't do that with fava, so the transactions pile up, I procrastinate, then finally I have to sit down and reconcile everything. Something that used to be fun is now a chore. (The problem is even worse if you have shared accounts and you miss accounting for something - I'll see something unfamiliar on my credit card and wonder, "Was this expense something I bought, or was it my partner? Maybe it's a fraudulent transaction?"). When I was using ledgible's transaction entry I pretty much never missed anything.
2. date entry is usually just one or two clicks, rather than any typing
3. autocompletion can "learn" from your data; eg. if my expenses at the payee "Costco" frequently go to my `Expenses:Grocery` account, `Expenses:Grocery` should show up first in the autocompletion list for the 'destination'/debit account. Likewise, if I pay for groceries with my credit card, that account would show up first for the 'source'/credit account. (To see this [in the demo](https://lipidity.com/cgi/ledgible/app.py/add), put the payee as "Uncle Boons" and see when you type an "e" in either the "to" or "from" account, the first result is based on previous transactions). It doesn't take long before tab-completion does most of the work, so just a few keystrokes take care of the most common transactions!

> [A public web service to add transactions, then sync with local fava] [...] This way I do not have to make my Fava instance publicly accessible

This sounds like a bigger privacy issue, since the web service is getting all your transactions!

It would seem to me much more sensible to use TLS and Basic HTTP password protection through eg nginx or httpd - which I am in fact doing already.

> What should the features be? A form-like input, with dropdowns etc., or just a normal editor with completion

Based on my experiences with ledgible, +1 to a web form. It shouldn't be difficult to achieve parity with, then surpass ledgible. I look forward to migrating my family to fava once this is implemented :)

Issue body:
With the Nearby feature using queries sent to Wikidata, (#289) I believe we have privacy issues to consider, for example the accidental disclosure of sensitive locations of the user (e.g. home address).

In my opinion, we should make sure that users are aware of the fact that:

1. the app may disclose the current location of the user's device to the Wikidata server when querying nearby places. <s>(And maybe explicitly ask the user to agree with the Terms of Use of the WMF?)</s>
2. the app may disclose the current location of the user's the device to the core app developers subscribed to the private mailing list when sending crash reports. (I believe the current app doesn't include coordinates to an error message, but it may happen in future.)

For developers, I would imagine something like:

1. Developers may use personal information obtained from the user only for the purpose of improving this app.
2. Developers may not disclose personal information obtained from the user.

I'm not sure in what way we want to deliver such a statement to the user. Maybe a wiki page and a link from the About screen to it? A dialog before a relevant action (e.g. sending a query) is done?

Issue body:
Allow the user to set a default location. This location would then be shown automatically when the app opens instead of the list of locations. This is a feature most weather apps have as it saves one click to the user.

Title at retrieval: Provide better privacy in the usage reporting
Status at retrieval: closed

Issue body:
I am the kind of people that systematically deactivate usage report "features", and Syncthing is no exception, even if I love it. As the target audience for Syncthing is more or less FOSS lovers / technical people, it is likely that the usage statistics published are largely underestimated. This is also prejudicial since the kind of people that deactivate usage reporting are possibly correlated to the kind of people that say, use a specific other feature, so you cannot simply extrapolate from the usage reports you have.

One way to gather more information about the real use of Syncthing, apart from using the limited information available to relays logs &cie, would be to increase the confidentiality of the usage reports
Google developed for Chrome a system called RAPPOR that provides usage information while being much more preserving of users' privacy. See [this design document](https://www.chromium.org/developers/design-documents/rappor).

The basic idea is to flip a coin, and report either the real value or a random value. No one can say if the reported value is actually true (and if the client does use an outdated and potentially vulnerable version!), but that's not relevant since what you are looking for is _trends_. The server can then correct reported information by adjusting for the probability that the reported usage is random. It has several complications such as its application on textual data (I guess we will be able to label build strings?) and how to deal with recurrent reporting (that would increase the probability of the reported information being true), but all of that can be worked on. I guess this would 1) increase privacy of Syncthing users, and 2) increase the trust in the Usage Reporting feature and improve its representativeness, if this feature is marketed in the UI.

For an introduction on the concept of Differential Privacy and RAPPOR, look at [this great article](http://blog.cryptographyengineering.com/2016/06/what-is-differential-privacy.html).

[edited to add some line breaks for readability]

Title at retrieval: Privacy issues with profile data on SD card
Status at retrieval: closed

Issue body:
In case the external SD card is formatted as mobile / removable storage (FAT32) and not as encrypted/bound to the device, the SD card can be removed and read out by any attacker, thief, or finder of a device.

The unencrypted, XML-style Osmand profile data easily reveals the saved and used locations of the device owner: home and work location, favourite places, tracks, and potentially even data of related people. This is like address badges on your keys and not compatible with EU privacy law (GDPR).

So, Osmand should retain privacy-related profile data (locations history favourite places, home and work locations, settings, GPX tracks, navigation settings and cache) separate from large "bulk" data (maps, sounds, fonts, ...) and keep privacy-related information in internal storage and/or let the user choose where to save profile and map / bulk data independently.

Software provided AS IS and it is hard to predict how it will be used on user device, so user should take separate precautions to avoid leak i.e. don't install 3rd party apps, use special security. 

I will vote against this issue cause it seriously harms usability between apps which user can control.

Thanks, but my main point was: Having personal information like names and home locations stored unencrypted and bound to the same directory if storage of the maps on external SD card is used, is a major threat in case of robbery or loss or unauthorized access to the SD card, especially as the user usually does not know that this information stored in plain text on SD card. Thus, the mandatory link between map storage and user data should be removed.

> I will vote against this issue cause it seriously harms usability between apps which user can control.

This I don't understand, neither technical (in terms of Android common practice or app interfaces) nor functional: The user is asked where to store the *maps*, not the *personal data* that is entered into Osmand. 

> I think there is no connection to EU privacy law (GDPR) cause this data is solely stored on user device and has no connection OsmAnd company.

GDPR and most other privacy laws cover all handling, storage, and protection of personal data, not only internet transmission. If a user saves data within favourites that reveals personal data of other people (e. g. name, geo location, relationship, reason of visiting, medical attributes of these people) within Osmand, and Osmand saves this on an exposed SD card without knowledge or consent of the user, there is indeed a GDPR issue that could be easily avoided, no matter if the Osmand company or the user could be legally held responsible for it. If the Osmand company knows about the issue but does not address it, this would be irresponsible to me.

Anyway I need to consult but it would be very stupid to make all Editors with Save As functionality legally responsible how the data stored.

Title at retrieval: Using Local Workbox Files Instead of CDN
Status at retrieval: closed
Retrieved issue comments: 6/6

Issue body:
## Feature request

Using local workbox files for the service worker, instead of loading them from a CDN.

#### What problem does this feature solve?

By using the CDN, any client will automatically open a connection to https://storage.googleapis.com/workbox-cdn/releases/... and inevitably transmit his IP address, which is regarded as personal information under EU law. As under the European General Data Protection Regulation, the site owner is responsible for any leak of personal information that is shared or made accessibly because of his site. Therefore, the site owner **must** obtain the clients permission in advance, or be able to ensure that no such information is shared/accessible.

This is especially a concern for services like workbox, since if many pages include it via a CDN, tracking a client between different sites becomes possible, which is even more restricted.

#### What does the proposed API look like?

Depending on the favoured solution, this would either need an additional config to let the site owner decide whether local files or the CDN should be used, or no changes at all if we could switch from CDN-only to local-only.

#### How should this be implemented in your opinion?

Instead of using the CDN, local files could be used as described under https://developers.google.com/web/tools/workbox/modules/workbox-sw

This would also be the easiest option compared to obtaining the clients permission beforehand. In addition, this also seems to comply with _Privacy by Design_ and _Default_ -- which is also a European General Data Protection Regulation requirement.

If I saw it correctly, the package `workbox-build` is used for this process, together with the `generateSW` function.

As of https://developers.google.com/web/tools/workbox/reference-docs/latest/module-workbox-build, the source could easily be switched from CDN to local by adding `importWorkboxFrom: 'local'` to the function call. As stated in the documentation, this should also cover copying all needed files.

#### Are you willing to work on this yourself?

Sure 👍 

I will gladly submit a pull request that adds `importWorkboxFrom: 'local'` to `generateSW` as well as making it configurable if required.

There is also a privacy issue with the current inclusion of Google Analytics, as the current configuration neither anonymises the IP address nor limits tracking. Since its not configurable as of now, we simply skipped the `ga` config option and implemented our own solution using `enhanceApp.js`, to adhere to EU law.

If you think this should also be extended in Vuepress core (as I could also imagine to move this into a plugin later on), I would create another issue and will also be willing to work on this.

Comment 2 (source ID 409842121) | Participant 1 | created 2018-08-02T08:04:15Z | updated 2018-08-02T08:40:55Z
Source: https://github.com/vuejs/vuepress/issues/539#issuecomment-409842121
Given that this is now 2 months old, I would like to bump this in order to get some feedback :)

So the main point was to make VuePress GDPR-compliant, especially the service worker implementation. On a side note, complying to modern data privacy standards could also be important to be prepared for future changes to other privacy laws. While changes are still discussed in the United States as far as I know, India for example already published a draft which was heavily inspired by the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR).

On the bigger picture however, the default Google Analytics (GA) integration is also not up to date with current (European) standards. However, this can easily and individually be fixed by using a custom theme and `enhanceApp.js`. Having that said, a quick default improvement could still be to add `ga('set', 'anonymizeIp', true);` and `forceSSL: true` to the default GA integration under `/lib/app/clientEntry.js`.

So what are your thoughts on this? Would it be easier to achieve the aforementioned changes (seeing my first post, or the summary below) to the workbox integration after the plugin system is released, or is this independently, so that I could/should start working on the pull request immediately?

The change I have in mind is to edit `/lib/build.js`, and either replacing

```js
await wbb.generateSW({
```

with

```js
await wbb.generateSW({
   importWorkboxFrom: 'local',
```

or adding an option like 

```js
await wbb.generateSW({
   importWorkboxFrom: SW_IMPORT,
```

to let each user choose whether `cdn`, `local`, or any other setting is sufficient.

Issue body:
**Description**

For the EU GDPR and other privacy laws, keeping logs only a limited amount of time (rather than a limited amount of overall data, like docker's `--log-opt max-buffer-size` allows) is essential to avoid fines for unnecessarily keeping sensitive data beyond a reasonable time window required for potential investigation of technical incidents.

Since this will affect a lot of those people who are using the docker engine directly (rather than an orchestrator like kubernetes) to run containers and manage their logs, I propose an option is added to handle this, e.g. `--log-opt max-buffer-days` or something. To handle this, docker would internally need to separate the log by days, so it can throw away not only based on overall log size but also based on age.

Sorry if such an option already exists, I made this ticket because I wasn't able to find it.

Edit: please note detailed "throw away granularity"/small interval, or a super exact throw away time (beyond not exceeding the interval) is really not required for this option to fulfill this use case. So I don't think any advanced detail intervals or making sure it's not thrown away a day *early* in some corner cases is important, and the simplest implementation that doesn't have horrible performance is probably good enough.

Issue body:
Hi there! is there a way to exclude elements that may contain PII info from BugSnag's breadcrumbs?
similar to this behavior: http://help.fullstory.com/spp/138664


Issue discussion (chronological; participant names pseudonymized within the case):
Comment 1 (source ID 250462088) | Participant 2 | created 2016-09-29T13:13:49Z | updated 2016-09-29T13:13:49Z
Source: https://github.com/bugsnag/bugsnag-js/issues/188#issuecomment-250462088
There isn't currently a UI for this like the behavior you described on full story. The best way to accomplish it would be with a [before notify hook](https://docs.bugsnag.com/platforms/browsers/customizing-error-reports/) . This let's you modify the exception payload before it is sent to Bugsnag.

``` js
Bugsnag.beforeNotify = function(payload, metaData) {
  // Filter out sensitive information
  payload.breadcrumbs = payload.breadcrumbs.map(function(crumb){
    // Check 
    if(crumb.metaData.targetSelector.match(/SOMEREGEX/) {
      crumb.metaData.targetText = 'HIDDEN';
    }
    return crumb;
  });
}
```

Issue body:
Ref. GDPR02

**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**

As a visitor when I visit a Decidim installation I could be tracked for analytics purposes, but it isn’t mentioned to me.

**Describe the solution you’d like**

We must offer a way to accept this tracking or to reject it.

Right now, the current behavior is a cookie warning that only shows the information that we use Cookies:
 

![header](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/717367/164201791-2592c33b-25f7-4cab-a675-46e6a0bb43fc.png)

We need to explain better what cookies do we use, why we’re using these cookies, and let the user choose which cookies they want to use.

**Describe alternatives you’ve considered**

There are JavaScript libraries that already tackle this issue, as it’s a classic.

1. Orejime
![orejime01](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/717367/164201764-1b5ac8a4-ed74-41a0-a074-1c1add844e38.png)
![orejime02](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/717367/164201768-04284076-7799-472f-916c-958862f7431d.png)

https://orejime.netlify.app/  
 https://github.com/Quentinchampenois/decidim-module_cookies 

3. Cookie Consent
https://github.com/osano/cookieconsent 
https://www.osano.com/cookieconsent/download/  

**Additional context**
 Cookie Law European Union and GDPR.
See [discussion on MetaDecidim](https://meta.decidim.org/processes/roadmap/f/122/proposals/15215)
See [Metadecidim proposal](https://meta.decidim.org/processes/roadmap/f/122/proposals/16970) 

We really like how this is solved in https://omastadi.hel.fi/  

**Does this issue could impact on users private data?**
 Yes, it’s about cookies and improving the (optional) tracking mechanisms that implementers can have on Decidim.

**Acceptance criteria**

- [ ]  As an implementer when installing Decidim I have a way of enabling this setting as a module
- [ ] As an implementer, I can configure which cookies are for which purpose and which are required for the app to work

Issue discussion (chronological; participant names pseudonymized within the case):
Comment 1 (source ID 1108273359) | Participant 2 | created 2022-04-25T08:51:45Z | updated 2022-04-25T08:51:45Z
Source: https://github.com/decidim/decidim/issues/9170#issuecomment-1108273359
I realized there is another issue related to this which is related to the embedded content on the website. E.g. MetaDecidim has a lot of YouTube embedded videos on it:
https://meta.decidim.org/conferences/DecidimFest21

The same also applies to other instances, such as Decidim.Barcelona, e.g. on this page:
https://www.decidim.barcelona/assemblies/audiencia-santsmontjuic/f/3983/meetings/4607

When you embed content from other sites, you will need to get consent from the user to use cookies before loading the content from the external website. In case of YouTube, you would need to get consent for the "marketing" cookie category (see below).

We are thinking to split this cookies task into two sub-tasks, of which we'll implement the first one in the current sprint:
1. Creating a framework for getting consent for the cookies + hiding **all iframe embeds** before the user has given their full consent for all cookie categories
2. Creating a way to define the "cookie category" for the iframe embeds when you add them to the site through the Quill editor

This second one would be part of the next sprint, i.e. a separate task after this initial implementation.

For the first task, we are considering the following approach:
- Define 4 cookie categories under which all cookies will be defined to
- Provide an editable section where the cookies can be documented for each of the categories
- Disable all cookie-related functionality until the user has given their consent

The cookie categories are:
1. Essential - Always enabled, forced (session cookie, cookie consent, load balancer related cookies, other infrastructure related cookies, etc.)
2. Preferences - Optional (cookies related to the user preferences, something that would edit the website behavior based on the user preferences, an example could be enabling dark mode)
3. Analytics and statistics - Optional (web analytics and other tracking cookies, excluding marketing related)
4. Marketing - Optional (Facebook/Google remarketing cookies, YouTube cookies, etc.)

Functionality-wise we need to consider the following:
- Disable all analytics scripts until the user has given their consent for the "Analytics and statistics" category
- Disable all iframe embeds until the user has given their consent for **all cookie categories** (because we are not currently categorizing the iframe embeds)

In the follow-up task we would create a way to categorize the iframe embeds for these categories but it is outside of the scope for the cookie consent task itself.

A common way to disable the iframe/video embeds is using the following kind of placeholder where the iframe would normally appear:
![Iframe placeholder](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/864340/165054189-bdf02eda-7886-446f-9dc9-8248bc52c6ad.png)

In Decidim we probably need to do that a bit more generic way, e.g. "In order to see **this content**, you need to...".

Comment 2 (source ID 1108277067) | Participant 2 | created 2022-04-25T08:54:58Z | updated 2022-04-25T08:54:58Z
Source: https://github.com/decidim/decidim/issues/9170#issuecomment-1108277067
And by the way, in general we are not only talking about "cookies" as these issues are normally presented, but the same applies for all data stored in the user device, including local storage, session storage, and other current or future means of storing data on the user's device.

Comment 3 (source ID 1110742014) | Participant 1 | created 2022-04-27T08:55:10Z | updated 2022-04-27T08:55:10Z
Source: https://github.com/decidim/decidim/issues/9170#issuecomment-1110742014
Nice catch! With @carolromero we were also talking about the cookie page that we've seen in other platforms, but we didn't have time yet to fully develop the User Story, and it could go to other sprints too. 

Comment 4 (source ID 1111869664) | Participant 1 | created 2022-04-28T07:58:59Z | updated 2022-04-28T07:58:59Z
Source: https://github.com/decidim/decidim/issues/9170#issuecomment-1111869664
As we've talked in our last meeting, just to let it in the same issue: 

1) We agree that this should also apply to all data stored in the user device (cookies, localStorage, sessionStorage, etc) 
2) In that case, although it'd be clear to talk about "Data policy", that approach has usability issues, so we'll keep referring to this to "Cookie policy". If in the future we see that other naming is better, then we can change it if so.

As an example look how the German government website handles it's cookies https://www.bundesregierung.de/breg-en before consent there is only one cookie that is required for consent because this is necessary for functioning of the website.  If no consent is given there are not more cookies.  Once consent is given then there are more cookies.

So how do I disable OWA cookies until consent is given?

If this means that OWA is totally disabled until consent is given then so be it, as long as there are no cookies beyond what is necessary for the basic functioning of the website (OWA is not part of the basic functioning of the website).

Issue discussion (chronological; participant names pseudonymized within the case):
Comment 1 (source ID 391918609) | Participant 2 | created 2018-05-25T01:59:59Z | updated 2018-05-25T02:17:20Z
Source: https://github.com/OneSignal/OneSignal-WordPress-Plugin/issues/132#issuecomment-391918609
@stefa98 You will need to first disable automatic init the OneSignal WordPress does. 

1. At the bottom of the OneSignal WordPress settings you will need to toggle on "Disable OneSignal initialization".

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/645861/40521376-244a6a8a-5f80-11e8-9ab9-73eb786f0687.png)

2. Then you can initialize OneSignal through javascript with the `requiresUserPrivacyConsent` setting.

```html
<script src="https://cdn.onesignal.com/sdks/OneSignalSDK.js" async></script>
<script>
  var OneSignal = window.OneSignal || [];
  window._oneSignalInitOptions["requiresUserPrivacyConsent"] = true;
  OneSignal.push(["init", window._oneSignalInitOptions]);
</script>
```
`window._oneSignalInitOptions` contains all the settings from the WordPress plugin including app_id are already set in here.

3. When the user accepts your privacy agreement you will need to call `userTappedProvideConsentButton`
```javascript
function userTappedProvideConsentButton() {
  // Will initialize the SDK and register for push notifications
  OneSignal.push(function() {
    OneSignal.provideUserConsent(true);
  });
}
```

Issue body:
For us maintainers it's really hard to judge which features of the admin interface people are using/not using.

It'd be nice to add opt-out analytics where we can collect (anonymized, obviously) information about what people are doing with the Keystone admin interface so we can adapt to what users are actually doing!

_Yes I realize this isn't a bug, but this wouldn't make sense to be on Product Pains since it's mostly maintainer-facing_

Could this issue relate to the overall architecture of the project, and more specifically to the potential split between a "core" codebase and "plugins"?
What I mean by that is that if we had a "core" package, and then "plugin" packages, you would know which additional features are being used just by looking at the number of downloads / issues created / PR submitted for each individual plugin.
I feel that adding another feature to the project (this time, analytics) is not a good solution to help shipping v4... Instead, it should be the opposite, the codebase should be getting lighter.
It doesn't really make sense that there are so many issues related to Cloudinary and so on, when a lot of users will never use that service and are just waiting for a stable release of basic v4 (like me :) )
The example of babel and their strategy for going from v5 to v6 seems a good example, don't you think? They isolated a core and externalized a lot of plugins, and in the process had to design a clear API for each plugin to integrate with core. I would love to see that with Keystone as well.


Comment 4 (source ID 228532266) | Participant 1 | created 2016-06-25T10:57:38Z | updated 2016-06-25T10:57:38Z
Source: https://github.com/keystonejs/keystone-classic/issues/3075#issuecomment-228532266
> They isolated a core and externalized a lot of plugins, and in the process had to design a clear API for each plugin to integrate with core.

That's what we're working towards and is one of the big reasons v4 is such a long update! (sorry about that…)
We are now using react, which will very easily allow us to split out and integrate new fields (like Cloudinary), which in combination with #3052 will make our life maintaining the core a lot easier.

We will definitely not make that happen for v4, since we do want to get that released asap, but it's very very high up on our roadmap!

> I feel that adding another feature to the project (this time, analytics) is not a good solution to help shipping v4...

This is not a feature per-se, as no user will ever see this. This is solely for us maintainers, and it's very important and I do want to get this in before the v4 release.

We maintainers have no clue what the hell people are doing with Keystone, and while Product Pains was a good first step to get more clarity it's not enough. Adding analytics to the interface (which will hopefully will not be too difficult, shouldn't really delay the release anyway) will help us massively to focus on making those features that people are actually using better!

Big thumbs down from my end. Remember when [Strongloop tracked user version distribution by abusing npm](https://github.com/strongloop/loopback/issues/1079)? Granted, this planned tracking in Keystone is a very different (and less shady) scenario but please read those user's reactions to being tracked by OSS.

Do other popular npm modules engage in this kind of opt-out tracking? I expect this kind of thing from SaaS but **never** in OSS.

If you want usability feedback there are less underhanded and frankly **more effective** ways of getting this data, including compensated IRL usability trials & voluntary usability surveys.

This kind of tracking blurs the line between commercial product & OSS in a way that I am not comfortable with.

Source: https://github.com/keystonejs/keystone-classic/issues/3075#issuecomment-232408934
@morenoh149 those are features we don't have yet, not how our existing features are used.

To provide my perspective on why this is valuable, we currently have several APIs that integrate file uploading to S3 and Cloudinary integrated with TinyMCE. I'd _love_ to rip them out and make room for better ones based on the new Storage stuff that's in the works. The problem is I don't know whether there are 5 or 5000 people using those features.

Knowing what's being used, and how, is only going to become more important in terms of understanding which features are safe to deprecate, which to invest in, and whether we're actually optimising Keystone for its real audience. We only interact with a small fraction of users here and in other channels, in terms of total installs. Most of our usage is totally opaque.

These aren't questions that usability trials can answer for us.

re: Strongloop's blip - that's hostile because it was sneaky, you couldn't opt out of it, was a technical abuse of peer dependencies, exposed a vulnerability, and caused install delays / errors. I didn't see a lot of complaints that would be relevant given the way @mxstbr is designing this for Keystone.

In terms of whether there's a precedent for OSS to track usage, I think that's mixed. I mentioned Yeoman already. Node itself obviously doesn't/can't; npm tracks heaps of things. If you're serving something, nobody questions whether you can do analytics; if you're charging people, the same. We're disadvantaged because we're building software, not services, and giving it away under the most liberal license possible for free. Kind of ironic :)

Something I'm really interested in is whether django, wordpress, and other apps similar to Keystone do any of this (unfortunately a search for "Wordpress analytics" is pretty useless). Although I'm sure wordpress have a tonne of usage data just from wordpress.com which is completely controlled by Automattic.

Comment 23 (source ID 232419537) | Participant 4 | created 2016-07-13T17:01:14Z | updated 2016-07-13T17:01:14Z

@JedWatson 

[Atom](https://github.com/atom/metrics) is another project that does this. Adding metrics to atom is/was a [contentious issue](https://github.com/atom/atom/issues/4966).

If you look at the dependents of the [yeoman insights package](https://www.npmjs.com/package/insight), you can see other projects that use Google Analytics to track users. Big players I recognized include Apache Cordova, GitHub command line tools and Jenkins command line tools. So there _is_ precedent.

I don't believe that tracking users via Google Analytics is the only way to get the information you want. That being said, if you _must_ do this, an **opt-in** approach is a satisfactory compromise. Obviously, you don't have to listen to me :smile:. I think this is the best way to communicate your intent-to-track to the user & allow them to explicitly provide consent.

@mxstbr You may not think this is a big deal but many other people in this community do (see linked atom thread). KeystoneJS risks alienating users if it adopts a cavalier attitude towards user privacy.

Title says it all, per Sandy's suggestion. I think if we decide to implement this, we should be careful with the following two issues:

- collected data should not be erased through the clear cache button.

Source: https://github.com/fesch/CanZE/issues/349#issuecomment-231595447
I have given this suggestion a bit more thought. In all fairness, I don't think we can implement this without cloud based storage. Phones live 2-3 years (with probably one or two full factory resets in that time frame); degradation to 75% for a ZOE is expected in the rough order of 200.000 kilometers, which is much more than the lifespan of the device.

Given the reluctance to implement and also maintain ANYTHING with remote data, partly because of Luxembourg and German legislation, I think this might be something we need to let go.

@fesch what do you think?

I'm not a lawyer I could be wrong here, but when it comes to user privacy why even risk it? We should take all precautions to not post real names and email addresses when we can. @murny the user agreement *explicitly* allows us to use submission data (which would include the publicly accessible metadata) and distribute it in any format, and would definitely cover testing / inclusion in GitHub. Our agreement was reviewed by both legal counsel and copyright office. Our privacy policy IS the UofA's privacy policy, but because this is information provided explicitly by users for these explicit purposes I'm confident we are not in breach of either it or any FOIP legislation.  @sfarnel @leahvanderjagt are both *very* well versed in FOIP and related policy and data management concerns and can likely provide very complete and detailed information if you would like to know more. The clause in the agreement that is most relevant is below. As long as we're respecting the access rules the user set, we could theoretically print a submission on shirts and wear them around the office if we wanted. 

"By accepting this agreement, you (the author or copyright right owner or designate) grant to the University of Alberta the non-exclusive rights to reproduce, translate (as defined below), and/or distribute your submission (including the abstract) worldwide in print and electronic format and in any medium, including but not limited to audio or video"

Think there is two different issues here. 

Item metadata is one thing. This is what @sfbetz is talking about with regards to our user agreement. (So by all means, we are protected legally. Ethically however should we be going around and posting people's names and other personal information found in ERA on 3rd party websites not associated with U of A?  I hope your not condoning that someone can post every single author/contributor/supervisor name that can be found in ERA here in github or somewhere else? I mean of course legally, you can and are protected. But should you?  Regardless why publicize people's names and other information on a 3rd party website not associated with U of A (regardless if you can legally or not)? What value does it give to publicize this information? There is no value added here if you include this information or not...

User data (CCID and other information that comes from CCID login) however I am pretty sure is a different can of worms. I would assume, they do not waive their right for this. And I am pretty sure IST and UofA wants you to protect this information (think we signed a document with IST with regards to privacy for this information even). I would really hate to see everyone of our user's ccid/email posted online (even though every one of our user's ccid/email is....publicly available in ERA currently: https://github.com/ualbertalib/di_internal/issues/2). We been told this information is so private, that we can't even put this information in 3rd party applications that we have full control of and only we can see that data (Rollbar/google analytics/etc). But yet we are posting it on github? This makes little sense.  And again, I have no idea why I am seeing such a big pushback here?

But If your saying we can, then sorry to everyone above, that I am wrong! If this is the case, we should probably stop caring so much about privacy issues around google analytics, putting logs and user's information on 3rd party services and other things. And probably should start pushing back on higher ups regarding this.

### Bug description
Random "Locked Message" notifications that supposedly just say: "Contact XYZ is on Signal!";
The thing is... they're not! On multiple occasions, I've called these people and they've never even heard about the app.
For most of my contacts, especially friends and family, I'm their "go-to IT person", so I'm pretty darn sure they would ask me if it's OK or safe to move from WhatsApp/Telegram/Messenger/whatever to Signal since they've done exactly that previously on other occasions. Issue body:
### Acknowledgements

- [X] I acknowledge that I have read the above items

### Describe the bug

LocalStorage of "greylisted" websites is not cleared at browser restart (and maybe also some other piece of data)
I detected the bug in particular with website https://www.lefigaro.fr/

The first time you access to this website, it asks for your consent to cookies, and records your answer, in order to do not ask you the same at your next access.
Your consent is not stored in a cookie (lefigaro.fr do not actually create any cookie) but in LocalStorage.

If there is no rule defined in CAD relative to this website, cleansing of this data (your consent) is correctlty done by CAD if you close the tab, a/o switch in the tab to another domain a/o restart the browser, and when the cleansing is done, re-opening the site asks again for your consent.

But if there is a "GreyList" rule defined on the domain, with all boxes checked ("Keep ... until restart"), the cleansing is not done if you "only" close the tab or switch to another domain (which is expected behaviour), but no cleansing as well is done EVEN IF YOU RESTART browser... whch is a bug.


### To Reproduce

Steps to reproduce 

Step 1:
To start on a "blank page", clear in Firefox all data relative to any website.
Do not create any rule in CAD, neither Blank nor Grey, relative to lefigaro.fr
Suspend automatic cleansing in CAD
Open www.lefigaro.fr and give (or reject) your consent to cookies
Close the tab, or switch to another domain, or restart the browser
Open again www.lefigaro.fr and see that your consent is no more asked
Activate automatic cleansing in CAD
Close the tab (the one opend on lefigaro.fr), or switch to another domain, or restart the browser
Wait for automatic cleansing
Open again www.lefigaro.fr and see that now your consent is again asked.

Step 2 :
To start also this 2nd step on a "blank page", clear again in Firefox all data relative to any website.
Create in CAD a "GreyList" rule, on "*.lefigaro.fr", with all boxes ("keep until restart") checked.
Activate automatic cleansing in CAD
Open www.lefigaro.fr and give (or reject) your consent to cookies
Close the tab, or switch to another domain.
Open again www.lefigaro.fr and verify that your consent is no more asked (normal, since "GreyList")
Restart the browser
Wait for automatic cleansing
Open again www.lefigaro.fr and see that your consent is still no more asked.... while it should if cleansing at restart has been effective.


### Expected Behavior

To have ALL data relative to GreyListed website (including the LocaStorage) cleared at browser restart,and then to have the website asking again for your consent to cookies.

### Screenshots

_No response_

### System Info - Operating System (OS)

Windows 10 Pro 21H1

### System Info - Browser Info

Firefox 90.0.2 (64 bits)

### System Info - CookieAutoDelete Version

3.6.0

### Additional Context
