Issue body:
The cookie settings is hidden under a menu which I wasn't even aware of when I first visited the site. 

https://gdpr.eu/cookies/
Via the gdpr directive it seems you must have explicit consent _before_ using any cookies except for "strictly necessary" cookies. This could be done with a popup on first visit.

Issue discussion (chronological; participant names pseudonymized within the case):
Comment 1 (source ID 705051261) | Participant 2 | created 2020-10-07T16:28:39Z | updated 2020-10-07T16:35:33Z
Source: https://github.com/datenanfragen/website/issues/430#issuecomment-705051261
Thanks for bringing this up. We have very deliberately opted not to have a cookie popup. We are not fans of cookie popups (they are annoying and provide little actual use to the user). One of our core philosophies is to design our sites in the most privacy-friendly way possible, mostly through data minimization meaning that we don't actually process any personal data unless absolutely necessary. As a result, we are of the opinion that our current implementation is in line with the relevant legislation. Nevertheless, we actually do have some changes planned to improve this aspect even more.

Let me elaborate. Note that this is our interpretation of the law. We are however not lawyers and cannot give legal advice.

The GDPR is actually not relevant in this case, it doesn't care about cookies, only personal data (see [our blog post](https://www.datarequests.org/blog/gdpr-cheat-sheet/) or Art. 4 GDPR for exact definitions of these terms) that is processed by a controller (which would be us in this case). In our case, we have made sure that we never even receive any of the data saved in the cookies, so we cannot process it.

The legislation that is actually relevant has the very compact name of ["Directive 2009/136/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 25 November 2009 amending Directive 2002/22/EC on universal service and users’ rights relating to electronic communications networks and services, Directive 2002/58/EC concerning the processing of personal data and the protection of privacy in the electronic communications sector and Regulation (EC) No 2006/2004 on cooperation between national authorities responsible for the enforcement of consumer protection laws"](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2009/136/oj) (and is thus usually just called the "cookie directive"). In particular, we are interested in this provision:

> Member States shall ensure that the storing of information, or the gaining of access to information already stored, in the terminal equipment of a subscriber or user is only allowed on condition that the subscriber or user concerned has given his or her consent, having been provided with clear and comprehensive information, in accordance with Directive 95/46/EC, inter alia, about the purposes of the processing. This shall not prevent any technical storage or access for the sole purpose of carrying out the transmission of a communication over an electronic communications network, or as strictly necessary in order for the provider of an information society service explicitly requested by the subscriber or user to provide the service.

This is where the "strictly necessary" is coming from. In order to interpret that, we can look at [this working paper by the Article 29 working group](https://ec.europa.eu/justice/article-29/documentation/opinion-recommendation/files/2012/wp194_en.pdf). Chapter 3 lists various use cases that can be classified as "strictly necessary". Of interest to us are "user-input cookies" ("typically used to keep track of the user’s input when filling online forms over several pages"), "UI customization cookies" ("used to store a user’s preference regarding a service across web pages") and "result display preference cookies" (used to remember the user’s preference regarding online search queries).

In terms of actual cookies, there are actually only two that are set automatically: `country` and `changed_saved_companies`. All other cookies are only set after the user has interacted with a relevant control.  
We have concluded that the `country` cookie is strictly necessary for our website. It is filled with a best guess when the user first enters the website. As the country determines the companies the user sees (among other things), it is very important to be consistent here. Without a cookie saving this information, we wouldn't be able to ensure that the user always sees the same companies.  
As for the `changed_saved_companies` cookie, legally speaking we think that it also falls under the "strictly necessary" definition. However, we have determined that we can also implement the wizard on the homepage in a way that only sets a cookie once the user has changed something. This is a change we plan to implement.

We also save some data in local storage (one of the local storage APIs anyway, as we are using [localForage](https://localforage.github.io/localForage/)). I won't go into detail on that here but we have of course also evaluated the necessity of those individual cases and have determined that our use is OK here. However, we also want to improve even more and limit data storage where possible.

Here are also some additional references that we considered (sorry, these are only available in German as they are in relation to a recent German court case on this topic): [1](https://www.bundesgerichtshof.de/SharedDocs/Pressemitteilungen/DE/2020/2020067.html?nn=10690868), [2](https://diercks-digital-recht.de/2019/10/zum-eugh-urteil-planet49-az-c-673-17-benoetigen-cookies-ab-jetzt-immer-einer-einwilligung-spoiler-nein/), [3](https://diercks-digital-recht.de/2020/05/eine-erste-einordnung-des-bgh-urteils-cookie-ii-i-zr-7-16-voreingestellte-einwilligungen-opt-outs-sind-unwirksam-und-das-gilt-grundsaetzlich-auch-fuer-cookies/)

Finally, regarding our [privacy controls](https://www.datarequests.org/privacy-controls): These actually don't (primarily) deal with cookies. They allow you to enable and disable certain features of the website that sometimes require the use of local storage. For each of them, we have evaluated whether it is appropriate to enable them by default. For the current privacy controls, we concluded that they are all "safe" and "private" enough as (apart from the search) they all work solely in the user's browser and never transmit any data to us (and of course, the search feature doesn't save any data either). Personally, I honestly see little reason to disable any of our current privacy controls but we have still decided to provide that ability out of principle.

As I have said, we don't believe in big popups that interrupt the flow (and that most users just accept anyway without reading). Instead, we have tried to incorporate links to the privacy controls when the user actually comes into contact with the relevant features. For example, take a look at the "entertainment" tab of the wizard on the homepage or the "My saved data" page.

I hope this explains our considerations of this topic. Sorry for the long wall of text but this is a complex topic that we have put a lot of thought into (after all, that is sort of what we do :D). We do of course welcome any input on how we can improve. Let us know what you think.

Linked pages and attachments are not fetched. Issue retrieved at: 2026-10-19T03:11:53.299066+00:00 Issue last updated at: 2018-05-16T10:59:23Z Title at retrieval: Possible Data Leakage Through AMP Load Cookie iFrame Status at retrieval: closed Retrieved issue comments: 11/11 Issue body: Just checking on this. It seems that the AMP Cookie Sync iFrame is loading against all possible bidders irrespective of whether they're being used on the page. In the two examples below e-planning and conversant are dropping cookies despite not being bidders. This would breach GDPR where the data is neither being used and presumably consent would not have been received to do this. I don't know if it's possible but it would seem that the possible solution may be to pass bidders through to the cookie sync in url vars. If my observations are correct. Issue discussion (chronological; participant names pseudonymized within the case): Comment 1 (source ID 386053199) | Participant 2 | created 2018-05-02T17:17:02Z | updated 2018-05-02T17:17:02Z Source: https://github.com/prebid/prebid-server/issues/490#issuecomment-386053199 That's a really good catch! @jaiminpanchal27, @mkendall07, @jsnellbaker ... thoughts? Comment 2 (source ID 386085051) | Participant 3 | created 2018-05-02T19:00:06Z | updated 2018-05-02T19:00:06Z Source: https://github.com/prebid/prebid-server/issues/490#issuecomment-386085051 @dbemiller https://github.com/prebid/prebid-universal-creative/blob/master/src/cookieSync.js#L97 Comment 3 (source ID 386133591) | Participant 4 | created 2018-05-02T21:54:15Z | updated 2018-05-02T21:54:15Z Source: https://github.com/prebid/prebid-server/issues/490#issuecomment-386133591 it looks like AMP is integrating some kind of consent framework. We'll need to look into that and see if it's possible to pass consent data into PBS. https://github.com/ampproject/amphtml/issues/13716 Comment 4 (source ID 386342428) | Participant 2 | created 2018-05-03T15:48:57Z | updated 2018-05-03T15:48:57Z Source: https://github.com/prebid/prebid-server/issues/490#issuecomment-386342428 @mkendall07 I dove through AMP a bit to understand the `amp-consent` tag, and how it relates to `amp-ad` and `amp-iframe`. The former is used for PBS auctions, and the latter for PBS cookie syncs. Here are some highlights: 1. [This comment](https://github.com/ampproject/amphtml/issues/13716#issuecomment-386115655) says that the `amp-consent` tag only exposes [an enum value](https://github.com/ampproject/amphtml/blob/master/extensions/amp-consent/customizing-extension-behaviors-on-consent.md#advanced-blocking-behaviors) to other elements. There won't be enough info there for us to make bidder-specific decisions. 2. Consent status [is available to `amp-ad` extensions](https://github.com/ampproject/amphtml/issues/14921), but `amp-iframe` ones are a [work in progress](https://github.com/ampproject/amphtml/issues/14877)... so we couldn't use it in our `amp-iframe` yet even if we wanted to. 3. We _may_ be able to pass this flag into the actual `auction` call, depending on the ad network being used. `amp-ad` implementations can define [their own macros](https://github.com/ampproject/amphtml/blob/master/extensions/amp-a4a/rtc-documentation.md#fast-fetch-implementation-defined-macros), which we could then encode into [our vendor URL](https://github.com/ampproject/amphtml/blob/master/extensions/amp-a4a/0.1/callout-vendors.js#L45). I doubt any ad networks are doing this yet, so we would have to submit PRs to the networks we care about, or convince them. As an example, the doubleclick code is [here](https://github.com/ampproject/amphtml/blob/master/extensions/amp-ad-network-doubleclick-impl/0.1/amp-ad-network-doubleclick-impl.js#L716) Comment 5 (source ID 386345847) | Participant 2 | created 2018-05-03T15:59:23Z | updated 2018-05-03T16:00:00Z Source: https://github.com/prebid/prebid-server/issues/490#issuecomment-386345847 @gramorris I'm not a GDPR expert, so... a question about this: > I don't know if it's possible but it would seem that the possible solution may be to pass bidders through to the cookie sync in url vars. If my observations are correct. I thought that GDPR required users to give their consent to _each company_ who wanted to use their personal info. If we added query string param support for bidders, how would the publisher [setting up their AMP page](http://prebid.org/dev-docs/show-prebid-ads-on-amp-pages.html#amp-content-page) know which bidders the user had consented to? Comment 6 (source ID 386348450) | Participant 1 | created 2018-05-03T16:06:57Z | updated 2018-05-03T16:06:57Z Source: https://github.com/prebid/prebid-server/issues/490#issuecomment-386348450 Yeah you're right, that doesn't satisfy GDPR. On the consent flags in the amp implementation I don't think that's fit for purpose yet. We've just got to the testing stage now but I don't think there's the ability (there should be and hopefully will be) to get optional consent for multiple vendors and have separate consent flags for each. Google are selling the AMP solution so I'm assuming they intend to have it complete at some point. Comment 7 (source ID 386392089) | Participant 2 | created 2018-05-03T18:27:11Z | updated 2018-05-04T17:17:54Z Source: https://github.com/prebid/prebid-server/issues/490#issuecomment-386392089 Actually... I may have spoken too soon here. [This Issue](https://github.com/ampproject/amphtml/issues/14877) is making sure that `amp-consent` info can be seen from `amp-iframe` and `amp-ad` tags. The [amp-consent docs](https://www.ampproject.org/docs/reference/components/amp-consent) say that the tag only supports a single `consent` ID instance (for now), and @mkendall07 found an [amp-story-consent tag PR](https://github.com/ampproject/amphtml/pull/15062) opened just yesterday. Note the `vendors` list in the example: ``` “story-consent”: { “title”: "Foo", “message”: "Bar", “vendors”: ["Item 1", "Item 2", "Item 3", "Item 4"], “color”: "#0379c4" } ``` All that in mind: it seems like their strategy is for publishers to use a single Consent instance/UI, and list all the vendors who they plan to share data with in their consent modal. If that's all accurate, then it seems like we _could_ pass query strings, the way you suggested. You could do the following ``` { "consents": { "some-id": { "checkConsentHref": "http://path.to.your/amp_consent_url", "promptUI": "consent-ui" } } } ``` And then make sure that the `consent-ui` element lists off the PBS Host company and all the Bidders who you plan to sync. We could enhance `/cookie_sync` to allow Bidders as arguments, as well as in query params to `cookieSync` script that @jaiminpanchal27 linked. It would then be up to the Publisher to make sure they include any Bidders who they drop cookie syncs for in their consent UI. Comment 8 (source ID 388043092) | Participant 2 | created 2018-05-10T12:46:56Z | updated 2018-05-10T12:47:58Z Source: https://github.com/prebid/prebid-server/issues/490#issuecomment-388043092 I was researching stuff for #501 (similar issue in non-AMP pages), and found that the IAB defines a spec for CMPs. These manage consent data across pages, and have some standards for use in iframes: - [Determine if a CMP is Present](https://github.com/InteractiveAdvertisingBureau/GDPR-Transparency-and-Consent-Framework/blob/master/CMP%20JS%20API%20v1.1%20Final.md#how-can-callers-determine-if-there-is-a-cmp-present-) - [Calling the CMP API from an iframe](https://github.com/InteractiveAdvertisingBureau/GDPR-Transparency-and-Consent-Framework/blob/master/CMP%20JS%20API%20v1.1%20Final.md#how-can-vendors-that-use-iframes-call-the-cmp-api-from-an-iframe-) If there's some way to load your CMP onto an AMP page and we can find a way to get the consent info into it, this would be a much better solution. Comment 9 (source ID 388428056) | Participant 5 | created 2018-05-11T17:17:25Z | updated 2018-05-11T17:17:25Z Source: https://github.com/prebid/prebid-server/issues/490#issuecomment-388428056 @dbemiller, Vamsee from the AMP team here. > It would then be up to the Publisher to make sure they include any Bidders who they drop cookie syncs for in their consent UI. This is exactly the assumption under which is currently developed. Having said that we are looking at supporting per vendor, per purpose based consent post May 25th if that's something publisher absolutely request. Comment 10 (source ID 389164866) | Participant 2 | created 2018-05-15T13:23:43Z | updated 2018-05-15T13:23:43Z Source: https://github.com/prebid/prebid-server/issues/490#issuecomment-389164866 @jasti Thanks for the details Vamsee. I did a bit more research, and I don't think [AMP's localstorage scheme](https://github.com/ampproject/amphtml/issues/13716) will integrate well with the IAB's [Transparency and Consent framework](https://github.com/InteractiveAdvertisingBureau/GDPR-Transparency-and-Consent-Framework). In particular, it's very difficult (if not impossible) to implement [the CMP APIs](https://github.com/InteractiveAdvertisingBureau/GDPR-Transparency-and-Consent-Framework/blob/master/CMP%20JS%20API%20v1.1%20Final.md#what-api-will-need-to-be-provided-by-the-cmp-) given the state: `amp-consent:${consentInstanceId}: true/false`. So... I don't think it's possible for publishers using the Prebids to be able to share the user's consent between AMP and non-AMP pages. All that in mind, I logged https://github.com/prebid/prebid-universal-creative/issues/19 to add the query params and update the AMP docs. Once closed, publishers will need to update their `amp-iframe` tags to send in the query params of the bidders they want to sync. Since Prebid Server's `/cookie_sync` endpoint [already accepts a list of Bidders to sync](https://github.com/prebid/prebid-server/blob/master/docs/endpoints/cookieSync.md), I don't think there's any more work to do for AMP in this project. @gramorris please close this and follow https://github.com/prebid/prebid-universal-creative/issues/19 if you feel like this sufficiently addresses your concerns. Comment 11 (source ID 389479248) | Participant 1 | created 2018-05-16T10:59:22Z | updated 2018-05-16T10:59:22Z Source: https://github.com/prebid/prebid-server/issues/490#issuecomment-389479248 @dbemiller @jasti Thanks I'll close this, in the immediate term with the amp-consent limitations I'd accept this as the solution. We have a non-optimal solution to ensure we have some level of consent on AMP pages.

In theory, all methods implemented by the tool are relevant for implementing privacy protection as required by the GDPR.

Issue body:
```
 Call to a member function getType() on boolean in /mysite/mod/search/views/default/search/object/comment/entity.php:15
```

i have seen these errors in my logs for over a year. having explored the cause, i found that this line does not find a container when i am logged out and the search results point to a specific comment (which apparently has been orphaned somehow):

```
$container = $entity->getContainerEntity()
```


Issue discussion (chronological; participant names pseudonymized within the case):
Comment 1 (source ID 227144594) | Participant 2 | created 2016-06-20T13:39:56Z | updated 2016-06-20T13:39:56Z
Source: https://github.com/Elgg/Elgg/issues/9911#issuecomment-227144594
We have a lot of code that fails to check the return of getContainerEntity() before using it.


Comment 2 (source ID 227152373) | Participant 1 | created 2016-06-20T14:08:05Z | updated 2016-06-20T14:08:05Z
Source: https://github.com/Elgg/Elgg/issues/9911#issuecomment-227152373
i don't really understand what the code is doing here enough to know the best solution. in my workaround i just intended to bypass outputting the comment in the search results completely if there is no container guid.. but _now_ when i run the search i see the comment appearing in the results correctly..
so either there is a duplicate comment in my database somehow, one of which has no container guid - or somehow the container guid got added to the comment in between the tests i ran (_unlikely_)!
my approach, in general, is to always maintain database integrity as the primary solution to such issues - so i would run a database patch to fix the database and any orphaned entities ideally.


Comment 3 (source ID 227221315) | Participant 3 | created 2016-06-20T18:05:28Z | updated 2016-06-20T18:05:28Z
Source: https://github.com/Elgg/Elgg/issues/9911#issuecomment-227221315
It's not that it has no container guid, it's that the container the guid belongs to isn't able to load (due to access_id).


Comment 4 (source ID 227226825) | Participant 1 | created 2016-06-20T18:25:05Z | updated 2016-06-20T18:25:05Z
Source: https://github.com/Elgg/Elgg/issues/9911#issuecomment-227226825
@beck24 ah, ok - yes that sounds more likely. so is that something that wasn't considered fully when comments became entities?


Comment 5 (source ID 227229577) | Participant 3 | created 2016-06-20T18:34:58Z | updated 2016-06-20T18:34:58Z
Source: https://github.com/Elgg/Elgg/issues/9911#issuecomment-227229577
no it was a problem before that as well, just an oversight when coding the views.  Someone used $entity->getContainerEntity(); and then started using $container without first making sure we actually have $container.


Comment 6 (source ID 227240286) | Participant 1 | created 2016-06-20T19:13:49Z | updated 2016-06-20T19:13:49Z
Source: https://github.com/Elgg/Elgg/issues/9911#issuecomment-227240286
in the case of the comments entity view on the search results page, i think the needed change will be further up the source file path than at this view level since a check needs to be made for the container before the view is rendered.. otherwise, the result is that the comment still appears in the search results but as an empty box.


Comment 7 (source ID 227243031) | Participant 3 | created 2016-06-20T19:24:39Z | updated 2016-06-20T19:24:39Z
Source: https://github.com/Elgg/Elgg/issues/9911#issuecomment-227243031
For that you would have to add container access to the search query, that will make the already heavy search queries even heavier and this is pretty much an edge case.  I would rather bail on the view if the container isn't fetchable, if an empty comment is unacceptable we could put in some placeholder message explaining the lack of comment.  Or render the comment without linking to the container.


Comment 8 (source ID 227250934) | Participant 1 | created 2016-06-20T19:55:27Z | updated 2016-06-20T20:23:55Z
Source: https://github.com/Elgg/Elgg/issues/9911#issuecomment-227250934
the issue for privacy is that if you have a placeholder message explaining the lack of comment, then it will be plausible that private data can be searched for and found, via a process of elimination. let's say you write "my password is muffins" in a private group and then i search for "my password is" - i will then see that private comments exist that contain that phrase since there is an empty comment rendered in the search results. i'm sure the average hacker can think of a few ways to exploit that.
is there a reason why it is a problem to just exclude such comments in the PHP, before the point of rendering an entity view for them?


Comment 9 (source ID 227256971) | Participant 3 | created 2016-06-20T20:19:20Z | updated 2016-06-20T20:19:20Z
Source: https://github.com/Elgg/Elgg/issues/9911#issuecomment-227256971
Technically it wouldn't be an issue for privacy, as you have access to the comment anyway


Comment 10 (source ID 227258512) | Participant 1 | created 2016-06-20T20:25:10Z | updated 2016-06-20T20:25:10Z
Source: https://github.com/Elgg/Elgg/issues/9911#issuecomment-227258512
if the container can't be loaded due to access reasons, doesn't that imply that the comment shouldn't be loadable either?


Comment 11 (source ID 227355621) | Participant 4 | created 2016-06-21T06:53:58Z | updated 2016-06-21T06:53:58Z
Source: https://github.com/Elgg/Elgg/issues/9911#issuecomment-227355621
As far as I remember comment access is synced with the container access. Maybe there are some old comments that weren't synced?


Comment 12 (source ID 227376116) | Participant 3 | created 2016-06-21T08:37:04Z | updated 2016-06-21T08:37:04Z
Source: https://github.com/Elgg/Elgg/issues/9911#issuecomment-227376116
Yes, it's a legacy edge case issue.
Regarding the question of whether the container access has any bearing on the comment access when not in sync - I think it's questionable.  It's the same thing with hidden groups wanting to publish public group content, depends on the needs of the site.  Given that this specific case is a legacy issue I don't really care either way what we do with the comment, just that we're not erroring out.


Comment 13 (source ID 227383348) | Participant 1 | created 2016-06-21T09:08:39Z | updated 2016-06-21T09:08:39Z
Source: https://github.com/Elgg/Elgg/issues/9911#issuecomment-227383348
if someone adds a comment to a private group, then the comments are expected by the author to be private regardless of technical issues. @beck24 why are you calling this a legacy issue? isn't the issue and its causes present in all current versions of code?


Comment 14 (source ID 227387494) | Participant 4 | created 2016-06-21T09:26:01Z | updated 2016-06-21T09:26:01Z
Source: https://github.com/Elgg/Elgg/issues/9911#issuecomment-227387494
The situation you are encountering is no longer possible - comment  access is always synced with the container. I don't think we ever implemented an upgrade script for older comments.
Try updating the container (edit and save) and see if the issue persists.

Title at retrieval: Separate coinbase and non-coinbase rings

Issue body:
# Summary

Monero should add a consensus rule to require spends of coinbase outputs to select only other coinbase output decoys, and for transactions to require rings with at least 1 non-coinbase output to only contain non-coinbase outputs. Wallets should select only coinbase rings when spending coinbase, and only non-coinbase when spending non-coinbase. There are a variety of other related improvements to improve privacy.

# Problem

Users currently include coinbase outputs in their rings, which are distinguishable from non-coinbase outputs. The vast majority of users do not conceivably spend coinbase outputs. This reduces the effective anonymity set by 1-2 outputs per ring. We are wasting about 15% of the rings in most transactions.

In addition to spends of coinbase outputs not aligning with conceivable user behavior, many public mining pools reveal blocks they mine and transactions paid to miners. With this information, these coinbase outputs may be considered heuristically dead for these other reasons. @sneurlax made a tool that looked at this public mining pool information for some common pools to trace heuristically dead coinbase outputs: https://github.com/sneurlax/xmreuse. I used these lists when running the Monero Blackball (Spent Output) tool at https://moneroblackball.com.

[More background](https://medium.com/@JEhrenhofer/lets-stop-using-coinbase-outputs-da672ca75d43?source=friends_link&sk=48cac958597ddc4be004bbb5d5f59f95)

# Fix

**Consensus changes**: Require rings to either contain all coinbase outputs or all non-coinbase outputs. If rings have 1 or more outputs of a different type, reject the transaction.

**Wallet changes**: When spending coinbase outputs, select only coinbase outputs as decoys. When spending non-coinbase outputs, select only non-coinbase outputs as decoys.

**Advanced wallet changes**: When spending a coinbase-only ring, send a warning, strongly recommending that users "churn" their funds before spending to an address not known to the wallet. If there is a coinbase output in the wallet's possession, warn that users who care about privacy should churn these outputs before spending. Ideally, there would be a wallet `churn-coinbase` spend option in that churns all of the coinbase outputs to the main wallet address. This should be accomplished by running a command in the CLI, or by a prominent button in the GUI or other wallets. Wallets should prominently display when there are unspent coinbase outputs and encourage a churn of them. Wallets should prioritize spending of non-coinbase outputs to others.

# Benefits

Users will no longer spend Monero with coinbase outputs as non-plausible decoys. Their effective ringsize will be greater by about 15%. This doesn't cost any efficiency.

Users will be warned when spending coinbase funds so that they are less likely to make spends with lessened privacy.

# Neutral

Public pools that already share information about what blocks they mine are unaffected. Users of mining pools, both public and private, are unaffected. Private pools *should* be mostly unaffected if they only pay miners.

# Downsides

Private pools should churn coinbase outputs if sending these to non-miners. Solo miners should churn coinbase outputs before sending them to someone else. Coinbase outputs, which are more likely to be deducible than non-coinbase outputs, are concentrated in rings; this is another argument in support of churning before sending coins to non-miners.

# Configurable Items, Related Items, and Areas for Improvement

## Selection algorithm

Sarang Noether looked at the spend histories of deducible, pre-RCT Monero outputs. The coinbase spends largely match up with non-coinbase spends:

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/12520755/85618857-04479000-b627-11ea-8f14-94622a2af3e5.png)

He also broke them out by 200k block chunks. While there are some differences over time, these differences are relatively small.

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/12520755/85618952-29d49980-b627-11ea-9d32-78306f609477.png)

Furthermore, the data is relatively old (and it's not possible to get newer data; go Monero privacy!). It would be best to have more recent data on Bitcoin coinbase spends.

We have an option to adjust the selection algorithms to treat coinbase and non-coinbase outputs separately. Given the data above however, I argue there is no significant reason to do this. If we learn of a strong reason to adjust, I think that's something we can approach when we get there.

## Wallet spends

We can optionally prevent wallets from spending coinbase outputs to others' addresses. However, this can not be enforced by consensus, and it would negatively impact mining pools who use this software.

## Ringsize

Ringsize can now be adjusted separately for coinbase and non-coinbase rings. Since information on coinbase outputs are often publicly shared, they are more likely to be deducible than non-coinbase outputs. However, if users already are assuming that these outputs will be deducible anyway, we may be able to drop the ringsize to make the blockchain more efficient.

Back when I wrote my article "Let's Stop Using Coinbase Outputs," I estimated that about 90% of outputs were directly deducible. With ringsize 11 and all-coinbase rings, a further ~35% of these remaining 10% would be deducible by chain reaction. Decreasing this proportion to 1% would take ringsize ~45. Ringsize 11 provides protection up to cases where ~60-65% of outputs are deducible.

Options are:

* Drop the coinbase ringsize to 1 or 3 for efficiency. Mostly write off coinbase outputs as a lost cause.

* Keep it the same

* Increase it knowing that coinbase outputs are a deducible bloodbath if we really feel that we need to protect coinbase outputs. It will cost us.

Note that if we drop the coinbase ringsize to 1 or 3, we can increase the non-coinbase ringsize by 1-3 at "no net cost." Something to think about. It's difficult to justify giving special privacy protections to coinbase outputs when pools make the info public anyway. If their funds ever are at risk of being blacklisted by other miners or of any other consequence that comes with potential graph traceability, then all they need to do is not make their own info public anymore. That being said, setting the ringsize to at least 3 is probably justified, even if there are large chain reaction impacts. It at least makes certain types of analysis on non-public pools more difficult at an extremely small cost. Pools will also likely appreciate slightly smaller transaction fees.

## Different pool selection algorithms

I opened up this issue about a year ago, focusing on mining pool transaction payouts https://github.com/monero-project/monero/issues/5222. The selection algorithm can be improved to reduce the deducibility of non-coinbase outputs. While related, these are different proposals and are not mutually exclusive.

## Pool outreach

In any case, pools should be informed about the way that they are sharing information to the public in a way that may be detrimental to the network. We should encourage pools to keep certain sensitive information private. Pools should only reveal payments to the miners involved in the specific payments, not to all miners or to the general public.

My thoughts on this is that while this a very valid issue, I cannot agree with the proposed fix. In order to place this into perspective it important to consider the actual impact on non coinbase transactions. We first take a look at the trend in non coin base transactions https://bitinfocharts.com/comparison/monero-transactions.html#log. When we consider that current non coinbase transactions have a minimum of 2 outputs we have coin base outputs are about 5% of total outputs, If the selection is algorithm is weighted towards current transactions then one would expect at most about 5% of compromised coinbase outputs in a ring. With a ring size of 11 the typical variance would be 0, 1, or 2 in most cases. The mitigation to this I see is to increase the ring size following out current sequence of primes: 13, 17, 19 etc with each hard fork as an interim solution until Triptych, Arcturus or a similar solution allowing for much larger rings can be used on the main chain. Increasing the ring size gradually is a way to mitigate the impact of increased transaction size and verification time, by taking advantage of improvements in bandwidth and processing power. With is in mind I have included an option in my fee and scaling recommendations for https://github.com/monero-project/research-lab/issues/70, should the community wish to increase the ring size along the above lines as an interim solution. Increasing the ring size together with overall trend in adoption will mitigate this issue over time. I must say that this issue was way more serious even a year ago than it is today. Furthermore it was orders of magnitude worse in 2016 etc. 

When one considers the trend in adoption together with the strong possibility of a significant increase in the ring size, even if my proposed interim mitigation is not accepted, I cannot support increasing the number of exposed coinbase outputs, from solo miners, private pools etc., that would result from separating coinbase and non coinbase rings.

Tor2Web is a proxy service that lets you browse Tor Hidden Services (.onion sites) without installing Tor. It was designed to facilitate anonymous publishing.

5:

Tor2Web only protects publishers, not readers. If you upload documents to us using Tor2Web, you are not anonymous and could be identified by your ISP or the Tor2Web proxy operators. source_templates/howto-disable-js.html 9:JavaScript exploit to de-anonymize Tor users. JavaScript exploits are also mentioned in documents describing the NSA's Egotistical Giraffe program, which also has the goal of targeting and de-anonymizing Tor users.

    • ``` We should consider the possibility that clicking any of these links makes it easier to deanonymize a source. In particular, I think of passive attacks such as website and circuit fingerprinting, especially combined with DNS observation. However, as not all are HTTPS, targeted MITM attacks against Tor clients who visit them is also a possible strategy, or targeted attacks against Tor clients who visit these particular pages in the case the site itself has been compromised (i.e., HTTPS in no guarantee of safety). Would it be better to just give our own brief description of why you should turn off JS? Does a source really need to read some article on Egotistical Giraffe before they submit a document? My opinion is yes, and that we should omit the the Tails website link as well. OTOH, the Tor2Web warning links make more sense because the user has already potentially compromised themselves, but we should at least cleanup the language there--"MITM'ed", "ISP", "capable adversary" are not exactly user-friendly terms, and we also shouldn't be claiming Tor2Web protects publishers. Search suggestions _should not_ appear because they are turned off in the settings.

### Actual behaviour

Search suggestions _do_ appear during step 4.

Google Pixel 3a

Android 12

Firefox

102.1.1

Issue discussion (chronological; participant names pseudonymized within the case):
Comment 1 (source ID 685070239) | Participant 1 | created 2020-09-01T18:59:26Z | updated 2020-09-01T18:59:26Z
Source: https://github.com/datenanfragen/website/issues/388#issuecomment-685070239
If we just try to follow these steps (go to the wizard, add some companies, click "Done" to be redirected to the generator, we are not able to reproduce the error. Luckily, the debug information is quite helpful in this case. It allows us to deduce two important facts:

* The error occurred in this line:

  https://github.com/datenanfragen/website/blob/d97ed79e7082db0cad9b2229f886c3e24d5638bf/src/Utility/RequestLetter.js#L122

  We can see that from the stack trace. The error occurred in `generator.gen.js`, line 29, column 41101. While not exactly pleasant, even the minified JS allows us to find out the actual position in the code. We are assigning to the `.signature.name` property of some object. In the line before, we are calling `formatData()` on some object. And in the line after, we are constructing an objects with properties like `erase_some` and `has_fields`. This only happens in `propsFromRequest()`.

  ![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/4048809/91893840-4410a080-ec84-11ea-8c7d-011f5d002d60.png)
* The user has custom privacy controls and has at least disabled "Save selected companies in the wizard". Otherwise, the wizard companies would not be passed via the URL but rather saved in localForage.

Now we need to do some experimenting. Even disabling "Save selected companies in the wizard" is not enough. It turns out, that actually disabling "Remember identification data" is necessary to reproduce the error.  
This does make sense, the signature is (usually) taken from the saved ID data. It seems like we forgot to handle the case where the saved ID data is disabled.

Comment 2 (source ID 685078840) | Participant 1 | created 2020-09-01T19:16:15Z | updated 2020-09-01T19:16:15Z
Source: https://github.com/datenanfragen/website/issues/388#issuecomment-685078840
Further, we can see that the generator doesn't work at all if "Remember identification data" is disabled, making this a pretty serious issue.

This highlights a problem with our current tests: We didn't think to test if things still work with modified privacy controls. Quite an oversight! I have opened #389 to change that.

Comment 3 (source ID 685078945) | Participant 1 | created 2020-09-01T19:16:27Z | updated 2020-09-01T19:16:27Z
Source: https://github.com/datenanfragen/website/issues/388#issuecomment-685078945
So, let's follow the money:

* `RequestLetter.propsFromRequest()` is only called in one place:

  https://github.com/datenanfragen/website/blob/d97ed79e7082db0cad9b2229f886c3e24d5638bf/src/Components/RequestGeneratorBuilder.js#L431

  This is in the `renderLetter()` function of the `RequestGeneratorBuilder` which is in fact called when we enter the generator, so we seem to be on the right track here.
* We are interested in the `request_object` parameter, which is the first argument. In this case, we are passing `this.state.request`.
* Since the error happens immediately after opening the generator, we can assume that the state will not have changed yet. So, what are we initializing the `this.state.request` to?

  https://github.com/datenanfragen/website/blob/d97ed79e7082db0cad9b2229f886c3e24d5638bf/src/Components/RequestGeneratorBuilder.js#L24

  A new `Request` object.
* This isn't the source of the issue, though, as the `signature` property is correctly initialized here:

  https://github.com/datenanfragen/website/blob/d97ed79e7082db0cad9b2229f886c3e24d5638bf/src/DataType/Request.js#L64
* Thus, we need to look for places where `this.state.request.signature` is modified without user interaction.
* The culprit is in the call to `this.resetInitialConditions()`, which happens soon after initializing the state.
* Here, we try to load the saved ID data and set the state accordingly:

  https://github.com/datenanfragen/website/blob/d97ed79e7082db0cad9b2229f886c3e24d5638bf/src/Components/RequestGeneratorBuilder.js#L81-L94
* And our initial suspicion is confirmed: We are indiscriminately setting `prev.request.signature = res.signature;` without checking whether there even is a `res.signature`. Luckily, that is very easy to fix.

Issue body:
**Originally posted by ByteCommander:**

It could be useful to know when an account has last been active in the server (e.g. events like sending messages, reactions, deleting messages, maybe changing nick) or even been visibly online in general. This could be integrated into the general user info command, or queried with a new bot command.

To avoid stalking/abuse potential, the reported time should probably be rounded to at least whole days, or for longer time spans even weeks for posting in public channels.

The data would have to be gathered by logging the time stamps (again, rounding this to e.g. full hours or maybe even full UTC days could be desirable) of user actions and status/visibility changes. Only the last value for both activity and visibility should be saved each, no history.

Additional things to do with this data include showing accumulated stats about how many people have been inactive/invisible for how long periods of time. Possibly it could even be used to notify and in a second step prune members that were inactive and never online for extended periods, like 6 months or a year (dead accounts).

Issue body:
We have websites that are hosted in Europe and we try our best to comply with GDPR laws.

With regards to storing cookie data, we are not allowed to store the cookie data `forever`.

The GDPR law states that `Data Retention` has to be set to a certain period and **not allowed to last forever**.

For example if you look at Google Analytics they changed their policy to **required** for users to select the data retention period. This period went up to a max period of 50 months for the old GA and the new GA4 is set to a max of 14 months.

Link: https://support.google.com/analytics/answer/7667196?hl=en

Storing data in a cache via a service worker I think would be under GDPR laws. We can easily store personal or tracking information via a service worker, intentionally or unintentionally.

Therefore the api found here: 
https://developers.google.com/web/tools/workbox/reference-docs/latest/module-workbox-expiration.ExpirationPlugin#ExpirationPlugin

Would probably fail under GDPR laws - because the data retention can be set to forever. 

Two options to fix this could be:

### 1. Change `maxAgeSeconds` to be required

#### Would fail GDPR

```js
workbox.routing.registerRoute(
    new RegExp("https://www.google-analytics.com/(.*)"),
    new workbox.strategies.CacheFirst({
        cacheName: "ga",
        plugins: [
            new workbox.expiration.ExpirationPlugin({
                maxEntries: 50,
            }),
            new workbox.cacheableResponse.CacheableResponsePlugin({
                statuses: [0, 200],
            }),
        ],
    })
);
```

#### Would pass GDPR

```js
workbox.routing.registerRoute(
    new RegExp("https://www.google-analytics.com/(.*)"),
    new workbox.strategies.CacheFirst({
        cacheName: "ga",
        plugins: [
            new workbox.expiration.ExpirationPlugin({
                maxEntries: 50,
                maxAgeSeconds: 30 * 24 * 60 * 60, // 30 Days
            }),
            new workbox.cacheableResponse.CacheableResponsePlugin({
                statuses: [0, 200],
            }),
        ],
    })
);
```

### 2. Add a max data retention to the `maxAgeSeconds` description and api

![Untitled](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/57409060/102131030-816ef780-3e49-11eb-9c17-2de85c2da566.png)

> The maximum age of an entry before it's treated as stale and removed. The maximum allowed data retention limit is set up to a 3 year period, to specify a shorter time scale use `maxAgeSeconds`.

Above description to be worded correctly by admins but gives a rough idea of what I'm suiggesting.

p.s. It would be even better to allow the website users to be able to set the `data retention` period for the service worker cache. This is what we do for all the other pieces of code running on our websites.

> Disclaimer: I'm not a lawyer, I'm just a developer. But the logic of what I'm saying here would make sense!

Issue body:
According to #750, this issue has been raised before, but was only partially addressed.

In its current version, Cura tells the user on first launch that Ultimaker is collecting anonymous slicing statistics and that this can be turned off in the settings.

While this is apparently better than before (where data would be collected without the user's consent), it may still be problematic for some people. If possible, there should be a link in the dialogue that allows disabling data collection immediately. The text doesn't even mention where said option is.

Personally, I would find it preferable to make this option opt-in instead of opt-out by changing the default to false and adapting the text accordingly.

From the feedback I received from fellow Debian maintainers, it seems like leaving this option as-is is not acceptable and will have to be changed for the Debian releases. We are currently discussing if the plugin should be removed altogether (which, I think, is unfair towards Ultimaker) or if we should just change the data collection default to `False`.

See above, closed that thread to continue the discussion all in one place.

I see this issue from three perspectives:

- **Moral:** Quite a few of us take this sort of issue very seriously and follow the politics closely. We do not, however, have a moral issue with the current practice as collecting IP addresses is a necessary part of how the Internet functions, and they are not saved. Also this is FOSS and anyone can make their own sandboxed version if they don't want to, say, use a VPN, or air-gap their machine, both of which are better privacy protections than relying on everyone else to protect it.
- **UX:** The "Disable" button should either be called what it does (e.g. "Modify in Preferences") or should do what its called (e.g. actually disable telemetry).
- **Legal:** As @Ghostkeeper says, this is now an impending issue to be handled. From a legal perspective, "it's a very complicated case, man. Lotta ins, lotta outs, man."

GDPR does appear to consider IP addresses personal information, which is a bit dumb, because as @nallath pointed out, the Internet doesn't really work without exchanging this information. Frankly GDPR puts virtually every website in existence right now out of compliance so in the back of my head this law already has "not really enforceable" written all over it. That being said, I think we should _try_ for the sake of liability.

Since IP addresses _do_ count as personal information and even if we do not store them, we do receive them, I don't think it's a very solid defense to say, "We super duper promise we destroyed the data immediately after receiving it," I do think this puts Cura (again, like literally everything ever) within the jurisdiction of GDPR.

_That_ means that the buttons need to do what they say. It's a very easy fix and we'll likely still have thousands and thousands of data points from all the cool people who are happy to help us improve the software, but, it should mean that we don't have to worry about GDPR compliance because it's explicitly opting in, and very clear what the buttons do.

It **is** a solid defence. Storing the data is not allowed, receiving it is. If we need information as a part of providing a service we are allowed to use and keep it without permission for as long as we need it to do the thing we need to do. 

What does that mean in this case (the "default" handling of a HTTP request)?
We get to store the IP for as long as it takes to send a request back (as this is an unavoidable requirement of HTTP).  Once the message is sent back, we lose this "right" as we no longer need to send a message, which puts us in violation if we keep it. So you are ever so slightly (but importantly) misunderstanding what GDPR is about. It's about _storing_ personal data. If we want to do it, we need permission. I'm obviously not up to date with the specifics regarding privacy laws in Norway, but I very much doubt that we are violating those. If we were, any and all websites or automatic update checks would be in violation. 

So as far as I'm concerned we are both morally and legally in the clear, which as far as I'm aware has been discussed with lawyers who know far more about this than me.

All that being said; The button does indeed not do what it needs to do, which should be changed. As far as legal goes; We don't need the permission in the first place. It's a **courtesy** to ask it in the first place. Morally speaking you want to explicitly mention that it's going on and provide instructions how to disable it if you don't want to. We do this already, but not as well as we can (and should therefore improve on it). Burning all old data is just silly and unnecessary.

To further argue the point. See the below definition what is defined as personal data. Note that personal data is **the only thing** that the GDPR protects. 

_"Defining “personal data” under GDPR
GDPR defines personal data broadly as “any information relating to an identified or identifiable natural person (‘data subject’); an identifiable natural person is one who can be identified, directly or indirectly, in particular by reference to an identifier such as a name, an identification number, location data, an online identifier or to one or more factors specific to the physical, physiological, genetic, mental, economic, cultural or social identity of that natural person.”
Under this definition, nearly ALL information about a EU resident is personal data–including, for example, names, ages, Social Security Numbers, email addresses, online identifiers and location data, IP addresses and mobile device IDs, cookies, and also more sensitive personal data such as genetic data and biometric data, including fingerprints, facial recognition and retinal scans."_

As the data we collect is not traceable to a natural person (and as long as we keep it that way) it's also not subject to GDPR. If we ever decide to become crooks and do make it tracable, we would be liable (and thus if it was ever found out, could be forced to pay tons and tons of money).

People are confusing "What data are we allowed to receive" with "What data are we allowed to store".

GDPR doesn't concern itself with the first. It concerns itself with storing data. So one could argue that we don't _need_ the request with the data to function (and therefore, don't need the IP). But that's a moot point. We don't keep the data. That's what this is about. That's also the spirit of the law imho; We don't know what person A made. We don't know how they did it. We just know that _someone_ did something. Thats why it's not _personal_ data but just _generic_ data. 

So yeah, the IP is personal data. _That's why we dont store it_. Storing it would require permission (and wouldn't make it anonymous anymore).

I get the impression that this discussion is going nowhere. Ultimately, it is up to Ultimaker to decide if and how they will comply with GDPR. The community can give input on how they think the user experience should be, but any legal questions should be answered by a legal counsel, or at least by those actually responsible (i.e. Ultimaker's management board). A public bug tracker is hardly the right place.

My expectations as a user of Cura are as such:

1. I want to be adequately informed that data is being collected
2. I want a description of what data is being collected, how, where and why
3. I want an easily accessible way of accepting data collection or denying it

Point 1. should already covered by the first-run message box.
Point 2. is a bit lacking - I don't see a link or other UI element that show this information.
Point 3. is there, but it's not presented in a very user-friendly manner.

My suggestion would be to improve this box; first by adding a link or button to the data collection policy (I assume it already exists somewhere). Secondly, there should be two buttons, one to enable SliceInfo and one to disable it. No data should be sent until this question is answered.
To make the option more palatable to users, the message should be formulated in an encouraging way, while also explaining clearly that no personally identifiable information is stored anywhere.

Something like:

> To improve Cura further, it is very important to us that we know how it is being used. For this reason, we are collecting fully anonymised slicing statistics on a server connected to the internet. The data we collect comprises a unique identifier calculated from the printed objects as well as the printing parameters. No personal information is stored at any point. Our full data collection policy can be found [here](link-to-data-collection-policy).
> Cura can be fully used without enabling these statistics, but we would be very happy if you would provide us with them. If you change your mind, you can always toggle the setting [here](link-to-settings-page).
> [ Accept ] [ Decline ]

We are going to add the "This is the data that is being collected". It was one of those things that was on the radar, but never quite got the attention that it deserves. This discussion has given it a lot higher priority.

As for the point that the data could, potentially, be used someday to identify a user. If this is ever the case, there is only one thing that Ultimaker can legally do with that information; Delete it. If we would not, we would be in violation of the GDPR.

Also note that "giving permission to access something" is not the same as giving permisison to "Send it somewhere and use it for datamining purposes". The GDPR is rather specific about it; For every type of use a specific agreement must be given by the user. So if you give the application permission to analyse a picture to say, detect if a camping tent is present, that is the only thing the company is allowed to do with it. If they were to add facial recognition (or use it on it) they would need separate permission for this.

In the interest of a quick implementation, I've cooked up a revision to the "Edit survey" view (which is also a proxy for the "Create survey" view) that helps us clean up that experience, and adds the ability to fine-tune the permissions around individual fields.

Some quick notes, though:

- This ignores "Tasks" for the moment.
- The "delete" button for surveys has moved to the "Surveys" listing, embedded in each survey's summary list item.
- All of this work is done using existing patterns in the PL.

Here's an average "Edit Survey" view:

![Edit Survey](https://cloud.githubusercontent.com/assets/1136279/22387424/39d2da96-e4a1-11e6-8823-1f10e1a8570e.png)

Some notable changes:

## Survey name and description
The survey's name and description take on a similar visual treatment to the actual survey form's display -- except they're editable:

![edit survey name](https://cloud.githubusercontent.com/assets/1136279/22387486/72fad008-e4a1-11e6-91e5-cb9c1fd065f6.png)

## Fields and settings
The survey's fields and settings have been grouped in a way that better lends itself to onboarding and new survey creation, by grouping them in tabs (e.g. Build, Configure, Share). By default (and first), you see "Build," which focuses entirely on building the data collection model.

"Configure" offers controls for visibility, permission, and color:

![configure](https://cloud.githubusercontent.com/assets/1136279/22387598/fd7cfb52-e4a1-11e6-9e79-04b8f061f447.png)

"Share" prompts you to share your survey's URL, grab the embed code, share on Facebook, etc:

![share](https://cloud.githubusercontent.com/assets/1136279/22387650/3c216f50-e4a2-11e6-86cc-f8416de8a3fb.png)

Now, to the matter of "private fields"...

## 'Who can see the response to this field'
In the "Build" tab, each field can be configured by selecting its name. And you can add a new field by selecting "Add field." In either case, you see a modal window with controls for each of its settings.

If I choose to "Add field," for example, I first select the field type (e.g. short text) and then I see:

![add field](https://cloud.githubusercontent.com/assets/1136279/22387759/d596e52a-e4a2-11e6-99c4-cb5010d54b2a.png)

The key new field here is "Who can see the response to this field," whose value is always "everyone" by default.

I can easily change this so that only "Editors" can see the response to this field:

![specific roles](https://cloud.githubusercontent.com/assets/1136279/22387848/3588527a-e4a3-11e6-8848-bcc2da59ae4f.png)

Now, when I save and close the window, that field will be appended to the list of fields with an indicator to the right of the field's label:

![list item](https://cloud.githubusercontent.com/assets/1136279/22387877/60a91d9a-e4a3-11e6-9078-c854881188b4.png)

It doubles as a tooltip, with more detail on hover:

![tooltip](https://cloud.githubusercontent.com/assets/1136279/22387901/756acf26-e4a3-11e6-93e5-59c35e295bcf.png)

Similarly, when I view a detail view for any response to this survey (assuming I have permission to see it), this field's label will have the same indicator/tooltip:

![detail view](https://cloud.githubusercontent.com/assets/1136279/22387962/bbf58242-e4a3-11e6-85b9-b0c6213bec5c.png)

------

All of this is demonstrated in [a feature-specific branch](https://github.com/ushahidi/platform-pattern-library/tree/f-fields_and_sections) in the Pattern Library, largely in [the "Edit survey" layout](http://preview.ushahidi.com/platform-pattern-library/f-fields_and_sections/assets/html/5_layouts/settings-survey-edit.html).

I'd really appreciate your feedback on this reasonably quick solution, @caharding and @jshorland.

Great catch, @willdoran and @rjmackay. And I think it calls for a revision to this direction that'll help simplify things.

In short, instead of asking deployers to choose a role that can "see responses to this field," let's do what we do with post status: Make it something you can lock (or unlock).

So when editing a field that you intend to make "private," you'll see a switch to "Make responses private":

![edit field](https://cloud.githubusercontent.com/assets/1136279/23970620/658cd99a-0998-11e7-87ca-6b94a8a0fc9b.png)

By turning this option "on," you see some help text:

![field locked](https://cloud.githubusercontent.com/assets/1136279/23970633/77928ffe-0998-11e7-8b4a-96a2c3794f52.png)

And when a survey response was submitted, only users with permission to edit that response would see the following in the response's detail view:

![detail view](https://cloud.githubusercontent.com/assets/1136279/23970889/9bfa556a-0999-11e7-8803-77fbb71887b2.png)

Otherwise, the user simply wouldn't see the field at all. The same logic would apply to the response's "edit" view.

So let's be clear. When a field's responses are marked private:

- A new, empty survey would display that field to the author, using the same survey-level permissions that already exist to restrict who can submit to the survey to begin with.
- Once a survey response with the field is submitted, its "edit" and "detail" views will only reveal the field to users with permission to edit it.

As I understand it, this would greatly simplify the cascade of permissions. True, @willdoran?

Try that on desktop and Fennec and you'll see that it's not normal behaviour.

Just because I forget to close a private browsing tab, doesn't mean that private browsing should hijack my browser experience. 

Maybe Fenix is evolving the private browsing experience, to provide more permanence, however that's not expected behaviour and as such, it's probably worth explaining that. But in doing so, what are the impacts to other aspects, do custom tabs act the same? 

With such an implementation though, of essentially making private browsing an isolated tab group/container, how is it possible that you all dropped the ball and collections glorified bookmarks when they too could've been a tab group/container?


Comment 3 (source ID 496133907) | Participant 2 | created 2019-05-27T08:48:21Z | updated 2019-05-27T08:50:00Z
Source: https://github.com/mozilla-mobile/fenix/issues/2867#issuecomment-496133907
> Try that on desktop and Fennec and you'll see that it's not normal behaviour.

There is no "normal" behaviour, you can argue for both behaviours. It's a decision made by the developers to use either the one or the other mode. And yes, there may be different opinions. But in my opinion the current behaviour of Fenix makes a lot of sense and I don't want the current behaviour changed.

Fenix has another UX than Firefox for Desktop or Fennec. The mask icon on the Fenix home screen acts as a kind of "permanent browsing mode toggle", Fenix remembers the choice. If I press the mask icon it's my explicit decision to use the private mode, also the next time when I start Fenix. Just try it without using an external app: Start Fenix, switch to private mode, exit Fenix via Android recent apps, start Fenix again. As you can see you're still in private mode. That's intended behaviour. So there is no reason why Fenix should behave differently when clicking a link in an external app.

And to be honest, being accidentally in the private mode is far less a problem than the other way around.

Funnily in #2868 you argued for privacy by default a few minutes ago but here you don't want the more private approach.

> 
> There is no "normal" behaviour, you can argue for both behaviours. It's a decision made by the developers to use either the one or the other mode. And yes, there may be different opinions. But in my opinion the current behaviour of Fenix makes a lot of sense and I don't want the current behaviour changed.

I disagree. Normal is legacy behaviour. To have browser traditionally act one way and then suddenly change that and is abnormal behaviour. It's confusing and bewildering.

> Fenix has another UX than Firefox for Desktop or Fennec. The mask icon on the Fenix home screen acts as a kind of "permanent browsing mode toggle", Fenix remembers the choice. If I press the mask icon it's my explicit decision to use the private mode, also the next time when I start Fenix. Just try it without using an external app: Start Fenix, switch to private mode, exit Fenix via Android recent apps, start Fenix again. As you can see you're still in private mode. That's intended behaviour. So there is no reason why Fenix should behave differently when clicking a link in an external app.
> 
> And to be honest, being accidentally in the private mode is far less a problem than the other way around.

I can totally see the benefits for such an approach, they don't fit how I use a browser's private mode, but then I've had years to learn my current behaviour model of wanting to open something privately and expecting my browser to treat everything else as normal browsing behaviour. I'm really not arguing against the change in browser behaviour, I just hope that users can be notified that there has been a change in behaviour and that desktop and mobile act the same. I would also, and this is the most important part, expect the UI to suggest that my actions entail a permanent change in state and thus I would like to advocate for switching out the button for a toggle.


> Funnily in #2868 you argued for privacy by default a few minutes ago but here you don't want the more private approach.

I advocated for an option, but you're ultimately right. That said, I continue to want users to be informed and in control. Also, once again I'd like to advocate for switching from a button to a toggle seeing that private browsing is a sticky mode now, I feel that the change should definitely be represented with a switch/toggle and not a button. That should allay some of the confusion that users are likely to feel.

According to [WCA's Privacy Statement](https://www.worldcubeassociation.org/privacy) a WCA member has a right to be forgotten. Call is accepted and proceed in both directions.

Comment 21 (source ID 211380015) | Participant 2 | created 2016-04-18T13:31:50Z | updated 2016-04-18T13:31:50Z
Source: https://github.com/signalapp/Signal-Android/issues/5421#issuecomment-211380015
OK, I can actually reproduce this behaviour if I make changes to the code, which to me indicates that there is a bug in your ROM of PH2. So I think the problem is this (for whatever reason):
1. The incoming call screen is displayed on PH2: `ResponderCallManager` is `wait()`ing in `synchronized waitForAnswer()`
2. You accept the incoming call: `RedPhoneService` calls `synchronized ResponderCallManager.answer(true)` through `onIntentReceived`, **but never returns**
3. `ResponderCallManager.waitForAnswer()` also never returns, so the call will not be initiated
4. As a result, after a while PH1 will automatically (or manually) end the call attempt
5. `SignalListenerTask` on PH2 will notice this and call `RedPhoneService.notifyCallDisconnected()`, which will hide the call screen, **but** it cannot call `synchronized RedPhoneService.terminate()` because it is still stuck in `synchronized onIntentReceived` since step 2

[Here](https://github.com/WhisperSystems/Signal-Android/blob/master/src/org/thoughtcrime/redphone/call/ResponderCallManager.java#L120) is the implementation that I assume is failing.

One could try to work around this by using `Lock` (and `Condition`) objects in the `ResponderCallManager` and just see if that works @moxie0 ?

Also, there is no `stopService()` anywhere.

#### Bug description

When I send a video on which I trimmed out the beginning, the resulting message on the sender's phone displays a thumbnail/poster that is based on the trimmed out part of the video.

#### Steps to reproduce
- Make sure you have a video more than 10 seconds long on your device.
- Open Signal.
- Open a recipient's conversation.
- Tap the `+` icon and select the video. The video preview opens.
- Use the slider at the top of the screen to trim out the first 10 seconds of the video.
- Send the video.

**Actual result:** On the sender's phone, the video thumbnail is a image taken from the first 10 seconds of the video. As a user, I am afraid that the recipient is seeing an image from the video I didn't want him/her to see. In reality though, the recipient sees a different thumbnail, one that actually matches the part of the video that was sent, so there is no "breach of privacy", but the UI is misleading.

**Expected result:** On the sender's phone, the video thumbnail should be an image taken from whatever part of the video that was actually sent to the recipient. Ideally, the sender and the recipient should just see the same thumbnail.

#### Device info

**Device:** OnePlus 5

**Android version:** Android 11 with LineageOS

**Signal version:** 5.22.8

Integrate IP anonymization into Google Analytics due to the May 2018 General Data Protection Regulation for the European Union.

https://support.google.com/analytics/answer/2763052?hl=en&ref_topic=2919631

In Google Tag Manager, I have added the Google Analytics `anonymizeIp : true` property.  I verified that the IP anonymization property is enabled by looking for `aip=1` in the google analytics traffic on openliberty.io.

Example of verification:
1.  Open new tab in Chrome
2.  Enable Chrome debug tools
3.  In tools, open the Network tab
4.  Go to openliberty.io
5.  Filter the network data with the word `analytics`
6.  Observe that the `collect` request has the `aip=1`, meaning IP addresses are anonymized.

> The IP anonymization parameter looks like this: &aip=1
> src: https://support.google.com/analytics/answer/2763052?hl=en&ref_topic=2919631

Issue body:
Hey there,

why do we want to support companies like google getting more user data?
We expect - or at least hope - that a lot of projects participate in the digital climate strike.

We

* piss off admins who see the google analytics by default
* give the data of users of websites, who previously didn't have google analytics, to google

and for what?...

Source: https://github.com/fightforthefuture/digital-climate-strike/issues/76#issuecomment-530223147

Comment 2 (source ID 530504793) | Participant 3 | created 2019-09-11T18:23:45Z | updated 2019-09-11T18:29:39Z
Source: https://github.com/fightforthefuture/digital-climate-strike/issues/76#issuecomment-530504793
Hey @NerdyProjects and @miloskroulik,

First up, thanks for this feedback. I'm aligned with you on not wanting to send user data to Google on websites that previously did not have Google Analytics. We thought about this default when we implemented this feature and settled where we did for a number of reasons. I'll try to outline them as best I can, along with what I recommend instead of changing the default:

- As you’re probably aware, this javascript widget is part of a much broader campaign to drive turnout on September 20th and raise massive, widespread public awareness about the Global Climate Strike. A critical data point for generating media coverage, promoting the strikes, and for using to convince large website targets is the total number of websites that have added the widget. For example, we can now say publicly that over 900 sites have added the banner. Without GA being on by default, we would be unaware of the vast majority of sites and lose this critical tactic from our campaign toolbelt. 
- Ancillary to this, GA has enabled us to follow up some of the large sites and ask them a) to post about it on social media, and b) join the participants list of the website (https://digital.globalclimatestrike.net/#participants). Not only have the websites we’ve spoken been delighted by this, but added more logos on the website provides legitimacy to the campaign and our outreach has been strengthened. Without GA we would be unlikely to have this feedback loop and opportunity. 
- Providing the option to disable balances these benefits with the real issue you mention about Google Analytics being added (intentionally, or unintentionally) to a website that doesn’t want it. 
- We have not and will not turn on any Google Advertising features that GA support (e.g Demographics and Interest reporting) and no Personally Identifiable Information (PII) is ever sent to Google. 

So, instead of flipping the default on this, I think we should update the README to be super clear (with some bolding, for example) that the widget adds Google analytics by default, but it can be disabled in the options. We could even include the specific additional script tag they will need so folks can just copy and paste it.

How does that sound? I totally hear y’all on the downside with this - but am also hoping this provides a bit more transparency / thinking into why it’s on by default.

I'd then either suggest running something self-hosted like Matomo or doing something simple as pinging the main server with a transparent POST request everytime the banner is shown.

Google Analytics is not needed for this and having it enabled by default is not compliant with the EU's GDPR. The last thing you want is bringing webmasters trying to raise awareness into legal trouble.

@krmax44 I hear you and agree it would be good to have this tracking self-hosted with Matamo. I created a Matomo account and an issue to migrate over to it (#77). Setting up a server (we don't currently have any running) would unlikely deliver on the acceptance criteria in the issue (or at least be a lot more difficult). 

But I also want to provide additional transparency as to why I am not confident we should complete the ticket before Sept 20th:

- We only have 8 days until the Global Climate Strike. The No.1 priority for this campaign is outreach to large websites, the No.2 priority is media/press and the No.3 priority is social media awareness. Our volunteer team is spread extremely thin and we just lost our developer who was leading on a lot of the tech. I can try to find some time to work on the ticket, but I'm not sure if I'll be able to. But that's why this is open source - so maybe someone can jump in! 
- Migrating to Matomo will break technical and human dependancies which will slow our team down. For example we would need to re-train volunteers to use Matomo and set up a new process to compare the event data with other data sources like we are now and has taken us numerous days to set up (E.g. form submissions here: https://digital.globalclimatestrike.net/#join-digital-strike)
- We now have almost 2,000 websites who have added the widget - some of which have gone with a self-hosted solution and should be notified of these changes. Because of this and how close we are to the strikes, we want to keep changes to the widget code as minimal as possible and any change should be very carefully implemented and very extensively tested. We would want to test in all available languages / x-browser / operating system combinations. In general I'd be nervous about making this sort of change so late in the campaign. 

So while the code changes might not be too complex, there will need to be quite a lot of non-code related work before we could consider it done, and we're spread super thin with widget updates being very low priority for our team. I hope that context is helpful in terms of my thinking around this. I really do want to support this community and campaign with the best possible approach that works for the most people - and most importantly, whatever makes the biggest impact (turnout, awareness) for the strikes.  Thanks :)

Issue body:
What happened so far:

1. We added a safeguard to not upload profiles with network resources URLs as they might contain PII

What's still there:

1. PII is still spread across profiles as URLs are included in markers and source file.

What's success:

1. Technical and non-technical users can upload profiles while knowing which aspects of their browsing session are shared (and which are not).
2. Engineers get enough information from anonymized profiles to make sense (single profile or in aggregate)

What is PII:
> "Personally Identifiable Information (PII), as used in information security, is information that can be used to uniquely identify, contact, or locate a single person or can be used with other sources to uniquely identify a single individual." 

- Any file and URL is PII
  - Long tail domains can contain PII, like subdomains (genderqueeries.tumblr.com, rickroll.smugmug.com).
- For the domain, a whitelist of top sites could be considered OK, as it doesn't tell anything about the user
- PII needs to be removed from any marker until we have refactored the system and removed all URLs

My past approach for a sanitation step that removes all URLs while keeping top site domains intact: https://github.com/digitarald/performance-foxfooding-ext/blob/master/src/purge.js

The thing with GPDR is that it requires an easy way for users to delete the data. So just a notice and confirmation like cookie law wont seem to cut it. Or 'you agreed to our terms of service' methodology. 

To chime in the general discussion before this point and some of the approaches voiced : GDPR shouldnt be treated like VAT - VAT was, and is something that pertains to local tax authorities and their action: For there to be consequences, a local (national) tax authority must think that some site is not paying the taxes due to their government, and then act on it. There first needs to be probable cause for this to happen - just like any citizen in any country being investigated for suspected tax evasion. So the authority must be informed of valid purchases by their own residents, then must conclude that the tax for those valid purchases were not paid that quarter, then initiate the procedure for following up and so on. And the consequences would be according to how that country would handle that VAT avoidance - owed VAT plus a measure of interest and fines applied on top, which would be totally pointless to pursue for small amounts.

But GPDR is different - users not being able to delete data is something obvious and it doesnt require reqporting to an authority, or the authority trying to confirm non compliance through long legal procedures and follow up with another series of long legal procedures. An official tasked with investigating such issues can just register and confirm that s/he has no way to delete the data. 

And the fine for non compliance is quite serious - nothing like what could potentially result from VAT avoidance.

For that, both WP and EDD and any major plugin must have their own way of handling GPDR by default, at least for the default features. Plugins may extend these, but such compliance must not be left to plugins alone.

@Spreeuw - To be fair, the plugin you mentioned is a commercial one, the one that was the origination of the concepts being added to WP Core was free and worked on standardizing things.
That plugin is effectively dead now as those are merged into core.

I personally don't like the idea of a commercial option here like the one you linked. The reason being they get to decide what plugins & things they will support, what order, and when etc.

By putting the guts into the core, you will get to 100% coverage on your site much quicker. IE each plugin will do what EDD & Popup Maker and others have done and quickly extend the core functions with their own data.

This means that within days or weeks you can have thousands of plugins supporting GDPR rather than a handful that the team of that one plugin can get put together on their own.

That said I recently had a small quarrel with an EU user who blamed WP core for the sluggishness of developing these features. The facts though are that nobody from EU contributed early on with exception to those who developed commercial solutions. Only when non-EU devs took up the mission did core progress get made. To clarify only 1 issue about GDPR was submitted prior to Feb 28 2018, and 80% of those submitted since are from a Canadian and an American.
